A brief drive around New York last year was enough to show that the Lucid Gravity had plenty of promise. However, ten days and 1,100 miles across the American West gave it nowhere to hide. I drove the Grand Touring around Los Angeles then to Las Vegas for a few days, on to Palm Springs and then down to San Diego, carrying three adults and a substantial amount of luggage through city traffic, fast highways and desert temperatures that reached 115 degrees Fahrenheit, or around 46C.

The result was a much more revealing test than a conventional launch route. The Gravity was fantastic. It drove brilliantly, remained comfortable over long days and delivered the space, refinement and luxury touches that impressed my passengers as much as they impressed me. The air conditioning had some serious work to do and did it without fuss, while the car itself did not miss a beat in some fairly extreme circumstances.

Some Lucid customers have reported quality problems, but there was no sign of them in my car. Nothing failed, no warning lights appeared and none of the technology threw a tantrum across the whole trip. One fault-free example cannot speak for every Gravity, but this one dealt with heat, mileage, people and luggage exactly as it should.

It also attracted plenty of attention. Hotel valet teams repeatedly made positive comments about it, which felt significant given that they spend their working lives getting into and out of more cars than even I do. The reaction was understandable. The Gravity offers the space of a large seven-seat SUV without looking like a bloated SUV. At 5,035mm long it is a big car, yet its low, sleek shape and clean surfaces disguise much of that bulk. It is a great-looking car with genuine presence, but it does not shout about it.

There is an interesting British connection, too. Lucid was set up and originally run by British former Tesla engineer Peter Rawlinson. His focus on powertrain efficiency shaped the Lucid Air, the company’s first model and the 2023 World Luxury Car winner – and it is central to the Gravity too. Lucid has also agreed to supply electric technology to Aston Martin for the British company’s future EVs.

The Gravity has now followed the Air by winning a World Car Awards title. I joined 95 other international jurors in voting it the 2026 World Luxury Car. Living with it for 1,100 miles has only enhanced my view that Lucid is doing something different and special. To almost borrow the phrase from an old American sitcom, I love Lucid.

How we tested

I spent ten days driving a Lucid Gravity Grand Touring 1,100 miles from Los Angeles to Las Vegas, Palm Springs and San Diego with three adults and plenty of luggage on board. In that time I could assess what Lucid ownership would be like from the sound system to the folding rear seats.

Lucid Gravity: From $94,900 Lucidmotors.com

open image in gallery The Lucid Gravity's crossover styling hides a huge amount of passenger and luggage space inside ( Steve Fowler )

Independent rating: 9/10

Pros: Exceptional space and comfort, impressive efficiency, seamless technology, superb performance, easy to manoeuvre, great roof

Exceptional space and comfort, impressive efficiency, seamless technology, superb performance, easy to manoeuvre, great roof Cons: Not available in the UK, inconsistent wireless phone charging, DreamDrive availability varies by freeway, tailgate edges need care

Lucid Gravity specs

Price range: $94,900 (£70,800)

$94,900 (£70,800) Battery size: 123kWh

123kWh Maximum claimed range: 450 miles

450 miles Miles per kWh: More than 3 miles/kWh on test

More than 3 miles/kWh on test Maximum charging rate: 400kW

Battery, range, charging, performance and drive

The Gravity Grand Touring uses a 123kWh battery and a 926-volt electrical platform, with two motors, all-wheel drive and 828bhp. Lucid claims a maximum EPA range of 450 miles for a five-seat car on the smallest 20-inch front and 21-inch rear wheels. A seven-seat model on those wheels is rated at 437 miles, while larger wheel combinations reduce the official figure further. The important point is that the headline range varies with the seating and wheel specification. I managed well over 320 miles in extreme conditions.

open image in gallery The big Lucid Gravity Grand Touring feels smaller than it is to drive. The big glass roof is a joy ( Steve Fowler )

Over my trip the Gravity returned more than 3 miles/kWh. That was seriously impressive for a car of this size carrying three adults and plenty of luggage, particularly as much of the route was covered at speeds broadly comparable with UK motorway driving. The figure was not achieved by crawling around or treating the accelerator as if it were made of glass. It came from using the Gravity as a large, luxurious road-trip car.

Charging performance is equally strong on paper. The Grand Touring can accept up to 400kW from a compatible 1000-volt charger, and Lucid says as much as 200 miles can be added in under 11 minutes in the right conditions – the fastest speed I managed on a Electrify America charger was 340kW, which is still impressively fast.

The Gravity’s boost-charging technology also allows up to 225kW on lower-voltage 500-volt chargers, including compatible Tesla V3 Superchargers. Actual speed will depend on the charger, battery temperature and state of charge, but this hardware gives the Gravity an unusually broad rapid-charging capability.

Performance is startling for a seven-seat SUV. The official 0–60mph time is 3.4 seconds, and the Gravity feels every bit as quick as that suggests. The response is immediate, yet the accelerator is easy to modulate, so there is no need to make passengers regret accepting a lift. One-pedal driving is intuitive and makes town running smoother.

The greater achievement is the way the Gravity combines that speed with comfort and control. Its air suspension dealt well with poor surfaces in New York during my earlier drive and remained first rate across the longer test. It rides with the calm expected of a luxury car, without allowing the body to feel loose or cumbersome. The steering has useful weight and response, while the available active rear steering gives the big SUV a decently tight turning circle and makes it far easier to manoeuvre than its dimensions suggest.

open image in gallery The Lucid Gravity is a long car, but four-wheel steering helps to make it feel more manoeuvrable than expected ( Steve Fowler )

That agility helps the Gravity avoid feeling like rival big SUVs. It is easy to place, stable at highway speeds and capable of covering long distances without tiring its occupants. The air conditioning coped with desert heat, the cabin stayed quiet and the overall sense was of a car developed as a complete package, rather than a huge battery and a lot of power wrapped in an SUV body.

Interior, practicality and boot space

Space is one of the Gravity’s defining qualities. It can be configured with five or seven seats, and the three-row car gives adults useful room in every row. The flat floor helps, particularly in the second row, where the powered seats slide to balance legroom between passengers. Access to the third row is made easier by long, wide-opening rear doors and middle-row seats that move forward at the touch of a lever. Other back row seats fold more easily into the floor, though.

open image in gallery The Lucid Gravity feels luxurious and spacious in the back – and there's room for a total of seven passengers ( Lucid )

My passengers were consistently impressed by the room, comfort and luxury touches. The middle row can feel limousine-like when pushed back, while fold-out tables on the front seatbacks provide a proper surface for a laptop rather than forcing somebody to balance one on their knees. The third row has usable headroom and legroom, so it is more than a pair of occasional seats reserved for children.

The glass roof is one of my favourite parts of the car. It blends into a windscreen that stretches back over the front occupants, creating a wide, uninterrupted view and making an already spacious cabin feel even airier. It gave a spectacular view of the New York skyline on my first drive. In 115-degree Fahrenheit desert heat, however, we made very good use of the pop-in sunshades. The view is wonderful, but reducing the solar load was sensible when the temperature climbed.

open image in gallery The Lucid Gravity's frunk can double up as a padded bench for a bit of sightseeing ( Steve Fowler )

Material quality and design support the sense of luxury. Lucid offers sustainable wood and vegan leather, and the latter looks and feels much like the real thing. The cabin is tasteful rather than showy, the seats remained comfortable over long days and the build quality of the test car stayed solid throughout. The squared-off steering wheel sits low enough to leave a clear view of the display and is really good to use. There are also conventional stalks for the indicators, wipers and gear selection – a welcome point of difference from recent Teslas.

Luggage space is substantial. Lucid quotes 594 litres with all seven seats in use and 3,143 litres of total carrying capacity when the five rear seats are folded flat. What that meant in practice is that four super-sized suitcases, plus associated small bags all fitted in the boot with room to spare.

There is also a large storage area under the bonnet, with an added party trick. Its floor can be turned into a padded perch, making the frunk somewhere to sit as well as somewhere to store charging cables or bags. We did it to enjoy the view from the Griffith Observatory overlooking LA.

open image in gallery In five-seat mode, there's room for four large suitcases and a whole lot more in the back of the Lucid Gravity ( Steve Fowler )

There is one practical warning around the rear. The powered boot lid has pointed lips at either side, and a taller person approaching the luggage space from the side could bring their head uncomfortably close to one. I had a couple of near misses during the trip. It’s a minor inconvenience rather than a verdict-changing flaw, but owners will quickly learn to approach the open boot with a little care.

Technology, stereo and infotainment

The Gravity’s technology is extensive, but the most impressive part is how naturally it fits into the car. It feels a little like a Tesla, but designed with the benefit of hindsight: software-led and modern, yet with lessons learned about the value of familiar controls and straightforward operation. Across ten days, the technology rarely demanded attention for its own sake.

open image in gallery The Lucid Gravity's tech suite was easy to use and felt high quality ( Steve Fowler )

The main display is a curved 34-inch 6K OLED screen that appears to float above the dashboard and combines the driver’s instruments with touchscreen functions. A second touchscreen sits lower down, just above the centre console, with quick access to ventilation settings. That arrangement keeps regular controls within easier reach and helps the large upper screen remain useful rather than overwhelming.

An augmented-reality head-up display projects information into the driver’s line of sight, including navigation guidance. Wireless Apple CarPlay is included, while the car’s own Lucid UX software can be updated over the air. The controls responded cleanly during the trip and the overall integration was seamless.

The exception was the wireless phone-charging pad. It did not seem to get on with my iPhone and would not always charge it. That was irritating on long days when navigation, music and photography all placed demands on the phone, although it remained a small issue in an otherwise convincing cabin.

Lucid calls its driver-assistance package DreamDrive. It uses radar, lidar and cameras, shows surrounding traffic and other road users on the display, keeps the car in lane and can change lanes to overtake when it decides that’s needed. In the right conditions it worked well and took some of the strain out of long freeway sections. Full hands-free ‘dream driving’ only appeared to be available on some freeways, though, rather than every road where it might have been useful.

open image in gallery Tech highlights in the Lucid Gravity include a 34-inch curved OLED screen with a second screen below and handy fast keys, plus a Dolby Atmos-equipped 22-speaker audio system ( Steve Fowler )

The in-house Surreal Sound Pro system was another highlight. It uses 22 speakers and supports Dolby Atmos, giving music a convincing sense of height and space. Listening through Tidal, the clarity and scale were first rate and the system became an important part of the road trip rather than a specification-sheet extra. The same was true of the climate control: in extreme heat it worked hard, quietly and effectively.

Prices and running costs

The 2026 Lucid Gravity Grand Touring tested was priced from $94,900 in the US, excluding taxes, registration, options and destination charges. The Touring version was announced at $79,900, bringing a lower entry price with a smaller battery and reduced performance. There is still no UK price because Lucid does not sell right-hand-drive cars and has no plans to offer the super-sized Gravity over here.

open image in gallery The Lucid Gravity will fast charge at up to 400kW – and we saw an impressive 360kW speed on our journey ( Steve Fowler )

Lucid has previously said it is interested in right-hand-drive production but has other priorities. That leaves British buyers watching from the sidelines and waiting for smaller Lucids to arrive, even though the Gravity’s mix of space, comfort, performance and efficiency would place it naturally among premium electric SUVs sold here. European left-hand-drive sales have begun, but that does not change the position for the UK.

The Grand Touring’s 450-mile maximum EPA range applies to the most efficient five-seat configuration, so buyers need to check the rating attached to their chosen seating layout and wheels. Even so, achieving more than 3 miles/kWh during a 1,100-mile trip with three adults and luggage suggests that its efficiency is not confined to a laboratory figure.

Lucid provides an eight-year or 100,000-mile battery warranty, with the battery expected to retain at least 70 per cent of its original capacity during that period. The test car’s fault-free performance across a demanding ten days was reassuring, although reported quality concerns from some owners remain relevant when assessing a young manufacturer.

Value is difficult to translate directly into pounds without a UK car or official UK pricing. In America, however, the combination of seven-seat space, 828bhp performance, long range, rapid charging and a high-quality cabin gives the Gravity a broad set of abilities for its price. My extended drive strengthened the impression formed by World Car Awards jurors: this is a luxury EV doing things differently.

The verdict: Lucid Gravity

The Lucid Gravity is a very different and very special luxury, seven-seat, all-electric SUV. It’s fast, efficient, quick-charging, super-spacious, comfortable and beautifully resolved. My 1,100-mile road trip only strengthened the case for 2026’s World Luxury Car of the Year.

open image in gallery The Lucid Gravity is big, but it still managed to fit inside the garage to keep call in 115 degree heat in Palm Springs ( Steve Fowler )

Lucid Gravity rivals

FAQs

How long does it take to charge?

Lucid says the Gravity Grand Touring can add as much as 200 miles in under 11 minutes when connected to a compatible charger capable of delivering more than 400kW. Peak charging is up to 400kW on suitable 1000-volt equipment and up to 225kW on compatible 500-volt chargers. We saw speeds up too 360kW, which in searing heat was seriously impressive

How much does it cost - is it worth it?

The 2026 Gravity Grand Touring tested was priced from $94,900 in the US, with the Touring announced at $79,900. There is no UK price because Lucid does not currently offer a right-hand-drive Gravity

Does Lucid replace batteries for free?

oes Lucid replace batteries for free? Lucid’s battery warranty lasts for eight years or 100,000 miles. It covers defects and guarantees that the battery will retain at least 70 per cent of its original capacity during that period, subject to the warranty terms.

Why trust us

Our team of motoring experts have decades of experience driving, reviewing and reporting on the latest EV cars, and our verdicts are reached with every kind of driver in mind. We thoroughly test drive every car we recommend, so you can be sure our verdicts are honest, unbiased and authentic.

Could poop be the answer to potentially life-threatening peanut allergies - or allergies to other foods?

Fecal transplants - dubbed “poop pills” - from people without food allergies have proven to help people with peanut allergies tolerate the nuts months later, a small but groundbreaking new clinical trial of 15 adults shows.

“This landmark study was the first to demonstrate that a microbiome-based therapy may improve food allergy in people while also revealing how gut bacteria, their metabolites and the immune system work together to influence treatment response,” Dr. Rima Rachid, director of the Food Allergy Program and the Allergen Immunotherapy Program at Boston Children's Hospital, said in a statement.

The findings could help the 33 million Americans who have at least one food allergy, as well as the nearly five million Americans who suffer from peanut allergies.

Peanut, nut, milk and egg allergies are some of the most hazardous food allergies, according to the American Academy of Allergy Asthma and Immunology.

open image in gallery Millions of Americans suffer from allergies to peanuts and other foods. But researchers say a new transplant using ‘poop pills’ shows promise for future treatment ( Getty Images )

Peanuts allergies are also one of the most common allergies among children, although recent research has shown allergy cases have declined among kids following recommendations to feed kids peanuts earlier.

Exposure to peanuts for just a few minutes can cause hives, vomiting, dangerously low blood pressure and airway swelling that makes it hard to breathe, the Cleveland Clinic notes. While rare, these reactions can be fatal in people without access to treatment: shots of the hormone epinephrine that reverse symptoms, often known as EpiPens.

An average of four peanut allergy deaths occur in the U.S. each year, the non-profit Institute of Clinical and Economic Review says.

All food allergies cause an average of up to 200 deaths nationwide, per researchers at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and state health departments.

That requires Americans to be on guard when they leave their homes - and one EpiPen dose isn’t always enough, the academy says.

“People with food allergies want freedom from constant anxiety and extreme vigilance and to not have be on guard for potentially dangerous exposures every time they leave the house,” said Rachid.

That’s why more testing is necessary, she said.

open image in gallery EpiPens are the main treatment for people with life-threatening food allergies. But carrying just one dose may not be enough ( AFP via Getty Images )

In this study, Rachid and her team used 36 frozen “poop pills” taken orally to transfer good bacteria to their gut and results showed people who took antibiotics before these transplants saw more success.

They also found that people who responded to treatments - most of whom were men - had increased levels of bile salts: salts that are made in the liver and help us break down fats.

Metabolizing these salts was linked to increased levels of immune system-regulating cells that protect us from allergic reactions.

The researchers also transplanted gut bacteria from participants’ stool samples into mice, finding that the bacteria from people who responded to treatment also protected mice from developing allergies to an egg protein.

Because the mouse studies tested a different allergen, the transplant is likely to work for more than just peanut allergies, study co-author Talal Chatila, an immunologist at Harvard Medical School, told Nature.

Rachid is now leading a new study in teens that will test transplants, including a purified form of microbes that can be stored in a home fridge.

But it’s still a long time before this method will be widely used, Alexander Khoruts, a gastroenterologist at the University of Minnesota who is collaborating with Rachid, told Nature.

Even with sufficient fundraising, “it would take about ten years” for the bacteria to be approved by regulators, he said.

Simon Cowell is facing a High Court challenge over a multimillion-dollar agreement “written on a napkin”, court documents reveal.

Ian Rosenblatt, who previously served as Mr Cowell's business adviser, has initiated the proceedings.

His representative, Katherine Ratcliffe, stated in the filings that Mr Rosenblatt is seeking an agreed percentage from a confidential deal made in 2025.

Alternatively, he is claiming £100,000 in damages for an alleged breach of contract.

Mr Cowell has not yet submitted a defence to the claim.

Mr Rosenblatt, himself a lawyer, began working for Mr Cowell in 2018, Ms Ratcliffe said.

He helped with the transfer of shares in Mr Cowell’s company SyCo Entertainment, from Sir Philip Green and Sony to the former X Factor judge, leaving Mr Cowell with a 100% stake from July 2020.

Mr Rosenblatt was then appointed director of SyCo, but in late 2022 he wanted to quit.

open image in gallery Simon Cowell has not yet submitted a defence to the claim ( Tim Markland/PA )

Ms Ratcliffe said: “By September 2022 Mr Rosenblatt intended to formally resign as director of Syco, and cease providing business advisory services to Mr Cowell, because of how challenging he had found working with Mr Cowell.”

She said it was “difficult to communicate” with Mr Cowell, who was “unpredictable” and “extremely emotional”.

A month later, over dinner at Mr Cowell’s London home, the two men made an oral agreement about Mr Rosenblatt taking a percentage of a deal, Ms Ratcliffe said.

She added: “The terms of that offer were written on a napkin which Mr Cowell then signed.”

They stated that Mr Rosenblatt would receive 8% of any deal over 30 million dollars (£22 million), 10% of any deal over 50 million dollars (£37 million) and 15% of any deal over 100 million dollars (£74 million).

This was later written up and signed by Mr Cowell in February 2023 at his Cotswolds home, Ms Ratcliffe said.

Mr Rosenblatt claims however that when he sent an invoice to Mr Cowell following the deal in 2025, the fee was not paid.

Ms Ratcliffe said: “In breach of the Dinner Agreement and/or the February 2023 Letter, the fee owed to Mr Rosenblatt has not been paid within 30 days of the date of the invoice or at all.”

A spokesperson for Mr Cowell declined to comment.

England have been given another possible injury worry after opening batter Emilio Gay retired hurt while playing for Durham.

Gay appeared to suffer discomfort while batting against Middlesex in the Metro Bank One Day Cup at Chester-le-Street, clutching at his right shoulder after driving a four off Toby Roland-Jones.

The left-hander faced one more ball but was unable to continue his innings, retiring on nine not out after receiving initial treatment from the physio. He is due to have a scan over the weekend, having played no further part in the 50-over game.

open image in gallery Emilio Gay appeared to suffer an injury ( Getty )

Gay, who made his Test debut earlier in the summer, was primed to reprise his role as Ben Duckett’s partner at the top of the order in the three-Test series against Pakistan after being named in a 16-man squad on Thursday.

England are already without No 3 Jacob Bethell for those games, with Jordan Cox in line to deputise for the injured Warwickshire batter.

A recalled Ollie Pope is the batting cover within the squad, though there is no specialist opening back-up. Cox has previously performed the role for Kent and Essex, while Dan Lawrence – slated to bat at No 6 – opened for England against Sri Lanka in 2024.

Any possible absence for Gay would be a significant blow to a player who looked assured in his first taste of Test cricket, and is seeking to secure his place in the side under new coach Stephen Fleming.

President Donald Trump is “in denial” about his unfavorable polling numbers and is “distracted” by his Washington, D.C., renovation projects, according to a report.

Polls across the board, which Trump claimed were “fake,” show that a majority of Americans are unhappy with the president’s job performance.

Ahead of the looming midterm elections, insiders expressed frustration to Axios that, despite the grim polls, Trump “has no desire to back off” when it comes to the war in Iran, his trade tariffs and the overhauling of Washington monuments — issues that are unpopular with voters.

“He concentrates on the hobbies that distract from his terrible polling numbers, about which he is in denial,” a Trump insider told the outlet. “The other issue is how the war, tariffs and monuments are demoralizing the base.”

The report cited the latest Economist/YouGov poll tracking the president’s net approval rating, which fell to a record low of - 25 percent this week.

open image in gallery President Donald Trump is ‘in denial’ about his unfavorable polling numbers and is ‘distracted’ by his Washington, DC, renovation projects, according to a report ( AFP/Getty )

“My REAL Polling Numbers, not those made up by the Fake News Media, are the best they have ever been, and why wouldn’t they be with the biggest tax cuts and employment numbers EVER,” Trump responded.

The president acknowledged Friday that his party was facing an uphill battle in the upcoming midterm elections, but insisted voters are not angry at him.

“I mean they’re angry at Republicans, but they’re not angry at me. They’re not angry at me but they are angry at Republicans,” he told Punchbowl News.

During Trump’s second term, he has fixated on putting his personal touch on D.C.’s landmarks, and embarked on a $400 million White House ballroom project, which he referenced approximately the same number of times as healthcare affordability and drug pricing, according to analysis conducted in April.

Other projects include a flawed repair job of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and plans to install a 250-foot Triumphal Arch.

open image in gallery Insiders expressed frustration that Trump ‘has no desire to back off’ when it comes to the war in Iran, his trade tariffs and the overhauling of Washington monuments, including plans for his 250-foot Triumphal Arch ( AFP/Getty )

While 32 percent of Americans feel enthusiastic or satisfied with the plans, 65 percent feel dissatisfied or upset, according to a Washington Post-Ipsos poll last month.

Before Trump launched his war on Iran on February 28, his aides had urged him to stay on message about affordability — one of the most important issues for voters ahead of the midterms — but the conflict has proved to be a major distraction.

The White House issued a release Friday touting the Trump administration’s work on “rebuilding the foundation for lasting prosperity.”

“Across the country, private sector companies are responding to President Trump’s call by delivering tangible price reductions on everyday goods and services — putting money back in the pockets of American workers and families,” the release said.

News.title: Gomes scores for Aston Villa in defeat by Bayern Munich in Hong Kong
News.content:
Aston Villa 1 Bayern Munich 2

Aston Villa’s tour of the Far East ended in defeat as they lost 2-1 to German champions Bayern Munich in a pre-season friendly at the Kai Tak Sports Park in Hong Kong on Friday.

Bayern took the lead inside the final 10 minutes of the first half, with defender Kim Min-jae heading in from Tom Bischof’s sublime free-kick. Villa goalkeeper Marco Bizot made a string of saves in the second half to keep Bayern’s lead at one goal until former Liverpool forward Luis Díaz smashed in Bayern’s second off the underside of the bar.

Just as the game appeared to be out of reach for Aston Villa, who had struggled to create much going forward for most of the game, Unai Emery’s side showed some life late on. Summer signing João Gomes’s goal from the edge of the box gave them hope before Tammy Abraham nearly brought them back onto level terms, only to be denied by a fine save from 40-year-old Manuel Neuer.

Aston Villa are next in action in six days’ time when they take on Paris St-Germain in the Uefa Super Cup before kicking off their Premier League campaign at Brighton. Bayern have one more friendly to come against RB Leipzig before the DFL-Supercup against Borussia Dortmund. They then kick off the defence of their Bundesliga crown against Stuttgart at home on August 28.

News.title: Suspected Ebola case on packed Congo river boat sparks testing rush
News.content:
Congolese health authorities have intercepted and detained a river boat on its way to the capital after a suspected Ebola case onboard.

Authorities have set up a mobile clinic to test more than 200 passengers after one of them disembarked and died earlier on the voyage.

The boat travelling from the northeastern commercial hub of Kisangani was stopped and held in Maluku, some 40 miles from Kinshasa.

Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is dealing with its worst ever outbreak of the viral haemorrhagic fever, which has seen nearly 4,000 cases and killed around 1,801 people according to the latest government figures.

Samuel Roger Kamba, the health minister, said a 32-year-old man had disembarked in Pimu in Mongala province, before developing ‌suspected Ebola symptoms and dying.

“We did not say it was Ebola. We said there was a suspected case for which we are being cautious,” the health minister told a press conference, according to MediaCongo, a local news site.

He said there had been no other reports of deaths among travellers.

The virus has so far spread to five provinces, though more than 90 per cent of cases have been recorded in the north eastern Ituri region.

News.content:

News.title: El Nino could cause explosion of rabid seals, animal health experts warn
News.content:
This year’s El Nino weather event risks propelling an outbreak of rabid seals around the world, the world’s animal health body has warned.

Countries in South America and Australasia are being urged to look for signs the deadly infectious disease has reached their waters, only two years after it was first confirmed in South Africa.

The 2024 discovery of rabies in South Africa’s Cape fur seals was the first significant outbreak ever found in marine mammals and has been described as a “significant shift in rabies ecology”.

More than 100 cases have been confirmed in South Africa and Namibia since then, raising fears that aggressive rabid seals could infect humans, pets and other wildlife.

Changing patterns in fish stocks caused by the El Nino phenomenon now potentially risk widening the spread, as uninfected seal populations migrate for food and come into contact with rabid colleagues.

Scientists believe warming sea temperatures off Antarctica could send seal populations northwards into Southern African waters, where they could be exposed to rabies.

They could then return to their home waters, taking the virus with them and infecting other seal populations.

News.title: ​Arteta’s ‘dynasty’ dream collides with Arsenal’s harsh reality
News.content:
Arsenal 1 Real Betis 3

Mikel Arteta says he wants to create a “dynasty” at Arsenal as he threw down the gauntlet to his players to retain their Premier League title and reach a “different level”.

Arsenal are on the verge of completing a £75m deal for Brazil midfielder Bruno Guimãraes from Newcastle and have not given up hope of landing Real Madrid winger Vinícius Júnior, who has been offered an improved contract by the Spanish giants.

The Premier League champions slumped to a 3-1 defeat to Real Betis in Dublin on Wednesday night, when they paid the price for individual errors and a lethargic, sloppy defensive display.

But that did little to quell Arteta’s ambitions for the new season. “I’m even more excited [about this season], and we’re going to go and attack every possible title because that’s the ambition that we have,” he said.

“We know that we have the ability. We will go from a strength to a strength as well, whether it’s with the players that we have to take them to a different level, and with the market that is still open to recruit as well, so we are very optimistic about it.

“All the work that we’ve done – that I’ve done through the summer – is to understand what we need to do to win again and to create a dynasty in this football club. That’s the aim.”

Despite Arteta’s bullishness, he conceded Arsenal would have to be a lot better than they were against Betis. When asked about the mood in the dressing room, he said: “Very upset, given a hard time. They are fuming, but this is good. That’s what we need.”

Telegraph Sport analyses some of the talking points from a disappointing evening at the Aviva Stadium.

No Saliba a concern

The importance of goalkeeper David Raya and centre-backs William Saliba and Gabriel Magalhães to Arsenal hardly needs overstating. Their title success was built on the foundations provided by that triumvirate at the back.

Raya has yet to report back from holiday after Spain’s World Cup triumph and Saliba is facing an extended spell on the sidelines with a back injury. Gabriel did appear for the second half but, watching this, Arteta is unlikely to have been dissuaded from the belief he needs another top defender to compensate for the loss of Saliba.

It may have been only Arsenal’s second game of pre-season, so a degree of legginess was understandable.

But the ease with which they were cut open and overloaded by the Spanish side, and the volume of individual errors, did not sit comfortably with Arteta with just over a fortnight until they kick off their title defence at home to newly promoted Coventry City.

Only once in 63 matches last season did Arsenal concede three goals in a single game but they were fortunate Betis did not score more. “In the first half there are two different things: to play well and to compete,” said Arteta, who saw his side trail 3-1 at the interval.

News.title: Ebola outbreak outpacing containment effort, WHO chief warns
News.content:
Caused by the rare Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, for which there are no vaccines or treatments, it has been extremely difficult to contain, according to experts on the ground.

“The outbreak is spreading faster than our scale-up of the response, with new cases doubling in some hotspots over the past week alone,” Dr Tedros said on X.

Part of the difficulty is that the virus was circulating undetected for weeks before the outbreak was formally declared in mid-May, leaving health officials even now racing to catch up with the spread.

Prof Placide Mbala, director of research, clinical trials and innovation at Africa CDC, told the Telegraph: “It’s mostly the fact we arrived a bit late. It took us some time before we detected this virus outbreak. And when we detected the outbreak, we already had a total of I can say more than 200 suspected cases. It’s been difficult to catch up. That’s where we are.”

While the DRC has a wealth of experience in tackling haemorrhagic fever outbreaks, the effects of that initial delay are still being felt.

Prof Mbala said: “We have some experience dealing with the cases, the labs, the communication, the infection prevention and control.

“We have some experience... But my observation is that we were very slow, and it’s why we’re in this situation.

“We are slow detecting the people, slow responding, we are slow deploying people, we are slow to recruit the community healthcare workers to improve contact tracing, we are slow to deploy the safe burials.”

DRC’s largest outbreak had previously been from 2018 to 2020, when 3,481 cases were recorded.

The West Africa outbreak recorded 28,616 cases and 11,310 deaths according to the WHO.

Prof Mbala said insecurity was also severely hampering attempts to curb the virus. The outbreak epicentre is in Ituri province, which has been wracked by ethnic strife for decades and is also home to militias competing to control mining.

He said: “There are many, many mining groups controlling most of the mining places. We have a big issue with those places, because they are places where the response team cannot go.”

Medics and aid workers have also been undermined by violent public distrust of their efforts.

Locals in the area have either doubted the existence of the virus, or have accused health teams of deliberately spreading the infection, or somehow benefiting from it.

More than a dozen health facilities have been set alight and several health workers have been killed.

Prof Mbala said: “The local people, they also sometimes are very upset, because they believe that it’s a kind of a business, and people who are coming here, they are getting a lot of money, [so] don’t want this disease to stop.”

He said he hoped that immunity was starting to rise in some areas and this would start to curb transmission.

However there was also a risk that people fleeing the outbreak would spread the virus further afield.

He said: “The second scenario is the fact we are seeing people moving from the affected area to new areas, to run away from the response team because they do not want to go to the treatment centre.

“And in complicity with their family members living in other areas, they are now the ones who are spreading the disease to new areas

“So we’ll see new places affected because people are moving around from the affected zone to the non-affected zone.”

News.title: Mykhailo Mudryk returns as Chelsea slip to Juventus defeat
News.content:
Chelsea 0 Juventus 1

Mykhailo Mudryk made his first Chelsea appearance since November 2024 as Xabi Alonso’s team succumbed to their second pre-season defeat.

Mudryk replaced Nicolas Jackson in the 82nd minute against Juventus, marking his return to competitive football after a long doping ban that was resolved this week thanks to changes in Wada regulations.

There were a couple of crosses delivered from the left flank by the Ukrainian winger, who could yet leave Chelsea on loan or on a permanent basis before the close of the transfer window.

Juventus were the victors though, thanks to a sumptuous 68th-minute goal by Kosovo winger Edon Zhegrova.

Alonso had 21 players on his bench, and made 12 second-half substitutions.

Levi Colwill and Cole Palmer featured in the defeat by 10-man Spurs on Saturday, but sat this game out as they continue to build fitness. Danny Welbeck did start though, reunited with former Brighton team-mate Joao Pedro up top.

Chelsea scored just one goal against Spurs and Juventus, but the thrust provided by right-back Marco Palestra in tandem with first Geovany Quenda and then Estevao was a bright spot for Alonso.

Chelsea continue their pre-season against AC Milan on Saturday, before they host Real Sociedad at Stamford Bridge on August 15.

They begin their Premier League campaign at Fulham in the Monday night slot on the opening weekend.

News.title: The underground lab where ‘princess mosquitoes’ are treated like royalty
News.content:
Beneath the grand Art Deco headquarters of the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine lies a vast labyrinth inhabited by weird and wonderful creatures.

In this maze of subterranean labs, store rooms and corridors live colonies of disease-bearing insects and arachnids from all over the world, from bed bugs, sand flies and microscopic dust mites to the so-called kissing bugs that spread Chagas disease – a sinister condition that can cause its victims to drop dead of heart failure without warning, albeit decades after the first (silent) infection.

Behind a series of doors, contained in stacks of mesh boxes, you can even find the flies that spread trachoma, the Dickensian eye disease that is still a leading cause of blindness around the world. But be warned: entering the room is not for the faint of heart – the flies feed on human excrement and the smell is impossible to forget.

There are also many varieties of mosquito, including several species of the Anopheles genus that spread malaria, Culex and Aedes mosquitoes that are also vectors for human and animal diseases, and even Toxorhynchites, perhaps better known as the elephant mosquito, a friendly giant which doesn’t bite people but preys on other mosquitoes.

These animals have been studied intensely since the insectaries were established in the building’s vaults in the 1960s, underpinning many breakthroughs in the control, surveillance, and understanding of vector-borne diseases in the developing world.

LSHTM researchers are now looking closer to home. They have established the UK’s first laboratory colony of Aedes vexans mosquitoes, a species native to the British isles, to study whether they could harbour diseases like West Nile virus, Rift Valley fever, Zika or Japanese encephalitis.

Sports.title: White: I know where the Fury-AJ venue is - I did the deal!
Sports.content:
The long-awaited heavyweight showdown between Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua will take place "where the money is", says Dana White.

White, who founded the UFC and new promotion Zuffa Boxing, is a major figure in combat sports. He revealed that he knows where Fury vs Joshua will take place.

"We're the ones that have done all the deals for this fight. I did the deal for the venue, that's why I know where the venue is. I did the deal. We at TKO [the company which owns UFC, WWE and Zuffa Boxing] did the deal for television and we did everything," White told Sky Sports.

Sports.title: Shergar Cup Sprint tips: Kate, Sam and Jamie are taking on Ascot favourite

Kate Tracey, Sam Boswell and Jamie Lynch reconvene to discuss the best betting angles for the Shergar Cup Sprint at Ascot on Saturday, live on Sky Sports Racing.

Thunder Call heads the market for this typically competitive heat having gone down on his sword when looking to complete a hat-trick in a hot three-year-old handicap at Newmarket last time out, but all three of our panellists are taking on the William Haggas-trained sprinter.

Senior form analyst Jamie Lynch:

"Quick conditions will help for Havana Hurricane, trained by Eve Johnson Houghton. He's up to six furlongs from five last time and this is only his third handicap start too. He was well liked last year and won the Windsor Castle.

"The key here is up in trip and being held up. The last five winners of this race have come from off the pace as they go a fair gallop. There is a lot to like with him here and he's a proper each-way price."

Host Kate Tracey:

"The horse for me is Figjam, who was second at Doncaster last season in a competitive handicap. She had been pitched into the deep end in the Firth Of Clyde and ran fourth. She makes her handicap debut.

"Her rating could be a little high but the thing with her is she's still so unexposed for a trainer who has done well with sprinting mares this season in Katie Scott. I think she's a lot more unexposed than these and has a good chance here."

Sports.title: Doyle: Thunder Call a big player in Ascot's Shergar Cup
Sports.content:
Our ambassador Hollie Doyle, who was the leading rider at the 2023 Shergar Cup, runs the rule over Saturday's international contest at Ascot - live on Sky Sports Racing.

Glamorous can have them singing in the Valleys

It's exciting for Welsh trainer Chris Mason to have a runner in this year's Dubai Duty Free Shergar Cup and they'll be singing loud in his Monmouth village on Saturday night if All Ways Glamorous takes the opening Dubai Duty Free Shergar Cup Dash (1.35) at Ascot.

His five-year-old, who will be representing Team Europe, already has a course-and-distance win to his name after impressing off a five-pound lower rating two weeks ago and can give French rider Marie Velon a great experience.

Europe's Bolo Neighs looks poised to get his head in front soon after flashing home in the same race last time but has work to do to turn the tables, while Ryan Moore can be relied upon to get the best out of my old friend Spartan Arrow who has been working well enough to put points on the board for Great Britain and Ireland.

Shady has Moore to offer in Stayers

Shrimp Shady is a young horse going places and can give Great Britain and Ireland maximum points in the Dubai Duty Free Shergar Cup Stayers (2.10).

Andrew Balding's four-year-old has landed big marathon handicaps at Chester and Newbury already this summer and looks made for this stiff two-mile trip with Ryan Moore set for another plum ride.

Europe, who haven't won the Shergar Cup since back-to-back triumphs in 2013 and 2014, are also well represented with the Ian Williams-trained Hermetic likely to build on his fourth at Newcastle under the classy Christophe Lemaire. This ex-French winner could be well treated off a mark of 81.

Castle in driving seat for Ferraris

It was good to see Richard and Peter Fahey come off the cold list at Southwell on Thursday, just in time for Castle Stuart's run in the Dubai Duty Free Shergar Cup Challenge (2.45).

Hong Kong, who are competing as a team for the first time, have a live contender in this reliable four-year-old who has been unfortunate to bump into two Roger Varian improvers at York this summer. South African Luke Ferraris, a well-known name in China, can be relied upon to get the best out of him.

Ian Williams has the services of Irish champion Dylan Browne McMonagle on his likely favourite Night Breeze, a consistent sort who was a good third at Goodwood but needs a career best to win this, which could make him a shade vulnerable. Insanity took this two years ago for Rachel King and can go well again under Europe's Velon.

Thunder a big player for Hong Kong debutant

Thunder Call didn't appear to enjoy Newmarket's undulations last time but can get back to winning ways for the Hong Kong team in the Dubai Duty Free Shergar Cup Sprint (3.20).

William Haggas' sprinter won in the style of a very nice horse at York before that and promises to be ideally suited to the stiff finish at Ascot, with British racing debutant Jerry Chau on board.

One to watch out for is Great Britain and Ireland's Cape Ashizuri who is unexposed enough to put a disappointing run in a big field last time behind him. John and Sean Quinn will be happy to have McMonagle in the plate.

Archers can hit the target for Ryan

Newmarket-based Italian trainer Marco Botti can put maximum points on the scoreboard for Great Britain and Ireland in the Dubai Duty Free Shergar Cup Classic (3.55).

Archers Bay, another strong chance for Moore, has been bumping into the likes of Ancient Egypt and Heraldry since winning at Newmarket - form that stands out in what doesn't look the strongest renewal.

Team-mate Hoseki is on a roll after rattling up a hat-trick in a course-and-distance fillies' race under a light weight. I'm not sure how much improvement she has left off this five-pound higher mark, though. A more interesting proposition could be Jessie Harrington's Pierre Grosse who is still a maiden but brings solid form to the race in first-time cheekpieces.

Bullet to make a Point in Cup decider

The closing Dubai Duty Free Shergar Cup Mile (4.30) could determine where the trophy goes this year with Europe's Bullet Point the one I expect to capitalise.

Lemaire partners Haggas' gelding, who has the sheepskins on for the first time after not hitting top stride in two starts this year. He is only a pound higher than when he won a big handicap at York's Ebor Festival 12 months ago.

I also like Rest of the World's Ebt's Guard, a course-and-distance winner who has run well in big handicaps at Royal Ascot and Sandown and looks a big player for Indian ace Suraj Narredu, who won the competition with Team Asia last year.

Special memories of the Shergar Cup

The Dubai Duty Free Shergar Cup has given me some of my most special days on a racecourse and I'm excited to watch the action unfold in front of what will once again be a big, enthusiastic crowd at Ascot.

I've been lucky enough to ride three winners in the competition including a double three years ago when I was presented with the Alistair Haggis Silver Saddle Trophy for the highest points scorer.

I was on the winning team in 2023 and 2018 and can tell you that lifting that cup is such a buzz. Being part of a team competition is something we don't often experience as jockeys so the rivalry out on the turf on Saturday will be intense.

Sports.title: Draper will play Cincinnati Open despite arm injury fears
Sports.content:
Jack Draper has been confirmed for next week's Cincinnati Open despite being left in a flood of tears following defeat at the National Bank Open in Montreal.

Draper's hopes of playing in the US Open had looked to be in doubt after his latest comeback attempt saw him break down in tears mid-match.

The 24-year-old was playing his first match since June in Canada having suffered a recurrence of the bone bruising that kept him out for almost seven months.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the first-round match at the Canadian Open between Draper and Terence Atmane

Draper looked in discomfort, with his serve badly affected against France's Terence Atmane. After being broken to trail 4-1 in the third set, Draper sat on his chair and sobbed, eventually losing 6-3 2-6 6-2.

"This is pretty emotional actually. He's been bent over and just literally erupting with emotion here. Very, very upsetting to see. It just happened at the change of ends, he leaned forward," former British No 1 Annabel Croft told viewers on Sky Sports.

Croft added: "He knows what's going on inside his body, and he knows the work he's done to try and get back on court."

The Brit has been given a wild card for the Masters 1000 event in Cincinnati beginning next week - live on Sky Sports Tennis, while the US Open - for which he would also need a wild card into the main draw - starts on August 30.

Draper is due to play in the mixed doubles at Flushing Meadows the preceding week with Jessica Pegula, and the American admitted their participation is now in doubt.

Speaking to reporters in Canada, Pegula said: "I know that he's been really struggling a bit with some injuries and I saw today he had a really tough day with his match.

"We're supposed to play. Obviously I know he's not healthy, so we'll see how that goes."

Pegula and Draper reached the semi-finals last year, and she added: "I've always since then been a very big fan, and it's been fun to watch him. He's a really nice kid, so I enjoy playing with him.

"Hoping that he can just get healthy and we can see him back out there."

Draper's injury woes

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Draper says his focus is on a 'rebirth' after suffering the 'perfect storm' of injury issues in recent times

If Draper is unable to play in New York, it would be a fourth consecutive Grand Slam that he has missed through injury.

Draper's problems first surfaced after a second-round exit at Wimbledon last year, with the former US Open semi-finalist forced off the tour with a bone bruise in his left arm.

He tried to make a comeback at Flushing Meadows but pulled out ahead of his second-round match and did not play again until February.

After initial positive signs, including victory over Novak Djokovic in Indian Wells, a changed service motion to try to help his arm problem led to a knee injury that kept him out for another lengthy spell.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the Indian Wells match between Draper and Novak Djokovic

Returning just ahead of Wimbledon in Eastbourne, Draper looked strong and reached the semi-finals only to announce on the eve of his home Grand Slam that his arm had flared up again and he would be unable to play.

Speaking to Sky Sports ahead of Montreal, Draper said: "It's important for people to recognise that the injury I have is very complex, it's very complicated, and everyone around me is doing everything we can to help this keep moving along.

"It really has been a perfect storm for me in a lot of ways. When I do get out of this storm, I'm going to be pushing on to hopefully get to where I want to be and beyond."

Sports.title: Newcastle stand firm on Hall after rejecting Man Utd approach
Sports.content:
Newcastle United have told Manchester United that full-back Lewis Hall is not for sale this summer, after an initial enquiry was rejected.

Manchester United are looking to strengthen at left-back this summer and 21-year-old England international Hall is a player they have long admired.

But Newcastle turned down their enquiry two weeks ago, and are in the market to add another full-back themselves.

Hall has three years remaining on his current Newcastle contract.

Sky Sports News has been reporting since March that Hall was among the names being considered by Manchester United for a summer move as they search for a long-term successor to Luke Shaw, who has one year left on his contract.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' Joe Thomlinson, William Bitibiri and Danyal Khan discuss Manchester United's interest in Newcastle left-back Lewis Hall.

Manchester United are currently going into the new season with Shaw as their only senior option at left-back, following Tyrell Malacia's departure on a free transfer.

Manchester United will continue to assess their options this summer as they look to strengthen Michael Carrick's side with an additional midfielder still a possibility at this stage.
