Analysis: Is Hall an achievable target for Man Utd?

Sky Sports News' Danyal Khan speaking on 'A big summer for... Manchester United' podcast:

"We first reported Hall's name [as a Man Utd target] in March, and a lot of people raised an eyebrow.

"People were like, 'oh, Lewis Hall, that's never going to happen'. And then, from my perspective, it has shifted a little bit.

"Hall is someone they really admire, and also actually feels a little bit achievable now this summer because of where Newcastle ended last season. They have no Champions League football to look forward to.

"You look at Newcastle's change in manager, the ownership and the players leaving...

"Newcastle wouldn't be happy to lose Hall, but I wouldn't say from a Newcastle perspective that he's irreplaceable.

"He was out of the team a little bit in April. From Manchester United's perspective, with all of these factors, they believe he is an achievable target this summer."

Sports.title: Man City reject Barcelona offer for Rodri
Sports.content:
Manchester City have knocked back an initial offer from Barcelona for Rodri that is considered far too low.

Barcelona's initial offer - which Manchester City rejected - was worth in the region of £40m. City are seeking upwards of £60m for the 30-year-old midfielder, who has entered the final year of his deal.

Talks over a deal have therefore halted for now.

Barcelona are not giving up on Rodri by any means. Plans are in motion for another offer to go in at some point in coming days.

Sources in Spain believe Rodri would prefer a move to Barcelona over Real Madrid.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player On the Transfer Show, the panel discuss which Spanish giant is favourite to sign Manchester City midfielder Rodri

City do not want to sell Spain's World Cup-winning captain and instead want to agree a new contract with him.

If Rodri asks to leave, however, then they would not stand in his way.

Chelsea's Fernandez would be 'dream' signing for Maresca

Image: Enzo Fernandez could be a target for Man City if Rodri leaves

As Manchester City assess their options for a replacement, Sky in Italy reports that Chelsea midfielder Enzo Fernández is manager Enzo Maresca's "dream" signing.

Sky Sports News reported earlier this summer that Fernandez was not a player City were considering signing, as their priority at the time was to retain Rodri.

The fluidity of the situation, therefore, means it remains to be seen whether circumstances change with regards to Fernandez, as City may look to bring in two players if Rodri joins Barcelona.

Fernandez is due back at Chelsea training next week after reaching the World Cup final with Argentina. Question marks remain over his future with the Blues despite the fact he has a contract until 2032. Chelsea value Fernandez at £120m.

The midfielder was left out of the squad for two games in April after admitting he would like to live in Madrid. The midfielder and his agent later apologised for the comments. They are also seeking improved terms at Chelsea.

Real Madrid released a statement last month denying any interest in signing Fernandez, while the Argentine enjoyed a strong working relationship with Maresca during the Italian's time at Chelsea.

Carra: Don't sell Rodri for £40-50m!

Sky Sports' Jamie Carragher:

"£40-50m? If you're Manchester City, what's the point in selling them? You might as well just keep them for the extra year.

"He's as good as anybody in that position in the Premier League, probably the best. Seeing what he was like in the World Cup, it was like he was back to his best.

"I thought the second half of the season him and Bernardo Silva were fantastic and almost took Manchester City to the title.

"So, if I was the manager of Manchester City, I'd be keeping Rodri at that price. It'd have to be something really special to want me to lose arguably the best midfield player in world football.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' Jamie Carragher urges Manchester City to keep midfielder Rodri for the final season of his contract rather than sell him in this transfer window

"I think it'd be really tough for them to win the Premier League without Rodri, even though they've got a lot of midfielders. He's the best, even though they've brought Elliot Anderson, who is one who I'm sure will learn off Rodri.

"And for me, I'd see those two as a pair. I see Elliot Anderson as almost the replacement for Bernardo Silva, who's gone to Real Madrid. So, I think that'd be a big hole. It'd be really difficult to fill.

"When Liverpool won the title under Arne Slot, Rodri got an injury in that season very early on, which helped Liverpool and was to the detriment of Manchester City. So if I was Manchester City, I'd be keeping him and letting him go on a free.

"City paid £60m for him. If they're getting £40m back now, what can they do with that type of money? Not a lot, really. So, I'd rather keep him."

Image: Real Madrid has also shown an interest in Rodri

Sky Sports' Laura Hunter:

Massive. Despite his age, and recent injury record, Rodri remains the most complete central midfielder to have operated in the Premier League over the past five years. "The best midfielder in the world by far," maintains Pep Guardiola.

Under Guardiola, City's in-play strategy revolved entirely around him, always impressing with his use of the ball and ability to receive in tight situations. He set the tempo for his team and controlled games as a result, doing the same for triumphant Spain this summer.

There is no current player who can condition a game like Rodri, and it is no coincidence City failed to retain their Premier League crown in the two seasons he was injury-plagued.

So, how is he replaced?

In short, he isn't.

But in Anderson City have got a surrogate of sorts. The England international might not yet be the dictator Rodri is but he can evolve to become something close. As a box-to-box midfielder, the 23-year-old is putting up numbers that at least mean he is comparable.

Sports.title: Mexico and Argentina line up behind Infantino to deepen football’s civil war
Sports.content:
Mexico’s football federation has broken ranks with the rest of Concacaf by publicly backing the beleaguered Gianni Infantino in a move that has deepened world football’s civil war.

Concacaf has called for a thorough review of Fifa’s governance in the light of the World Cup sell-off debacle, and is backing Uefa’s demands for meaningful change, although has yet to follow its European counterparts by threatening to boycott tournaments if they do not achieve their objectives.

In a statement issued on Thursday night, the FMF went some way towards explaining Concacaf’s reticence, as its second-biggest member after the US was unequivocal in its support for the Fifa president. In a Fifa statement released under Infantino’s name on Wednesday, the world governing body had called for its institutional practices to be respected, a coded way of condemning any leadership challenge before next March’s scheduled presidential election, which the FMF endorsed.

“The Mexican Football Federation is convinced that football is its fundamental value and that its best defence lies in institutional integrity and respect for the governance and processes that safeguard it,” the FMF said. “Therefore, the FMF will not recognise or approve any process convened outside of this institutional framework, and it embraces the call issued by president Infantino on 5 August 2026 to collectively continue developing football for the benefit of its 211 member associations.

“The FMF supports president Infantino’s leadership in continuing to promote the development of football through institutional strengthening.”

The Argentina Football Association (AFA) followed Mexico’s lead by backing Infantino in a gushing tribute and expressing support for his leadership over the past decade. Unlike Concacaf, South America’s Conmebol appears united behind Infantino, while in an intriguing subplot there is growing speculation that Mexico would like to switch confederations to join the latter.

“In relation to the recent events that are public knowledge, we must recognise the decision of the administration to withdraw a project that generated, within the football family and from its inception, many more uncertainties than certainties,” the AFA statement read.

“That is why it is worth highlighting the acceptance of the errors made in this process and the apology expressed in the heartfelt message displayed to the 211 member associations of Fifa. Prioritising governance standards is a fundamental pillar for strengthening good relations between Fifa, its member associations and the confederations.

“In the same way, and as we have already expressed, you are leading a management that led to a profound transformation of Fifa, which opened the doors of the organisation to all member associations and confederations, so that with a frank and direct dialogue, we can, together, continue to promote football at all levels and disciplines.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“This transformation was based on a model of transparent governance, respect for statutory structures and the monitoring of democratic procedures, essential principles for the football family to be united, firm and working to continue generating improvements in sports and institutions, which have an impact on a better quality of life for millions of human beings who practise our beloved sport.

“Accordingly, with the upcoming Fifa congress approaching, the association that we proudly preside over firmly believes and reaffirms that the way forward is to continue to work under your leadership, so that we can continue to develop better and even more inclusive football.”

Earlier on Thursday, the Confederation of African Football had reaffirmed its support for Infantino, providing him with further allies as he fights to extend his 10-year reign.

Sports.title: Norway’s Klaveness tells Fifa president Infantino to resign: ‘There is no trust now’
Sports.content:
The Norwegian FA will ask Gianni Infantino to resign with immediate effect after his doomed attempt to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

Norway is the first federation to call directly for the Fifa president to step down after a series of controversies that came to a head with the crisis engulfing his Fifa Forward Enterprise scheme.

The decision was made at a meeting of the Norwegian Football Federation board (NFF) on Thursday night. Norway has consistently taken a lead in efforts to scrutinise Fifa’s governance and recent events have taken any faith in its leadership beyond the point of no return.

“We decided that there is no trust in Infantino now,” the NFF president, Lise Klaveness, told the Guardian. “We have been worried consistently and there has been one more step in worrying direction every year, every part of the year. The trust is now gone for us, there is no way back for Infantino.

“We’re left in a very polarised cooperation globally and, I would say, chaos. So we will ask him to resign immediately so that the global football community can look ahead and cooperate going into the future.”

The NFF is expected to formally write a letter requesting Infantino’s resignation in the coming week. Norway was among a handful of countries not to back his re-election as president next March, although several European federations have withdrawn their endorsement in the past week.

“We understand that we’re one country, but it’s our position,” Klaveness said. “It’s just one step further for us. We did not vote for him in 2023 but we hoped we would support him, he was elected and the reason why we were so clear in our statements was to really give the signal that we wanted him to implement the good reforms he was part of. But he didn’t, and now we will ask him to resign.”

The NFF agreed to demand a full review into the package of reforms passed upon Infantino’s ascent to the presidency in 2016, which were intended to extricate Fifa from the corruption crisis that had previously dogged the governing body. Klaveness said the investigation should ask “what was implemented, what was not, what should have been implemented and what we should also implement to make this a functioning organisation”.

Norway will also formalise a fresh complaint to Fifa’s ethics committee on three fronts, taking in the FFE scandal, the award of Fifa’s peace prize to Donald Trump and the Folarin Balogun affair at the World Cup. It will attempt to bring a number of major European federations on board for its submission in an effort to further increase the pressure on Infantino.

“We want the ethics committee to show their work transparently because this is a very big part of the issue,” Klaveness said. “There are all kinds of control mechanisms in place but they are not really holding the council and president accountable.”

View image in fullscreen Gianni Infantino leaves after attending the Wafcon match between Malawi and Zambia in Rabat. Photograph: AP

In June, the NFF wrote to the ethics committee supporting a complaint by the advocacy group FairSquare, which centred on alleged breaches of political neutrality by Infantino. It will now make a new submission that asks for the three situations to be considered individually. “We will join them in one letter but they are very different cases and we want the ethical committee to treat them separately,” Klaveness said.

The NFF is understood to have particular concerns that the timing of Infantino’s FFE offer, which promised federations significant financial gains if accepted, may constitute an abuse of position at this proximity to a presidential election. It has also been observed that the FFE scheme, had it been passed, would have locked in commitments extending well beyond Infantino’s term.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to The Recap The best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s action Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Similarly to its call for Infantino to step down, Norway is the first federation to adopt a public stance regarding the peace prize or Balogun case. Fifa’s decision to suspend the USA striker’s red card during the World Cup, meaning he was free to face Belgium in the last 16, came after Trump had called Infantino to discuss the ban.

Uefa’s federations have stood together in backing a potential boycott of Fifa competitions, a stance it reasserted on Thursday despite Infantino’s shelving of FFE. Klaveness said the move is not merely symbolic and is intended to bring swift results.

“There’s no point in Uefa standing in a war position for half a year,” she said. “That would not be good at all. Now it’s crucial that we do it because global football cooperation is at stake. It’s very good to see we have strong leadership in Uefa that knows now is crunch time for this case. We cannot sell out this core of football.”

The first competition in line for a boycott would be the Under-20 Women’s World Cup, which is due to start in Poland on 5 September, but Klaveness expects the continued turmoil to have been resolved by then.

“I hope and think it will not come to that,” she said. “A lot of water will go under the bridge before that. But this is why we ask Infantino to resign. It’s so unstable now that it’s a matter of time. He cannot recover this and we cannot put the sport on the spot. The biggest priority is to be together with Uefa and have this strong position.”

Klaveness and the NFF have held a consistent line in calling for scrutiny of Fifa’s operations since she assumed her position in March 2022. She has been vocal on human rights issues and governance standards within Fifa, criticising failings surrounding the Qatar World Cup and questioning the process that awarded Saudi Arabia the 2034 edition of the tournament.

Sports.title: England striker Ivan Toney charged with assault after Soho nightclub incident
Sports.content:
The England footballer Ivan Toney has been charged with assault after an incident at a nightclub in Soho in December last year.

Scotland Yard said the striker had been charged on 31 July with assault causing actual bodily harm. Toney, who plays for the Saudi Pro League club Al-Ahli, is due to appear at Westminster magistrates court on 24 September.

The Sun newspaper reported in December that Toney had been arrested after an alleged head-butt. It claimed a fan recognised the footballer and grabbed at him while seeking a photograph with him before the incident.

On Friday the Metropolitan police said the charges related to an incident on 6 December at a nightclub on Wardour Street in central London, reportedly the now-closed 100 Wardour Street.

A spokesperson for Toney said: “Ivan acknowledges the charge and although he is naturally shocked, he looks forward to being given the opportunity to clear his name in court.”

Toney was at the centre of one of the most curious transfers on deadline day in August 2024 when he completed a late move from Brentford to Al-Ahli worth a reported £40m. He has also played for Newcastle United and his home town club Northampton Town, as well as several others on loan as he looked to establish himself.

Seen as a late bloomer in football terms, he had made only two Premier League appearances before his 25th birthday, but went on to score 67 goals in 128 appearances over the next three seasons at the top level.

He has played 10 times for England, scoring once in a friendly match against Belgium in 2024, and was part of the 2026 World Cup squad, making appearances against Argentina in the semi-final and in the win over France as England finished third.

Sports.title: Boardroom struggle deepens gloom as West Ham prepare for life on the outside
Sports.content:
There have been 10 summers of West Ham’s London Stadium tenancy and a number of winters of discontent. As the Hammers kick off the new season on Saturday, a Carabao Cup first-round fixture with Portsmouth is a stark reminder of reduced circumstances, further confirmation of last season’s relegation from the Premier League. The summer has been as bleak as any of those winters, with a number of factors colliding to deepen the gloom of relegation.

Certain clubs, including West Ham back in 2011-12 when promotion was achieved at first time of asking under Sam Allardyce, have used the Championship to take a beat, to refresh and replenish. Can this be the case at West Ham 2026? The Hammers are short-odds favourites for promotion but behind the scenes it has been a summer of turbulence, particularly in the boardroom, where a power struggle is being fought.

Portsmouth will bring 9,000 supporters on Saturday but will David Sullivan be present? This week it was revealed the operators of London Stadium had recommended the former joint-chair (but still co-owner) stay away, because of the “potential for demonstrations and anti-social behaviour by some spectators”.

It is expected that Sullivan will turn up, despite a fans’ advisory board statement that his attendance would cause “offence and upset”. It has been suggested that he wants to enjoy the coming season as a fan and is happy to bide his time before any consideration of selling his 38.8% stake. Considering his personal circumstances, his attendance would be a brazenly unpopular act. On 25 May, when relegation was confirmed despite a home win over Leeds, Sullivan was forced to leave the stadium early for his own safety.

View image in fullscreen Daniel Kretinsky wants to increase his shares in West Ham to just under 50.1%. Photograph: David W Černý/Reuters

Sullivan continues to deny allegations of sexually exploitative and predatory behaviour towards women over several decades made by the BBC’s Panorama documentary in early June, though he stepped down from his role on the eve of the broadcast “to avoid disruption to the club while he addresses the matter privately”.

Even before those allegations became public, Sullivan was a lightning rod, lambasted for his stewardship of a club in vertiginous decline since winning the Europa Conference League in May 2023. The £100m fee received for Declan Rice that summer was frittered away. Fellow Prague hero Jarrod Bowen, the club captain, has pledged to stay on, tasked with leading the club back up.

Until his defenestration Sullivan had acted as the club’s de facto director of football, often to the frustration of those in the football department. His chief ally, Karren Brady, stepped down in April as storm clouds gathered, severing a working relationship that dated as far back as 1990.

Among the club’s support, 50,000 season tickets have been sold for the attempt at re-entry to the Premier League. The overriding desire among fans is for Sullivan to completely depart the scene. His announced departure had installed a modicum of optimism.

Potential new sheriffs are circling but the picture is complicated, any future direction opaque as a result. As Sullivan stepped down the expectation was that Daniel Kretinsky, the Czech billionaire owner of Royal Mail who has owned 27% of West Ham since 2021, would make his move. Instead, this week, he cut that share down to just under 25%, though this was part of a strategy.

Last weekend, the familiar face of Amanda Staveley entered the picture. In July 2024 she departed Newcastle, after her leading role in bringing in the Saudi Arabian Public Investment Fund, but now Staveley wants to return to football. Last September, she was linked with a takeover at Tottenham, and it is suggested she will use a similar source of funding to engineer her move for West Ham. Among Newcastle fans, with their club faltering this summer, Staveley’s energy is lamented. With her connections, some Hammers fan hope she could have a similar galvanising effect.

View image in fullscreen David Sullivan’s closet ally, Karren Brady, left the club in April. Photograph: PA Images/Alamy

The key is the 25% that belonged to the late David Gold, Sullivan’s former joint-chair. As Staveley loomed, Kretinsky appeared ready to take up his first refusal on purchasing that 25% from Vanessa Gold, David’s daughter and current co-chair. Adding that to his 27% would take him beyond 50.1%, leaving him liable for a formal takeover offer. But shifting 2% to a Czech ally, the entrepreneur Jakub Havrlant, now means he would be short of that obligation should he cut across Staveley’s ambitions by buying Gold’s stake. Sullivan’s shares also hold the balance of power and Staveley’s next move is keenly awaited.

While that plays out, what of football? The arrival of free agent, the former Brighton and Ajax defender, Joël Veltman, was the first addition of a summer where the sales of Mateus Fernandes to Tottenham and Crysencio Summerville to Al-Hilal fetched a collective £140m, commensurate to a year of Premier League TV money. Youth product Freddie Potts’ departure to Club Brugge for £10m disappointed some fans. Needs must if further players are to arrive. There is interest in Ireland’s World Cup playoff hero Troy Parrott, the striker at AZ Alkmaar, though attracting players to the Championship has its difficulties.

View image in fullscreen West Ham have cashed in on key players, such as Mateus Fernandes to Tottenham, to cushion their descent into the Championship. Photograph: Phil Walter/Getty Images

In the dugout remains Nuno Espírito Santo, who stayed when his departure had been expected. Nuno’s zen-like calm is required at a club where panic regularly sets in. The vacuum created by Sullivan’s situation, relegation and lack of transfer business heightens anxieties. A new season has arrived, with uninviting league fixtures against Burnley, Charlton, Watford and Wolves by 1 September. Karim Virani, previously a club employee who departed in 2020, more recently at Glasgow Rangers, has returned as interim chief executive. Attempts are being made to stitch West Ham into a semblance of unity.

This summer, the London Stadium played host to concerts from Take That and Metallica, and staged the Diamond League athletics meet in July, where Josh Kerr broke the world mile record. Thursday saw a bid confirmed to stage the 2029 World Athletics Championships, following an impasse between the club and the stadium owners. Further reminders that West Ham’s home will never be fully their own, 10 years after departing the Boleyn Ground.

Such were the terms Sullivan, Gold Sr and Brady agreed for a stadium that fans continue to resent, where Sullivan is unlikely to be made to feel welcome.

Sports.title: Football Daily | Vinícius Júnior and a fantasy world of transfers in the football lull
Sports.content:
THE CAPTIVE VOID OF NOBLE RAGE

“We were so close … At the end of the day, really, they made him an offer he couldn’t refuse … It shows where we’re trying to aim for the club … There has been a lot of stuff written in the papers that you have to take on the chin I’m afraid – they should be talking about how well the England cricket team are playing at the moment.” Words said not by Mikel Arteta about Arsenal missing out on Vinícius Júnior after the Brazilian megastar signed a new Real Madrid contract, but by Glenn Hoddle in 2002, as Tottenham missed out on signing … yes, Rivaldo. That last sentence was probably a dead giveaway. Tottenham’s solution to the Brazilian-shaped hole in their transfer ambitions was to sign Robbie Keane to his boyhood club. What might Arsenal do next? Eye up Cristian Romero, you say?

Arsenal’s unrequited chase for Vinícius brought to bear the fantasy world that fans reside in when the transfer window is open and no actual competitive football is being played. Just imagine what he might have done to defences in Our League. In that netherworld of reverie there are no wet Tuesday nights at Stoke, nobody gets knacked, nobody fails to settle, they just score a gazillion goals and outperform their xG. Imagine football heaven, it’s easy if you try.

There is a flip side. Transfer business, or lack thereof, can also lead to a summer of angst. See the social media disgrace wails of certain vocal fans at Liverpool and their exasperation that Virgil van Dijk, 73, is the sole senior Red Men centre-back. Perhaps the balm of signing Bradley Barcola will soothe, though that is not yet a DONE DEAL. Arsenal fans have already consoled themselves with the imminent addition of Bruno Guimarães; who needs Big Vin when the other Brazilian can supply passes to, er Gabriel Martinelli?

Each summer includes a deal that unlocks others. In a sign of the times, Madrid ponying up for a mega Vinícius deal rather than his doing one will likely shift tectonic plates. With him set to stay, Rodri whose winning of the 2024 Ballon d’Or caused an almighty strop from the Brazilian and his club, lest we forget, is now highly unlikely to head to the Bernabéu. With Kylian Mbappé already on silly money, and now Vinícius too, thus there is no room at the inn for the Spain captain. Instead, Manchester City’s main man and the Geopolitics World Cup’s very best player is said to want to join Barcelona, which would be a huge loss to his current club and Our League. Such is the transfer window, where it is far better to have loved and lost than never to have signed anyone at all.

Sports.title: Manchester City reject Barcelona’s opening £38.5m bid for Rodri as talks continue
Sports.content:
Manchester City have rejected an offer of £38.5m (€45m) from Barcelona for Rodri and want at least £60m before allowing Spain’s World Cup-winning captain to depart.

Barcelona have emerged as Rodri’s preferred destination after talks with Real Madrid broke down this week. It is understood that the 30-year-old, who is now in the final year of his contract at City, has agreed personal terms with the Spanish champions after indicating that he would like to return to his homeland following the departure of Pep Guardiola.

Rodri moved to the Etihad in 2019 from Atlético Madrid and has turned down the offer of a lucrative extension. Yet City are believed to be adamant that he will not be allowed to leave for less than their asking price. Barcelona are continuing negotiations in the hope of reaching a compromise.

Rodri, who won the World Cup Golden Ball as the tournament’s best player last month, spoke to Barça’s manager, Hansi Flick, and sporting director, Deco, about a potential move on Wednesday.

The Spanish champions will be without Frenkie de Jong for several months after the Netherlands midfielder sustained a knee injury and have targeted Rodri as a replacement. He has had minor surgery on his back and will miss most of City’s pre-season programme.

City have signed Elliot Anderson from Nottingham Forest for £116m and remain in negotiations with Lille over a deal for Ayyoub Bouaddi. The Morocco midfielder could cost up to £80m but they could be tempted to bring in a more experienced replacement for Rodri should he depart, with Chelsea’s Enzo Fernández among those thought to be under consideration. The 25-year-old is also wanted by Real, whose manager, José Mourinho is said to not to have the news of being gazumped by their great rivals well. Reports in Spain have claimed that the 63-year-old is unhappy after making the signing of a central midfielder his priority on returning for a second stint at the Santiago Bernabéu.

Real have already brought in the winger Yan Diomande for £115m and Marc Cucurella, Bernardo Silva, Ibrahima Konaté, Denzel Dumfries and Carlos Espí, so they may have to balance the books by selling either Aurélien Tchouaméni and Eduardo Camavinga if they want to pursue Argentinian Fernández.

Crystal Palace have confirmed the signing of Takehiro Tomiyasu after a successful trial period. The former Arsenal defender has been training with Palace during pre-season and has done enough to earn an initial 12-month deal with the option of extending that by another two years. Tomiyasu becomes new manager Pierre Sage’s second signing of the summer after the arrival of Óscar Mingueza on a free transfer. Palace are expected to complete a deal for the USA youth international Zavier Gozo from Real Salt Lake in MLS.

Sports.title: Tottenham and Atlético in talks over Romero with Van de Ven set to sign new deal
Sports.content:
Tottenham are in talks with Atlético Madrid over the sale of Cristian Romero after categorically rejecting Arsenal’s approach for the Argentina defender and are expected to agree a new five-year deal with Micky van de Ven.

Romero has made no secret of his desire to leave Spurs despite signing a new four-year contract at the start of last season and had looked set to join Inter for a fee of around £35m. But Atlético are long-term suitors of the 28-year-old and are thought to be his preferred destination, with Diego Simeone’s side understood to be prepared to match Inter’s bid.

Reports in Spain on Friday suggested that personal terms have already been agreed with Romero, although his move may have to wait for Atlético to free up space in their squad before they can complete the transfer. Nahuel Molina, Romero’s Argentina teammate, is expected to join Roma while Aston Villa are hoping to sign Matteo Ruggeri.

Arsenal had also made their interest known as they search for a replacement for William Saliba, with the Frenchman out for an extended period due to a back issue. However, Tottenham – who have signed defenders Jan Paul van Hecke and Marcos Senesi this summer – insisted that they did not want to sell to another Premier League club, least of all their north London rivals. Arsenal are also interested in Villa’s Ezri Konsa.

It is understood that Van de Ven had been considering his future in north London at the start of the summer after Tottenham narrowly avoided relegation last season. But the impact of the new manager, Roberto De Zerbi, has persuaded the Netherlands international to commit his future to the club after talks with his representatives.

Tottenham have already spent more than £200m on six new players this summer and are still in the market for a new attacker. Last week, De Zerbi said that they had “completed 60% of our project in the transfer market”.

Sports.title: Afcon’s biennial switch cost African governing body deal worth more than $1bn
Sports.content:
A deal worth at least $1bn in secured income over eight years was abandoned by the Confederation of African Football (Caf) because the governing body decided to switch the Africa Cup of Nations from a biennial to a four-yearly event, the Guardian can reveal.

On 5 July 2025, the eve of the delayed Women’s Africa Cup of Nations in Morocco, the Caf president, Patrice Motsepe, told the Guardian in Rabat, after a prolonged discussion of the bidding process at an executive committee meeting, that a decision on a winning bid would be made “in due course”.

“We announced in Addis Ababa this $1bn partnership that we are looking at over the next eight years. There is a lot of good progress that has been made,” he said.

On 23 July, four days after the World Cup final in New York, Caf opened a fresh tender for the marketing and commercial rights of the 2028, 2032 and 2036 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) tournaments, with bidders given until 24 August to hand in their bid books.

The tender is in complete contrast to the 2025 bidding round, in which the entirety of Caf’s competition portfolio was bundled for sale.

Luxolo September, Caf’s head of communications, confirmed that the change in Afcon frequency is wholly responsible for the abandonment of the 2025 bidding round that was on the verge of completion.

“As foreshadowed by the president in his comments last year, following the receipt and evaluation of bids and presentations from the bidders, in the second half of 2025, Caf entered into detailed discussions with shortlisted bidders regarding the precise terms and conditions of their proposals.

“However, at its meeting on 20 December 2025, the Caf executive committee took a unanimous decision – in the interest of African football – to move the Afcon to a four-year cycle, bringing the competition into alignment with the international match calendar,” September said. “This was a significant decision for African football. That executive committee decision materially changed the scope of the commercial rights available for tender, with the result that the 2025 ITT (Invitation To Tender) process could no longer proceed in its existing form.”

View image in fullscreen Patrice Motsepe (left) said in 2025 that ‘good progress’ was being made over a $1bn deal for Caf. Photograph: Angela Weiss/AFP/Getty Images

It has been seven years since Caf has had a long-term deal to secure its financial future. The 2016-2028 billion-dollar “minimum guarantee” revenue contract that it signed with the French company Lagardère during the tenure of Issa Hayatou, the late Cameroonian president of Caf, was the first of its kind for the organisation.

“The Memorandum of Understanding with Lagardère was agreed by a team I led with Hicham [El Amrani, then Caf general secretary] in May 2015, in Zurich,” Suketu Patel, then chair of Caf’s finance committee, said in 2019.

“On that same day, we met with Infront. Their indicative offer on the table was a $450m minimum guarantee for eight years, as opposed to the $1bn, for 12 years, from Lagardère.

“If you look at our earlier contract of 2009, we had a minimum guarantee of $150m, but our income for the period was actually around $350m. We anticipated that the 12-year contract would have yielded about $1.3bn.

“I can tell you that whilst President Hayatou and I had differences on political matters, we never had one on the management of Caf finances. He did not interfere with the processes established for good governance.”

But that agreement was unilaterally terminated in December 2019 during the tenure of Ahmad Ahmad, Hayatou’s successor as Caf president.

A protracted legal dispute at the International Chamber of Commerce led to Caf, just over a year into the presidency of Motsepe, paying Lagardère a final settlement of $50m, as compensation for the breach of contract, just before the 2022 World Cup in Qatar.

“There is no way that any sponsor will be prepared to pay the same amount of money for a deal in which you would normally have four Afcons over an eight-year period, when you will now only have two. That is certainly a no-brainer,” said a former FA president with expertise in financial matters.

Sports.title: Inside Jake Paul's plot to overthrow the UFC: How influencer plans to recruit Dana White's biggest stars... and hand an olive branch to Ronda Rousey
Sports.content:
Jake Paul has never been shy about declaring war on the establishment.

He has spent years accusing Dana White of underpaying fighters, publicly challenged the UFC president on everything from athlete welfare to revenue sharing and repeatedly insisted there is room for a genuine rival in mixed martial arts.

Now, he believes he finally has one.

This week, Most Valuable Promotions (MVP) completed a landmark merger with the Professional Fighters League (PFL), creating a combat sports company that combines boxing, MMA and entertainment under one banner.

The PFL name will gradually disappear over the coming months before being retired completely in January 2027, when the organization officially becomes MVP MMA. The combined company boasts almost 400 athletes worldwide, blending PFL's roster with MVP's rapidly growing boxing stable.

It is the biggest structural shake-up in MMA since the UFC cemented its dominance more than a decade ago.

Jake Paul (pictured above) has never been shy about declaring war on the establishment

He has spent years accusing Dana White of underpaying fighters, publicly challenged the UFC president on everything from athlete welfare to revenue sharing

Nobody inside MVP is pretending Dana White's empire is about to crumble overnight. But behind the scenes, the ambition is crystal clear.

'We know we're not going to overtake the UFC in the near future,' MVP co-founder Nakisa Bidarian said. 'This is a long term plan and over time we can close in on their position and create a Nike-versus-Adidas dynamic, or a Pepsi-versus-Coke dynamic, over the next seven to 10 years.

'We started this company five years ago and have been pioneers in boxing and in changing the way people consume content. We delivered the first live professional sporting event on Netflix.

'When we decided to enter MMA, we always said that if it proved successful, we would do more. Now, we the advantage of world-class infrastructure, elite fighters and the leadership of John Martin as CEO of the overall platform. We are not here to mess around.'

The merger instantly transforms MVP from a boxing promoter into a genuine multi-sport combat sports company.

Former PFL chief executive John Martin now oversees the wider business as CEO, while Jake Paul and Bidarian remain on the board, with Bidarian continuing to lead MVP Boxing alongside the promotion's blockbuster events.

Yet while the structure has changed, the philosophy has not.

From day one, Jake Paul has built his business around one message: fighters deserve more money. That message now sits at the heart of MVP's long-term strategy.

Daily Mail Sport sat down with Nakisa Bidarian to talk about how he and Paul are looking to reshape the economics of MMA

'The focus has always been to give at least 50 per cent of revenue back to the athletes,' Bidarian explained. 'If you look at traditional stick-and-ball sports that operate with those kinds of revenue-sharing models, they've created enormous enterprise value.

'When athletes receive a fair share, they're more invested, more committed, the product improves, and there's greater alignment across the sport.'

The comments represent another direct challenge to the UFC's long-standing business model, where fighter pay has remained one of the sport's most fiercely debated issues.

But simply paying athletes more is only one part of the plan. MVP believes it can also create stars in a way its rivals cannot.

'It's about branding, storytelling, exposure, engagement and producing content 24/7,' Bidarian said. 'It's about presenting our athletes for what they are - some of the best fighters in the world.

'Nobody does that better than MVP and Jake Paul. Our first MVP MMA event was a tremendous success and this merger turbocharges our ability to build on that momentum.'

The next battle will be fought in free agency.

MVP knows it cannot approach contracted UFC fighters, but once those deals expire, the landscape changes.

Bidarian believes PFL star Dakota Ditcheva has what it takes to become a global super star

'In MMA, just like in boxing, if a fighter is under contract you can't interfere with that,' Bidarian said. 'You have to wait until they become free agents.

'For example, the 155-pound champion Usman, who fought on Friday night, has just completed the final fight of his contract. I'm sure the UFC will try to re-sign him.

'But whenever a fighter comes out of contract with the UFC, of course we'll take a look. If they're the right fit for us, and we're the right fit for them, we'd love to make that partnership happen.'

The ambition stretches well beyond signing one or two marquee names.

'Our goal is to become the Pepsi to their Coke, the Adidas to their Nike, and eventually make this a genuine two-horse race,' Bidarian said. 'Sometimes we'll be ahead, sometimes they'll be ahead.

'But make no mistake, there's a real opportunity for a fighter-first platform. Very quickly, we're going to establish ourselves as the leading alternative.

'And in seven to 10 years' time, MVP will be the culturally relevant, empowerment-driven brand that Gen Z, Gen Alpha and even Gen Beta are focused on.'

One major advantage MVP believes it holds is flexibility.

Former UFC heavyweight champion Francis Ngannou remains central to the company's plans

Unlike publicly listed companies, Bidarian insists remaining privately owned allows the organization to pursue aggressive deals without shareholders dictating every financial decision.

'We intend to remain a private company for the foreseeable future because it provides us with a level of financial flexibility that public companies simply cannot match,' he said.

'In many ways, I would love for the UFC to announce tomorrow that they were increasing fighter pay to 50 per cent of revenue. But they can't. Doing so would significantly impact their margins, lower their enterprise value and ultimately affect the wealth of their owners.

'We have the freedom to be more aggressive in how we structure agreements and attract the best talent in the world.'

The roster itself is expected to evolve rapidly. Former UFC heavyweight champion Francis Ngannou remains central to the company's plans.

'That's absolutely what we want,' Bidarian said. 'Francis and I have spoken several times. He's excited to get back competing. He already has a relationship with the PFL, so it's just a case of making sure everyone is aligned on how we move forward. But yes, absolutely, Francis Ngannou is going to be part of what we're building.'

Women's MMA will also become a cornerstone of the new promotion.

Bidarian revealed he has already spoken to former UFC superstar Ronda Rousey about the future of the sport.

MVP already enjoys a close relationship with Matchroom through their recent boxing alliance, and Bidarian believes the partnership could eventually stretch beyond the squared circle

'Ronda Rousey is the most dominant female combat sports star in history in terms of popularity,' he said. 'She'd be more than welcome to be involved in MVP MMA in whatever role she wants. I spoke to her yesterday and listened to her thoughts on what we need to do.'

He also believes the promotion already possesses its next crossover superstar.

'Women's MMA will be a major focus for us. We have Dakota Ditcheva, who I believe is the most marketable female MMA fighter in the world.

'She's still young, undefeated, an outstanding striker and has enormous potential. We're excited to build around that.'

There may even be opportunities for crossover with boxing.

MVP already enjoys a close relationship with Matchroom through their recent boxing alliance, and Bidarian believes the partnership could eventually stretch beyond the squared circle and into their 'talent agency'.

'Listen, if Matchroom's talent from their talent agency become free agents, of course we'll have those discussions. We have a great working relationship with Eddie and Matchroom.

'The two MMA athletes they announced - Tom Aspinall and Ian Machado Garry - are both under UFC contracts, so there are no discussions to be had there for the moment but should they become available that's different.

Bidarian revealed he has already spoken to former UFC superstar Ronda Rousey (winning her contest with Gina Carano above) about the future of the sport

'I do think there's a huge long-term opportunity for Matchroom and MVP as combined entities. That's not today, and probably not three years from now. But when you think about Eddie's position in men's boxing, what we've built in women's boxing, and what we're going to build in MMA, I think there's a very clear path to what's possible over the next five to 10 years.'

For now, the UFC remains comfortably on top.

Dana White has already dismissed the merger between MVP and PFL, joking that it combines 'two organizations that struggle to sell tickets', while TKO president Mark Shapiro has taken a more measured stance, welcoming legitimate competition.

But inside MVP, nobody is looking for a quick knockout.

Instead, Jake Paul and Nakisa Bidarian are preparing for a long fight – one they believe could eventually reshape the economics of MMA.

They are not promising to replace the UFC.

They are trying to become something the sport has never truly had before: a genuine alternative.

Sports.title: Some of the elites criticising Gianni Infantino are sheer hypocrites. How can the money-obsessed leeches behind the Super League expect us to listen to their confected moral outrage as they bleed our beloved game dry, writes IAN HERBERT
Sports.content:
Some of the elites criticising Gianni Infantino are sheer hypocrites. How can the money-obsessed leeches behind the Super League expect us to listen to their confected moral outrage as they bleed our beloved game dry, writes IAN HERBERT

Unlock more of the best of our football coverage with a DailyMail+ subscription - brilliant exclusives, in-depth insight and the writers you love every day

The most preposterous man in football is staggering on, drowning in such vanity and ego that he cannot see how he embarrasses himself, so perhaps that’s why the biggest hypocrites of another dark week for football appear to have got away with it.

On Sunday, Real Madrid decided to weigh in on the Gianni Infantino scandal, instructing their media people to put out a sanctimonious statement welcoming the scrapping of the egghead’s plans to sell off a slice of the World Cup, and thanking UEFA for fulfilling their ‘duty’ to ‘protect football’.

You really could not make some of this stuff up. Yes, that moralising really did come from the same Real Madrid whose avarice stank football out when they led the contemptible group of 12 clubs who attempted the European Super League breakaway coup, a few years back.

Infantino’s intellectual and moral decrepitude may have been there for us all to see in his email offering nations a small cash consideration if they back his plans to raise $20billion, but have we forgotten the European club men with whiteboards and coloured marker pens, explaining their own despicable little earner in 2021?

Real’s executives back then were just as atrocious as Infantino is now – worse, in fact, given that the FIFA scheme was not actually a breakaway proposal designed to leave the have-nots behind – while the money men they indirectly inveighed against on Sunday are the one and the same suits from JPMorgan Chase, hired by them to advise on the Super League.

Given that the US finance house were forced to apologise for their part in that episode, you might have fancied they’d learned their lesson about how ferocious the backlash to a sell-out like this would be. No. They just couldn’t resist getting their snouts in the football trough again.

Gianni Infantino is somehow staggering on as FIFA President, drowning in such vanity and ego that he cannot see how he embarrasses himself

But many of his critics do not have a leg to stand on. These are clubs that tried to form the breakaway European Super League - and only buckled after immense fan pressure (pictured)

So, please let’s get this right. The new flank in football's civil war is not between the idealists and the profiteers, but between competing profiteers fighting over who gets to cash in on the game.

UEFA, under Aleksander Ceferin, are currently casting themselves as the defenders of football's traditions, protectors of the meritocracy, guardians of the fans against billionaire opportunists. Yet this is the self-same organisation which expanded the Champions League into a sprawling competition with 64 extra fixtures in 2024, to create greater TV income and more sponsorship revenue.

The self-same organisation which has been engaged in a pitched battle for territory with FIFA. That fight has spawned the Nations League and the expanded Club World Cup, with each governing body viewing the other’s new tournament with deep suspicion. UEFA’s objection is not to football becoming more commercial but to someone else collecting the commercial rewards.

Our own Premier League claim a moral high ground for themselves, too, proclaiming to be the world's greatest and most unpredictable domestic competition, while generating more money than any such league in history. Yet it is driven by the same monopolistic greed, behaving as though sharing a fraction of the wealth with the rest of the football pyramid would be an act of unconscionable sacrifice.

Don’t let it be forgotten that its biggest clubs, led by Liverpool and Manchester United, made their own power grab through Project Big Picture in 2020. Or that the Premier League held talks with CVC Capital Partners, one of the world's largest private equity firms, about selling a stake in future broadcasting and commercial revenues, at the same time.

That came to nothing, either, but here was an elite equally willing to explore new ways of extracting financial value from our game. The people’s game.

Whenever the redistribution of Premier League wealth is discussed, we witness the language and narrative suddenly change and those overseeing the competition which has negotiated television contracts worth billions begin to fret about the pennies.

It was clear when a White Paper on football governance was published a few years back that a greater flow of money down from the Premier League would be egregiously hard to extract.

UEFA, under Aleksander Ceferin (right), are casting themselves as the defenders of football's traditions. Yet they expanded and distorted the Champions League to generate more revenue

It shouldn't be forgotten that the Premier League's biggest clubs, led by Liverpool and Manchester United, made their own power grab through Project Big Picture in 2020

The gilded elite division continued to maintain the fallacy that they were helping the rest, when 70 per cent of the money they sent down below was Championship parachute money. An insurance policy for the division’s own members laughably dressed up as ‘solidarity payments’.

It has taken Government intervention to force a more equitable share of the Premier League’s wealth throughout the game, in the shape of the Independent Football Regulator, with its ‘backstop’ power to force a settlement if none is agreed.

Faced with such a prospect, the Premier League have finally just voted for an additional £1.5billion from those in the gilded cage, to be shared with the EFL’s clubs, though even that is not allocated yet. The cash, to be funded by a two per cent lift in the transfer levy on all top-flight deals, will clearly need to be crowbarred from clubs swimming in wealth, given the opposition led by Manchester City’s petro-dollar billionaire owners – another of the merry little European Super League band.

We understand other members of the so-called ‘Big Six’ are also unhappy that they may now find themselves coughing up more than less elevated Premier League clubs. It’s been left to the more moderately wealthy members of the division, who faced down the big clubs over the Super League, to challenge them again.

If there was one positive to come out of the Super League scandal, it was the way it cut the grasping, spiritually remote 'Big Six' down to size. 'It's like emerging from a slightly abusive relationship,' the owner of one of the smaller Premier League clubs told me at the time.

This weekend, the FA Cup begins its beautiful seasonal arc once more, carrying the customary thrill and sense of pride among all who will compete in its extra preliminary round. North Ferriby, at home to St Helens, Northwich Victoria, playing away to Beverley Town, and Nelson, entertaining Stockport Georgians, are just three of those taking part who know what a precarious financial reality and existential threat look and feel like.

For all the weekend’s 438 competing clubs, reaching the first round proper – six ties away, in November – would be monumental, with £47,750 prize money for those who win at that stage.

But any who progress that far will also experience the chill of strictures forced down from the top of the game. This will be the second season with no replays from the first round proper onwards – a diminishment the FA said was necessary because of increasing pressure on the calendar, particularly following UEFA's expansion of their club competitions.

The early rounds of the FA Cup still bring with them a sense of thrill and pride - though replays with England's top clubs are now sadly a thing of the past

Infantino is taking the logic of those presiding over the elite game to its natural conclusion, not dragging them somewhere they do not wish to go

Critics, especially in the EFL and non-League, have argued that a vital source of income is being removed from smaller clubs, who can no longer earn lucrative replay gates against bigger opponents.

But those little people are shouting in the dark. The abolition of replays, fourth-round matches spread over five days and the scheduling of the 2027 final before the Premier League campaign finishes, rather than as the climax to the season, belong to the story of the competition’s devaluation and diminishment. The Cup has been crushed into virtual irrelevance by football's high and mighty.

As of last night, Infantino’s brazen conceit and vanity were keeping him in a job which any intelligent and self-respecting industry would by now have forced him from. He is no doubt banking on the relentless news cycle moving on and UEFA’s threat to boycott FIFA’s competition receding into the distance.

Qualification games for the 2030 World Cup are just a year away and Infantino can safely calculate that national associations will not want to take the financial hit that a boycott would carry. It seems significant, and concerning, that a mere 11 national associations, including England and Wales, have voiced opposition to him remaining in post.

Yet for all the sound and fury, there is something deeply unsettling and incomplete about some of this moralising. Infantino is taking the logic of those presiding over the elite game to its natural conclusion, not dragging them somewhere they do not wish to go. He is the most despicable emblem of a game which is slowly devouring itself, but by no means the only one.

Sports.title: Man City reject £40m bid from Barcelona for Rodri as Catalans look to pip bitter rivals Real Madrid to land Spain captain in bitter blow to Jose Mourinho's title hopes
Sports.content:
Manchester City will demand upwards of £60million if Barcelona are to complete a sensational move for Rodri this summer.

Spain’s World Cup-winning captain has agreed terms with the Catalans ahead of the new season and is seeking a fresh challenge.

Barca instigated talks between the clubs and are understood to have had a derisory bid of nearly £40m rejected.

City have a history of allowing unhappy players to leave should the club’s valuation be met - and are standing firm in talks.

Rodri had been in negotiations with Real Madrid but communicated to them earlier in the week that Barca represented his preferred destination and has agreed personal terms.

While they are working on a transfer worth more than £80m for Lille teenager Ayyoub Bouaddi, City sources indicated that they are ready to land an experienced replacement for Rodri were he to depart.

Barcelona have begun talks with Manchester City over a move for Spain's World Cup winning captain Rodri

Man City are set to demand upwards of £60m if Barcelona are to seal the sensational move

The 2024 Ballon d’Or winner had remained coy over his future while away on international duty but is believed to have been open to a return to Spain once Pep Guardiola’s reign came to an end.

Guardiola had suggested last season that Rodri would not return to his best until the World Cup, as he battled various injury problems after the devastating ACL injury sustained two years ago.

Rodri underwent back surgery, revealed by Daily Mail Sport, immediately after lifting the World Cup.

City have kept an offer of a new contract on the table for the 30-year-old, whose deal expires next summer, and he is scheduled to link up with Enzo Maresca’s squad next week.

Sports.title: Revealed: Man United made another enquiry for Newcastle and England defender Lewis Hall - as Michael Carrick looks to strengthen left back options
Sports.content:
Revealed: Man United made another enquiry for Newcastle and England defender Lewis Hall - as Michael Carrick looks to strengthen left back options

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Manchester United made a fresh enquiry for Newcastle United left back Lewis Hall at the end of last month but were told he is not for sale.

As reported, Hall has been on United's radar this summer as it is clear they need to strengthen that position with Luke Shaw, now 31, in the final year of his contract while youngster Harry Amass has been told he may be best leaving for first team football.

Hall, 21, has three years left on his current contract, and would require a substantial fee with Newcastle looking to stabilise with Matthias Jaissle now in place.

The club want to add players to ensure they are competitive, having already lost the likes of Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali, while Bruno Guimaraes is on the verge of signing for Arsenal.

They will do all they can to keep hold of Hall, who is now seen as one of their biggest assets after joining from Chelsea in 2023.

United, meanwhile, feel they are light in the position. Shaw started all 38 Premier League matches last season, though there is no obvious back-up, with Patrick Dorgu viewed as a winger by Michael Carrick.

Manchester United moved to sign Lewis Hall (right) last month but were told he is not for sale

United have signed the likes of Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Karl Darlow this window, but aren't done yet.

Newcastle, meanwhile, want to strengthen at left back themselves and also want a right back with Tino Livramento likely to move on soon.

They are among the clubs who have checked on 19-year-old Jorge Salinas at Racing Santander along with Aston Villa. But Newcastle see Salinas as one for the future rather than ready to go now.

Sports.title: Rodri tells Real Madrid he wishes to join Barcelona as Man City legend prepares to leave Premier League - as Atletico Madrid push on with deal for Cristian Romero: WINDOW WATCH
Sports.content:
Rodri tells Real Madrid he wishes to join Barcelona as Man City legend prepares to leave Premier League - as Atletico Madrid push on with deal for Cristian Romero: WINDOW WATCH

It's that time of the year again – the transfer window is now open until September 1 and it's sure to be a busy period with clubs looking to make big signings ahead of next season.

Here are today's latest developments from Simon Jones and the Daily Mail Sport team...

United keeping tabs on Hall

Manchester United made a fresh enquiry for Newcastle left back Lewis Hall at the end of last month but were told he is not for sale.

As reported, Hall has been on United's radar this summer as it is clear they need to strengthen that position with Luke Shaw, now 31, in the final year of his contract while youngster Harry Amass has been told he may be best leaving for first team football.

Newcastle want to strengthen in that position themselves and also want a right-back with Tino Livramento likely to move on.

They are among the clubs who have checked on 19-year-old Jorge Salinas at Racing Santander along with Aston Villa. But Newcastle see Salinas as one for the future rather than ready to go now.

Palace sign ex-Arsenal man

Crystal Palace have signed former Arsenal defender Takehiro Tomiyasu on a free transfer.

Daily Mail Sport understands the 27-year-old has signed a one-year contract, with the option to extend it by a further two years.

Tomiyasu, who made 65 appearances for Arsenal from 2021-25, spent last season at Ajax but missed most of the campaign through injury.

The Japanese international will provide depth at centre-back and wing-back for Pierre Sage’s side.

BOBBY MANZI

Eagles swoop for Gozo

Crystal Palace have agreed an £11million deal to sign Real Salt Lake winger Zavier Gozo.

The 19-year-old has been given permission to have a medical.

Real Salt Lake winger Zavier Gozo looks set to join Crystal Palace

Tigers pounce on Norwegian midfielder

Hull have signed midfielder Jens Hjerto-Dahl from Tromso for a fee around £8million.

The 20-year-old has penned a five-year contract until the summer of 2031, becoming the Tigers’ sixth summer signing.

Lukic likes look of Ipswich

Fulham midfielder Sasa Lukic has completed his Ipswich medical ahead of a £9m move. He is expected to sign a four-year deal.

Atletico remain in pole position for Romero

Atletico Madrid remain in talks with Tottenham for Cristian Romero.

Numbers have been discussed between the two clubs, though Atletico have yet to make a formal offer.

Daily Mail Sport reported in July that Atletico had rekindled their long term interest in the Argentina centre back, who also has Inter Milan keen to sign him.

Atletico Madrid remain in talks with Tottenham over Cristian Romero but are yet to table a formal offer

However, the Italians are struggling to meet his personal terms despite offering £34m to Spurs.

Arsenal had enquired to Romero's representatives but that is unlikely with Diego Simeone and Atletico in pole.

Rodri sets sights on Barca

Rodri has informed Real Madrid that he wishes to join Barcelona.

The Spanish champions are now in official contact with Manchester City to try and agree a fee though their initial proposal is understood to be closer to £40million, well below their £68million valuation.

His representatives say out of respect to Madrid who were 'class in their approach', they were informed that the 30-year-old's preference is to link up with Hansi Flick's squad.

Rodri has informed Real Madrid that he wishes to join Barcelona

Wrexham target Ipswich keeper

Wrexham have asked about Ipswich Town's Alex Palmer as an alternative solution to find a new goalkeeper for the Championship season.

The 29-year-old is valued around £3.5million.

Wrexham have also been talking to Sunderland about Anthony Patterson though he is priced around £8m.

Leicester City's Harry Souttar remains a target too though Sheffield United are also in the mix for the Australia centre back.

Wrexham have asked about Ipswich's Alex Palmer as a potential goalkeeping option

Coventry remain in talks over Hamer return

The Blades, meanwhile, are continuing talks with Coventry City over the sale of midfielder Gus Hamer.

The Brazilian is keen to return to Coventry and the chance to play in the Premier League. He has also spoken to manager Frank Lampard.
