World.title: Restricting civic space and battering democracy, By Jibrin Ibrahim
World.content:
The administration should immediately withdraw the Foreign Aids (Regulation, Transparency and Disclosure) Bill, 2026 (SB.1034), the Bill requiring social media platforms to establish physical offices in Nigeria, and all other pending bills that unjustifiably restrict civic space, the rights to freedom of expression, association, peaceful assembly, media freedom, access to information and democratic participation.

The news circle has been dominated for some time by the visit of Catholic Bishops to President Tinubu to draw the attention of government to their concerns over the policy direction of the administration. Speaking about the visit in a television interview thereafter, the Archbishop Emeritus of Abuja, John Cardinal Onaiyekan has done Nigeria a good turn by boldly coming out and showing that President Tinubu’s administration is determined to win the 2027 elections “by all means.” All the indicators are blinking red, showing the single-minded determination of the Tinubu administration to use state resources to undermine the credibility of the electoral process. The problem, according to the Cardinal, is that ordinary Nigerians are in distress, suffering from the misery and hardship of the harmful policies imposed on them by President Tinubu.

The response of the government has been to launch a campaign of calumny against Onaiyekan. In a statement on Saturday, the Senior Special Assistant to the President on Media and Publicity, Temitope Ajayi, described Onaiyekan’s action as an abuse of privilege. Ajayi said that there was something fundamentally inappropriate about Cardinal John Onaiyekan granting a television interview to offer his own account and interpretation of what transpired during the private meeting between the Catholic Bishops’ Conference of Nigeria (CBCN) and President Bola Tinubu. It is strange that in a democracy, visitors to the president are denied the right to complain about his strong disagreement with their analysis. They had gone to see him to articulate a different vision for the country. He had rejected their position. They owed it to Nigerians to explain to them that President Tinubu is determined to stay in power to pursue the same anti-people policies he has been pursuing.

We thank the Catholic Bishops for their candour and commitment to the plight of the Nigerian people. It is clear to all that as the 2027 elections approach, an arsenal of executive, legislative and judicial powers have been mobilised, using the abuse of the powers of incumbency to deregister and disrupt opposition parties and politicians. The Electoral Body, INEC, is acting in a partisan and pro-administration manner. The media is under threat. Money and positions are in use to push opposition members into the ruling party.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

We must not be prevented from saying the truth that Nigerian democracy is on trial, as articulated in a recent Joint Civil Society Press Conference on Protecting the Civic Space, Constitutional Freedoms and Democratic Governance by Auwal Rafsanjani and other leaders. They expressed the view that human rights organisations and civil society organisations are gravely concerned by the growing number of restrictive and repressive bills currently before Nigeria’s National Assembly. If enacted, these bills would significantly expand executive control over civic life and further undermine the rights to freedom of expression, peaceful assembly, freedom of association, media freedom, access to information, democratic participation, and the rule of law.

These legislative proposals are being considered at a time when the civic space in Nigeria is experiencing one of its most serious declines since the country’s return to democratic rule in 1999. Since President Bola Ahmed Tinubu assumed office in May 2023, the authorities have increasingly relied on restrictive laws, politically motivated prosecutions, strategic lawsuits, arbitrary arrests, intimidation and judicial harassment against journalists, bloggers, media organisations, human rights defenders, civil society organisations and other individuals peacefully exercising their constitutional rights.

Civil society also expressed its concerns at legislative proposals seeking to compel social media platforms to establish physical offices in Nigeria or face prohibition from operating in the country. Although presented as regulatory measures, such proposals would substantially increase governmental leverage over digital platforms, thus limiting their ability to facilitate public debate, access to information and civic participation.

Recent examples include the continuing prosecution of activist and publisher, Omoyele Sowore, reprisals against the Socio-Economic Rights and Accountability Project (SERAP), the misuse of the Cybercrimes Act to target journalists and government critics, and repeated attempts to intimidate independent media and civil society organisations. International monitoring has also documented this deterioration. In May, the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) reported 91 cases of journalists being arrested, attacked or otherwise harassed across 13 states and the Federal Capital Territory during the first three years of the current administration.

The timing of these proposals is particularly concerning as Nigeria prepares for the 2027 general elections. Rather than creating an open environment in which citizens, journalists, civil society organisations and political actors can participate freely, these measures risk entrenching fear, self-censorship, and intolerance of dissent. Independent advocacy, investigative journalism and public scrutiny are not threats to democracy; they are essential safeguards of constitutional governance and accountability.

One of the most concerning Bills is the Foreign Aids (Regulation, Transparency and Disclosure) Bill, 2026 (SB.1034), which would confer sweeping powers on the authorities to monitor, regulate, sanction, suspend and potentially shut down non-governmental organisations, civil society organisations, and private entities receiving foreign assistance under the guise of promoting transparency, accountability and the prevention of the misuse of foreign aid.

Civil society also expressed its concerns at legislative proposals seeking to compel social media platforms to establish physical offices in Nigeria or face prohibition from operating in the country. Although presented as regulatory measures, such proposals would substantially increase governmental leverage over digital platforms, thus limiting their ability to facilitate public debate, access to information and civic participation.

Conditioning access to Nigeria’s digital market on the physical establishment of offices, backed by the threat of prohibition, is neither necessary nor proportionate to any legitimate regulatory objective. Such measures risk facilitating censorship, restricting access to information, discouraging innovation and investment, and encouraging private companies to prioritise political pressure over internationally recognised human rights standards.

Nigeria is further bound by the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR). Articles 19, 21, 22 and 25 protect freedom of expression, peaceful assembly, association and participation in public affairs, while Article 2 requires Nigeria to ensure that domestic laws give full effect to these rights. Under Article 2 of the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (ICESCR), Nigeria must ensure that its domestic legal framework remains consistent with its treaty obligations.

Both the Foreign Aids (Regulation, Transparency and Disclosure) Bill and the proposed legislation requiring social media platforms to establish physical offices in Nigeria are incompatible with Nigeria’s constitutional, regional and international human rights obligations. Sections 39 and 40 of the Nigerian Constitution 1999 (as amended) guarantee the freedom of expression, peaceful assembly and association, while Section 22 recognises the vital role of the media in holding government accountable.

Nigeria is also bound by the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights, which forms part of Nigerian law through the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights (Ratification and Enforcement) Act. Article 1 requires Nigeria to adopt legislative and other measures to give effect to the rights protected under the Charter, including freedom of expression (Article 9), freedom of association (Article 10), freedom of assembly (Article 11) and participation in public affairs (Article 13).

Nigeria is further bound by the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR). Articles 19, 21, 22 and 25 protect freedom of expression, peaceful assembly, association and participation in public affairs, while Article 2 requires Nigeria to ensure that domestic laws give full effect to these rights. Under Article 2 of the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (ICESCR), Nigeria must ensure that its domestic legal framework remains consistent with its treaty obligations.

Any restriction on these rights must satisfy the requirements of legality, legitimate purpose, necessity and proportionality under Articles 19(3), 21 and 22(2) of the ICCPR. The proposed bills fail to meet these standards.

The Foreign Aids Bill is also inconsistent with the United Nations Declaration on Human Rights Defenders. Article 13 recognises the right of everyone, individually and in association with others, to solicit, receive and utilise resources for the peaceful promotion and protection of human rights. Article 3 requires that any regulation of such activities should be consistent with the UN Charter and international human rights obligations.

The administration should immediately withdraw the Foreign Aids (Regulation, Transparency and Disclosure) Bill, 2026 (SB.1034), the Bill requiring social media platforms to establish physical offices in Nigeria, and all other pending bills that unjustifiably restrict civic space, the rights to freedom of expression, association, peaceful assembly, media freedom, access to information and democratic participation. It should ensure that all future legislation affecting civil society organisations, digital rights, media freedom or civic participation complies fully with the Nigerian Constitution, the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights, the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and other applicable international human rights standards.

A professor of Political Science and development consultant/expert, Jibrin Ibrahim is a Senior Fellow of the Centre for Democracy and Development, and Chair of the Editorial Board of PREMIUM TIMES.

World.title: Sanwo-Olu, Fashola advocate non-interest finance to drive Nigeria’s economic growth
World.content:
Lagos State Governor, Babajide Sanwo-Olu, and former Minister of Works and Housing, Babatunde Fashola, have called for greater adoption of non-interest finance to mobilise long-term capital to support Nigeria’s productive economy.

They spoke on Thursday at the ‘Beyond Interest’ private intelligence forum organised by The Alternative Bank in Victoria Island, Lagos.

The forum brought together investors, entrepreneurs, wealth creators, institutional decision-makers and public-sector leaders to examine the role of patient capital in driving sustainable economic growth.

Opening the forum, Chairman of The Alternative Bank, Muhtar Bakare, said Nigeria’s challenge was not a lack of capital but the absence of trust required for long-term investment.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“What we lack is not effort. We lack capital that stays long enough to turn effort into capacity, capacity into durable jobs and durable jobs into stability. That is why the distinction between extractive and productive capital matters,” Mr Bakare said.

Keynote address

Delivering the keynote address on behalf of Governor Sanwo-Olu, Lagos State Commissioner for Finance Abayomi Oluyomi said governments should serve as enablers of private investment rather than competitors.

“The future of finance is not only about the price of capital; it is increasingly about the quality of the economic activity that capital enables. Lagos is not only open for business; Lagos is prepared to do business,” Mr Sanwo-Olu said in the address.

The governor cited the Lagos infrastructure programme, the recent dual bond issuance and the Lekki corridor as examples of public investments that have improved the environment for private capital.

In his special remarks, Mr Fashola said capital anchored to real, productive assets and the public good delivers more enduring value than investments driven primarily by short-term returns.

He urged investors and institutions to consider the long-term social impact of their investments alongside financial returns.

Case for Ethical Capital

Speaking on “The Business Case for Ethical Capital,” Abubakar Suleiman, Promoter of Non-Interest Banking in Nigeria and Board Member of Sterling Financial Holdings Company Plc, said The Alternative Bank had demonstrated that non-interest banking could achieve commercial success while supporting economic development.

He noted that the bank, which started as Sterling Bank’s non-interest banking window in 2014, now holds assets approaching ₦500 billion and serves nearly one million customers.

“The Alternative Bank has shown that non-interest banking can grow, win customers, and generate profit. The business case for ethical capital already exists. Our task is to apply it with discipline,” Mr Suleiman said.

He cited WasteBanc, The Alternative Bank’s recycling initiative with the Lagos Waste Management Authority (LAWMA), and Nigeria’s sovereign Sukuk programme as examples of values-aligned finance connecting capital to productive assets while maintaining commercial standards.

Other speakers, including Stanley Jacob, Group Chief, Innovation and Technology at Meristem, and Ajibola Tobi-Osho, Executive Director of Tugrande Alliance Limited, argued that Africa’s financial challenge is increasingly one of infrastructure and capital allocation rather than liquidity.

Mr Jacob said the convergence of the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (PAPSS) and the tokenisation of real-world assets could give Nigeria a first-mover advantage in continental capital markets.

Mr Tobi-Osho, meanwhile, said Nigeria’s challenge had shifted from inflation to capital allocation, noting that banks were parking record levels of liquidity with the Central Bank of Nigeria rather than lending to businesses capable of creating jobs and driving growth.

The forum attracted senior business executives, investors and public-sector leaders, including Sterling Bank Chairman Olatunji Mayaki, Managing Director of The Alternative Bank Hassan Yusuf and Aruwa Capital founder Adesuwa Okunbo Rhodes.

Others included Sahara Group co-founder Tonye Cole, Noor Takaful Vice-Chairman Aminu Tukur, and Africa Business Angel Network President Yemi Keri.

World.title: Otedola acquires additional 138 million First HoldCo shares worth ₦18.1 billion
World.content:
Femi Otedola, chairman of First HoldCo Plc, has acquired an additional 138 million shares in the financial services group, valued at about ₦18.1 billion.

The transaction was announced on Friday in a regulatory filing signed by the group’s Company Secretary, Abiola Baruwa.

Mr Otedola acquired an additional 138,041,465 shares at ₦131.2 per share through Calvados Global Services Limited.

The new share purchase represents 0.30 per cent of the company’s outstanding shares, bringing Mr Otedola’s total stake in the financial services group to 27.16 per cent of the company’s issued share capital.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Mr Otedola now holds approximately 11.9 billion shares in the financial institution, valued at about ₦1.74 trillion based on the company’s share price of ₦146.20 as of 12:35 p.m. (WAT) on 7 August.

The First HoldCo chairman has steadily increased his investment in the company since emerging as its largest shareholder in 2021.

On 30 July, Mr Otedola increased his stake in the financial services group by acquiring an additional 1.78 billion shares, valued at about ₦222.2 billion.

About a week earlier, on 22 July, he acquired 706.1 million shares valued at ₦77.6 billion. This was separate from the 672.9 million shares worth ₦29.6 billion that he purchased in June.

The June acquisition was completed during the ₦45 billion second tranche of First HoldCo’s ₦350 billion private placement programme, in which shares were offered at ₦44 per share.

The group said it plans to inject the proceeds from the capital raise into First Bank of Nigeria Limited, its flagship commercial banking subsidiary, as part of its capital restoration and broader balance sheet strengthening programme.

World.title: JRS launches project to strengthen oil spill resilience in Akwa Ibom community
World.content:
The Jesuit Refugee Service (JRS) Nigeria has launched a new project aimed at strengthening the resilience of an oil-producing community in Akwa Ibom State against the devastating impacts of oil spills.

The project, funded by CARITAS Canada and titled “Strengthening Community Resilience to Oil Spill Impacts in Akwa Ibom State,” was inaugurated during an inception meeting held on Thursday in Eket, bringing together government officials, community leaders, traditional rulers, civil society groups and development partners.

The initiative will focus on the Okoro Utip community in Ibeno Local Government Area, where residents have complained for years about the environmental and socio-economic consequences of oil pollution.

PREMIUM TIMES reported how oil spills contaminate rivers and destroy livelihoods in Ibeno. The newspaper also reported how communities affected by oil spills have threatened legal action against oil firms over pollution.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

According to JRS Nigeria, the project is designed to strengthen the resilience of climate-vulnerable residents by promoting meaningful community participation in addressing the environmental, social and economic effects of oil contamination.

The organisation said decades of oil spills across the Niger Delta have degraded ecosystems, affected public health, weakened food security, reduced biodiversity and undermined the livelihoods of many residents.

Community-centred approach

JRS Nigeria said the project would adopt the African Palaver approach which is a traditional model of communal dialogue to create inclusive spaces where residents can share their experiences, deepen understanding of environmental challenges and collectively identify locally driven solutions.

It explained that the initiative is not intended to replace the responsibilities of government agencies but to encourage collaboration among communities, government institutions, civil society organisations, traditional institutions and other stakeholders in advancing environmental restoration and ecological justice.

The project will also promote awareness campaigns, community advocacy and community-based environmental monitoring to strengthen local capacity to respond to the long-term impacts of oil pollution.

The inception meeting, according to the organisation, introduced stakeholders to the project’s implementation strategy and expected outcomes while seeking their support for its successful execution.

‘Communities must have a voice’

Speaking at the event, the Country Director of JRS Nigeria, Temple Anuforo represented by the Deputy Head of Programmes, Iniobong Ikpang, said meaningful community participation is essential to building resilience in environmentally vulnerable communities.

“For communities like Okoro Utip, resilience begins with ensuring that people have a voice in decisions affecting their environment and their future,” Mr Anuforo said.

“Through this partnership with CARITAS Canada, we are creating opportunities for communities, government institutions and civil society to talk, walk and work together in promoting environmental justice, restoring livelihoods and strengthening hope for both present and future generations.”

He added that the project reflects JRS Nigeria’s mission of accompanying, serving and advocating for vulnerable communities by placing them at the centre of developing lasting solutions.

Community welcomes intervention

The youth leader of Okoro Utip, Nsoh Nsoh, welcomed the project, saying years of oil pollution and gas flaring had significantly affected the community’s environment, livelihoods and public health.

“Our environment, livelihoods and health have been severely affected by oil pollution and gas flaring,” he said.

“Pollution has become part of our lives to the extent that we are beginning to accept it as normal. With this project, we are hopeful that we will learn legitimate ways to resist it so that we can have a better life.”

NOSDRA pledges support

The Assistant Director of the National Oil Spill Detection and Response Agency (NOSDRA) in the Uyo Zonal Office, Akaninyene Odungide, reaffirmed the agency’s commitment to responding promptly to oil spill incidents and holding polluters accountable.

Mr Odungide also urged residents to refrain from engaging in crude oil theft and illegal bunkering, advising them instead to report such activities to the appropriate authorities.

READ ALSO: JRS launches project to strengthen oil spill resilience in Akwa Ibom community

He assured stakeholders of NOSDRA’s readiness to collaborate with JRS Nigeria and other partners to ensure the successful implementation of the project.

JRS Nigeria, which has operated in the country since 2018, said it remains committed to supporting displaced and vulnerable communities through education, livelihoods, peacebuilding, mental health and psychosocial support, advocacy and community resilience programmes. Together with CARITAS Canada and other partners, it said the new initiative seeks to empower communities to advocate for a healthier environment while promoting sustainable livelihoods and long-term resilience.

World.title: Omidiran pledges support for ABU’s 2028 NUGA, sports excellence drive
World.content:
The Executive Chairman of the Federal Character Commission (FCC), Ayo Omidiran, has pledged support Ahmadu Bello University’s plans to host the 2028 Nigeria University Games (NUGA) and develop one of the country’s National Centres of Excellence in Sports.

Ms Omidiran made the commitment on Thursday when the university’s management, led by Vice-Chancellor Adamu Ahmed, paid her a courtesy visit at the FCC headquarters in Abuja.

An alumna of the institution, Ms Omidiran said Ahmadu Bello University (ABU), Zaria, played a defining role in shaping her leadership journey and reaffirmed her commitment to supporting initiatives that promote education, youth empowerment and national development.

“I remain immensely proud to be an alumna of Ahmadu Bello University. The university shaped my character, broadened my perspective and prepared me for the responsibilities of leadership and national service. I will always cherish the institution and remain committed to supporting initiatives that promote education, national development and youth empowerment,” she said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

She welcomed the university’s request for closer collaboration, describing its selection to host the 2028 NUGA Games and its designation as one of Nigeria’s National Centres of Excellence in Sports as significant opportunities to promote youth development and strengthen the country’s sports ecosystem.

The former member of the House of Representatives also accepted an invitation to attend the university’s 64th anniversary celebration scheduled for 4 October.

Earlier, Mr Ahmed described Ms Omidiran as one of ABU’s distinguished alumni, praising her contributions to public service and sports administration.

“As an alumna of Ahmadu Bello University, where you obtained your Bachelor of Science degree in Biochemistry and served as Student Union Government Secretary of Queen Amina Hall, you exemplify the values of leadership, excellence, integrity and service that our university seeks to instil in its graduates,” the vice-chancellor said.

He also highlighted her record as a two-term member of the House of Representatives, a pioneering member of FIFA’s Women’s Committee, Secretary of the Board of Trustees of the Nigerian Olympic Committee, founder of Omidiran Babes Football Club and now Executive Chairman of the Federal Character Commission.

Mr Ahmed said the university looked forward to drawing on Ms Omidiran’s experience in sports administration as it prepares to host the 2028 NUGA Games and establish a world-class sports development centre.

“These landmark developments present enormous opportunities for the university to contribute to sports development, talent discovery and youth empowerment. We look forward to drawing upon your vast experience, guidance and support as we prepare to deliver a memorable NUGA Games and build a Centre of Excellence that will become a national model for sports development,” he said.

The vice-chancellor also formally invited the FCC chair to participate in the university’s 64th anniversary celebration, describing her as an inspiration to students and alumni alike.

The ABU delegation included the Registrar, Rabiu Samaila; Director of Public Affairs, Awwal Umar; Director of Sports, Omeiza; Professors Danladi Amoh, Sani Ibrahim and Aliyu Salihu; Deputy Registrar Ingino Danjuma Voh; and Liaison Officer Haruna Ajo.

World.title: “Our mum asked Paul and Jude to apologise before she died, but they never did” — Mr P
World.content:
Nigerian singer Peter “Mr P” Okoye has alleged that his late mother, Josephine Okoye, repeatedly urged his brothers, Paul and Jude Okoye, to apologise to him and his wife, Lola Omotayo-Okoye, over the family’s treatment of them, but said the apology never came before her death.

PREMIUM TIMES earlier reported that the singer’s mother died in 2012 at a hospital in India following heart surgery. Doctors initially admitted her to St. Nicholas Hospital on Lagos Island before transferring her abroad for further treatment.

Mr P made the claim in the latest instalment (part eight) of his ongoing tell-all video series on social media, where he has been revisiting the events that led to the collapse of P-Square and the strained relationship within the Okoye family.

The singer, who married Lola in 2013 after several years together, said his relationship with her was strongly opposed by Jude and, at times, Paul, long before their wedding. He alleged that the hostility continued even after the birth of their first child and persisted despite efforts by their late mother to reconcile the family.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Apology

According to Mr P, only his eldest brother apologised after his mother intervened, while Paul and Jude never did before she died in 2012.

The 44-year-old said, “While our mum was still around, she felt my pain. She said, ‘Don’t worry.’ When I was telling her everything, I said, ‘Mum, look at it this way: you thought you were telling me some good news, that the child is mine, but see how everyone left.’ She said, ‘No problem, I’ll talk to your brothers — they will apologise to you.’ I said, ‘No problem.’ My mum went back to Jos, and after about a week, she called me.

“She asked me, ‘Have they apologised?’ I said, ‘Only the first son, our firstborn, has apologised.’ She said, ‘Don’t worry, they will all apologise.’ After a few more weeks, Henry apologised too, except Paul and Jude, the ones I live with; they never did. One month, two months, three months, four months, five months, our mum died, and the apology was never made. My mum told them to do it, but they never did.”

Lola and Psquare’s mother’s relationship

Furthermore, the singer dismissed his brothers’ claims that their late mother never liked his wife.

He explained that his mother and Lola enjoyed a cordial relationship before her illness led to her hospitalisation in Lagos.

According to him, his mother had already accepted Lola and often referred to her as “our wife.”

“When our mum was sick in Jos, we flew her all the way to Lagos; we took her to St Nicholas Hospital on the Island, we live on the Mainland. Our mum was admitted, and four of her pastors came all the way from Jos to be with her. Guess where they stayed? Lola’s house. Lola got up as early as six o’clock every morning to make food for them, breakfast, everything. By seven o’clock, she would take them to the hospital and stay there. We lived on the Mainland so that we would arrive around eleven. When we came, Lola would leave for work.

“We stayed with our mum in the hospital with the pastors. By around six o’clock, Lola would leave work; her office wasn’t far from St Nicholas, and she would come back to the hospital. As soon as she arrived, we would leave. She stayed at the hospital until midnight, then took the pastors back to their house. The next morning, the same routine was repeated for over two months. During that time, in that hospital, they still tried to create a narrative that Lola and my mum never had a relationship, even though before I married Lola, my mum was already addressing her as ‘our wife’”, said Mr P.

Wedding

Mr P expressed concern that Jude was using his own twin brother as a pawn in what he described as his “evil games”, insisting that he had never been at odds with his brothers.

He also alleged that Jude scheduled a show for him in Ghana a day before his wedding to Lola.

According to him, despite personally giving Jude the fabric for the ceremony, Jude failed to attend the wedding.

“When I had my own wedding, my elder brother, our so-called manager, never attended. Let me tell you how bad it was: the night before my wedding, Jude booked a show with Globacom in Ghana, and showed me a return ticket for the next day, my wedding day, on a 2 o’clock flight. I said no, and insisted until they got us a private jet. I was at my own wedding. I was trending online for the wrong reason; Jude had posted a picture of himself at Mavin studio with Wizkid, Dr SID, Phyno, Don Jazzy and the rest of them.

“Jude posted that picture and started trending. Someone commented, something like, ‘You didn’t attend your brother’s wedding.’ He responded along the lines of, ‘If our mum were alive, this wedding wouldn’t have happened’, or something like that. And people said Jude was with Don Jazzy, Dr SID, Wizkid and Phyno, but all of them still left that studio and attended the wedding. My own senior brother, my manager, refused. I even arranged a barber for him and everything.”

Rudeboy responded to Mr P regarding their late mother’s legacy

Meanwhile, Rudeboy responded to Mr P’s claims about their mother. In a statement posted on his Instagram page, he said he regretted that their mother was no longer alive to defend herself.

He wrote, “Unfortunately, you’re not here to defend yourself and us. Continue resting, mum.”

As of the time of filing this report, Jude hasn’t responded to Mr P’s latest allegations.

The newspaper also reported that the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) investigated the dispute, leading to criminal charges against Jude over alleged money laundering involving about ₦1.38 billion, $1 million and £34,537.59.

Jude pleaded not guilty to the charges, and the case remains before the Federal High Court in Lagos.

During the court proceedings, Mr P testified for the prosecution, while Rudeboy publicly defended Jude, further exposing the rift within the family. The court initially remanded Jude in custody before later granting him bail.

Before P-Square split and the controversies that followed, the duo released several hit songs, including “Bizzy Body”, “Do Me”, “Personally”, “No One Like”, “You” and “Chop My Money”.

World.title: Tinubu’s reforms yielding results, GDP rises to $375bn — Yilwatda
World.content:
The National Chairman of the All Progressives Congress (APC), Nentawe Yilwatda, has defended President Bola Tinubu’s economic reforms, stating that Nigeria’s Gross Domestic Product (GDP) has risen from below $300 billion to about $375 billion in two years.

Mr Yilwatda made the claim on Thursday in Jos, Plateau State, while speaking at a colloquium organised to mark his 58th birthday.

He said the increase in GDP, which he attributed to the Tinubu administration’s economic policies, showed that the reforms were beginning to produce results despite the economic difficulties associated with their implementation.

According to him, Nigeria’s economic growth is now outpacing population growth, while improved investor confidence and increased exports are signs of a recovery in the productive sector.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“For the first time, our exports have exceeded our imports. Investors are returning to Nigeria because confidence has returned. The productive economy we have long desired is beginning to emerge,” Mr Yilwatda said.

The APC chairman said the administration’s investments in deep seaports, railways, highways and inland dry ports were intended to reduce the cost of doing business and expand Nigeria’s capacity to compete in regional and international trade.

He said the infrastructure projects would also support the federal government’s ambition of growing the Nigerian economy to $1 trillion.

“Every kilometre of road constructed represents increased commerce, improved security and accelerated economic development,” he said.

Mr Yilwatda described the reforms as a long-term economic restructuring programme rather than measures designed to produce immediate political gains.

“President Tinubu has a master plan. He is not building for today alone; he is building a future that our children and grandchildren will inherit,” he said.

Yilwatda links reforms to 2027

The APC chairman also linked the administration’s economic performance to the party’s prospects in the 2027 general elections.

Mr Yilwatda said he would mobilise support for Mr Tinubu’s re-election, describing himself as the president’s “chief campaigner.”

He expressed confidence that the APC would win the 2027 elections.

The remarks came against the backdrop of the APC administration’s controversial economic measures, including the removal of petrol subsidy and ongoing tax reforms, which have triggered significant economic adjustments and public debate.

Mutfwang backs $1 trillion target

Plateau State Governor Caleb Mutfwang, who delivered the keynote address, also referenced the Federal Government’s $1 trillion economic target.

Mr Mutfwang identified subsidy removal, tax restructuring and increased investment in infrastructure, agriculture, manufacturing and technology as some of the measures being pursued to achieve the target.

He, however, focused largely on Mr Yilwatda’s career, describing him as an academic, technocrat and administrator.

“Leadership is ultimately a sacred trust. It demands vision beyond personal ambition; history does not merely record titles; it remembers impact,” the governor said.

The governor’s participation in the event is notable because he recently defected from the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) to the APC, a move that has altered the political dynamics in Plateau State.

APC leadership commended

Imo State Governor Hope Uzodimma, represented by the Minister of Steel Development, Shuaibu Abubakar Audu, commended Mr Yilwatda for his leadership of the APC.

Mr Audu said the APC chairman had contributed to the expansion of the party’s membership and the conduct of its nationwide primaries with minimal disputes.

The national convener of the colloquium, Gaknung Seri, said the event was organised to examine Mr Yilwatda’s contributions to education, leadership and national development.

The event was attended by political leaders, academics, youths and other stakeholders.
