World.title: Former governor of Guerrero arrested on Ayotzinapa-related charges
World.content:
Federal authorities on Thursday announced the arrest of former Guerrero Governor Ángel Heladio Aguirre Rivero in connection with the 2014 abduction and presumed murder of 43 teachers college students.

Aguirre, governor of Guerrero from 2011 until his resignation in October 2014, was detained in México state on charges of concealment and/or destruction of evidence related to the whereabouts of the students, according to the Federal Attorney General’s Office (FGR).

“Ángel Aguirre”:

Porque fue detenido por su presunta participación en el ocultamiento de evidencias de Ayotzinapa pic.twitter.com/00qyDYyn1J — ¿Por qué es Tendencia? (@porktendencia) August 6, 2026

The FGR said on social media on Thursday morning that “as part of a new investigative model,” it carried out a reexamination of the September 2014 disappearance of 43 students from the Ayotzinapa Rural Teachers College in Guerrero. The students — all young men — disappeared in Iguala, Guerrero, on September 26, 2014, after the bus on which they were traveling to Mexico City was stopped by municipal and state police.

Police allegedly handed the students over to members of Guerreros Unidos, a crime gang.

The FGR said that “new acts of investigation” allowed it to “confirm the possible participation” of Aguirre, a Democratic Revolution Party governor, “in the concealment of evidence” related to the whereabouts of the students.

Consequently, a warrant for the arrest of the ex-governor was “requested, obtained and executed,” the FGR said on Thursday morning.

The FGR subsequently released a statement from Attorney General Ernestina Godoy, who said that the FGR has evidence that Aguirre ordered the concealment of video footage that showed the bus on which the students were traveling at the time it was stopped by police.

“On the night of September 26, 2014, the ‘Estrella de Oro’ bus number 1531, on which the group of teacher-training students was traveling, was captured on video by security cameras 12 and 15, located outside the State Palace of Justice in Iguala, at the time it was stopped by municipal and state police officers,” Godoy said.

“The first official statements claimed that the material in question did not exist due to alleged technical failures in the [security camera] system. However, subsequent investigations confirmed that this claim was false,” she said.

Godoy said that in January, a cooperating witness provided testimony that “confirmed the existence of the video recordings.” That witness, the attorney general said, identified the person who “removed” the recordings in order to “deliver them directly” to Aguirre.

Godoy said that the witness also provided information about threats they had received, which “explained their previous silence.”

The attorney general said that in May, “a second protected witness strengthened said testimony” by declaring that Aguirre “ordered, in a meeting with top officials from his government,” the concealment of “any evidence related to the events that occurred in the vicinity of the Iguala Palace of Justice.”

“The Attorney General’s Office has evidence that confirms that said instruction of concealment was issued directly by the then governor, with the participation of high-level state public servants,” Godoy said.

Near the start of her statement, the attorney general said that a reexamination of the Ayotzinapa case “confirmed with full evidence and adherence to due process the possible participation of Ángel ‘N,’ ex-governor of the state of Guerrero, in the destruction of evidence [needed] to determine the whereabouts of the students.”

Godoy said that Aguirre was arrested on Thursday in México state, but didn’t specify exactly where he was taken into custody. However, according to the National Arrests Register, the ex-governor was detained on Thursday morning in Tepotzotlán, a México state municipality north of Mexico City. He was subsequently transferred to the Altiplano federal prison in Almoloya de Juárez, México state.

The arrest of Aguirre is one of the most prominent detentions in connection with the Ayotzinapa case, which sparked outrage in Mexico and around the world, and triggered large protests in Mexico City and across the country.

In a 2023 report, the previous federal government led by former President Andrés Manuel López Obrador outlined three “possible reasons” for the abduction of the students, one of which was “the possible presence of drugs, weapons or money” on buses Ayotzinapa students had commandeered to travel to a protest in Mexico City.

The disappearance of the 43 young men — a “crime of the state,” according to a top official in the previous federal government — was a major blight on the 2012-18 presidency of Enrique Peña Nieto, but he survived widespread calls for his removal from office. The remains of just three students have been found.

Scores of people have been arrested in connection with the case, but no has been convicted of the crime and some suspects have been released from prison. Among those who have been detained are soldiers and high-ranking members of the Mexican Army, police officers, Guerreros Unidos members and Jesús Murillo Karam, federal attorney general at the time of the students’ disappearance.

Murillo was detained in 2022 on charges of forced disappearance, torture and obstruction of justice in connection with the Aytozinapa case. He was released from prison in 2024 after a judge ruled he could await trial under house arrest. The 78-year-old former attorney general suffered a stroke in April.

With reports from La Jornada and AP

World.title: Vatican envoy prays for Mexico’s missing at CDMX Basilica Mass
World.content:
Vatican Secretary of State Cardinal Pietro Parolin, who’s in Mexico as part of a multi-day official visit that began on Tuesday, presided a Mass at the Basilica of Our Lady of Guadalupe in Mexico City, where he called for prayers for missing persons and “searching mothers.”

After reading a few passages from the Bible regarding the miracles of the Virgin Mary and concern for one’s neighbor, Pietro spoke of the arduous search undertaken by mothers with a missing loved one.

En Palacio Nacional, recibí al secretario de Estado del Vaticano, Pietro Parolin; abordamos temas como la primera encíclica del papa León XIV, Magnifica Humanitas, donde plantea que el desarrollo de la inteligencia artificial debe estar guiado por criterios éticos, dignidad… pic.twitter.com/HU7yc9S9Zp — Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo (@Claudiashein) August 5, 2026

“Their example resonates with particular force here in Mexico, where so many mothers continue to search for their missing children with steadfastness and faith,” he said, calling upon the faithful to support them with solidarity and prayer.

During his homily, Parolin noted that too many communities are “scarred by violence and aggression” and that a significant number of families have experienced the pain of loss. He urged that prayer be translated into concrete actions of solidarity with victims, migrants, and marginalized groups.

The Mass followed a one-hour meeting between Pietro and President Claudia Sheinbaum, during which both officials discussed the formal invitation for Pope Leo XIV to visit Mexico.

Sheinbaum reiterated her invitation for the pope to visit the country at her Wednesday morning press conference, saying, “We’re going to insist on the visit of the pope to Mexico.”

The meeting also addressed the challenges posed by artificial intelligence in light of Pope Leo XIV’s latest encyclical Dilexi Te.

“The Pope’s calls for peace, fraternity, and closeness to the most vulnerable represent a humanitarian vision—one that is indispensable at a time when the world needs to strengthen dialogue, solidarity, and cooperation among nations,” Sheinbaum wrote on her official X account along with a picture of the meeting.

The message of the pope’s emissary carries significant weight in Mexico, the country with the second-highest Catholic population in the world after Brazil. Nearly 80% of Mexico’s population (101.3 million people) identify as Roman Catholic.

Pietro’s statement comes as Mexico continues to confront a disappearance crisis, with over 132,000 people officially listed as missing or unaccounted for, and mothers and relatives often leading the search themselves.

With reports from El Universal and Vatican News

World.title: Reward for CJNG’s new leader jumps to $25 million after ‘El Mencho’s’ death
World.content:
The U.S. government on Wednesday raised from US $5 million to $25 million the maximum reward it is offering for information leading to the arrest of Juan Carlos Valencia González, the alleged new leader of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG).

The U.S. State Department announced the higher bounty as part of reward offers totaling up to $102 million “for information leading to the arrests and/or convictions, in any country, of eight leaders and associates” of the CJNG, one of eight Mexican criminal organizations that have been designated as foreign terrorist organizations (FTOs) by the U.S. government. All of the eight people — seven men and one woman — face criminal charges in the United States.

“The reward offers include up to $25 million (an increase from up to $5 million) for Juan Carlos Valencia González, aka ‘Pelón,’ the new leader of CJNG following the recent death of his stepfather, CJNG founder Nemesio Rubén Oseguera Cervantes, aka ‘El Mencho,'” the State Department said in a statement titled “Degrading CJNG: Announcing over $100 Million in Reward Offers and Visa Restrictions.”

Oseguera, the founder of the CJNG and longtime leader of the powerful cartel, was fatally wounded by soldiers during a military operation in Tapalpa, Jalisco, on Feb. 22.

His 41-year-old stepson — a California native who is also known as “El R3,” among other aliases — was subsequently identified in media reports as a leading contender to become the new leader of the CJGN.

According to an online Department of State wanted poster, Valencia González was charged in October 2020 in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia with “conspiracy to distribute a controlled substance for purpose of unlawful importation into the United States and use of a firearm during a narcotics transaction.”

US raises reward for a suspect already in custody

The U.S. State Department announced a reward of up to $15 million — an increase from up to $5 million — for the conviction of Audias Flores Silva, aka “El Jardinero” (The Gardener), who was detained by the Mexican Navy in Nayarit in April.

Prior to his capture, the 45-year-old Michoacán native was a “regional commander” of the CJNG, according to the State Department.

“In addition to his narco-trafficking activities, Flores Silva is the alleged leader of CJNG’s timeshare fraud operations in Nayarit, including a major operation centered around the Kovay Gardens resort targeting vulnerable Americans,” the State Department said in an online poster.

“… The U.S. Department of State is offering a reward increase of up to $15 million for information leading to the conviction of Flores Silva,” the State Department said.

Rewards of $2 million to $15 million for 6 other suspects

The State Department said it is also offering a reward of up to $15 million for information leading to the arrest and/or conviction of Gonzalo Mendoza Gaytán, aka “El Sapo” (The Toad), who is said to be a godson of Oseguera.

Mendoza is a “senior leader” of the CJNG and “controls most of the cartel’s operations in Jalisco,” according to the State Department. The 37-year-old Michoacán native was also mentioned in media reports as a possible successor to “El Mencho.”

The State Department is also offering a reward of up to $15 million for information leading to the capture and/or conviction of Julio Alberto Castillo Rodríguez, a son-in-law of the now-deceased Oseguera.

Castillo, known as “Chorro” and “Ojo de Vidrio” (Glass Eye), is a “senior member” of the CJNG and runs the cartel’s “daily operations in Colima, including by exercising control over parts of the port of Manzanillo, one of Mexico’s busiest ports,” according to the State Department. The 49-year-old is also a native of Michoacán, the state where “El Mencho” was born.

The State Department is offering rewards of up to $10 million each for Ricardo Ruiz Velasco, aka “Tripa” and “Doble R”; Julio César Montero Pinzón, aka “El Tarjetas”; and Carlos Andrés Rivera Varela, aka “La Firma.”

Ruiz, who was also mentioned in media reports as a possible successor to Oseguera, is a senior CJNG “lieutenant” and “leader of ‘Grupo Élite,’ a CJNG paramilitary group known for its extreme violence,” according to the State Department.

Montero is an “alleged high-ranking leader” of the CJNG who “allegedly directed an international complex fraud scheme targeting Americans who own timeshare properties in Mexico.”

Rivera, a native of Colombia, is “an alleged high-ranking leader” of the CJNG who also “allegedly directed an international complex fraud scheme targeting Americans who own timeshare properties in Mexico,” according to the State Department.

The State Department is offering a reward of up to $2 million for information leading to the arrest and/or conviction of Griselda Margarita Arredondo Pinzón, an “alleged high-ranking financial operator” for the CJNG. She is Montero’s half-sister, according to U.S authorities.

State Department announces US visa restrictions on relatives and associates of people linked to CJNG

In the same statement, the State Department announced that it was “imposing visa restrictions on 65 individuals who are family members or close personal or business associates of persons linked to CJNG” and who have been sanctioned under Executive Order 14059: Imposing Sanctions on Foreign Persons Involved in the Global Illicit Drug Trade.

It said that 26 of those individuals “had existing visas, which have now been revoked.”

“Since announcing this visa restriction policy in June 2025, a total of 93 visas have been revoked from family members and associates of sanctioned drug traffickers connected to FTO-designated cartels,” the State Department said.

“Under President Trump and Secretary Rubio’s leadership, violent cartel operatives and their criminal facilitators are no longer able to enter our country and terrorize the American people.”

Secretary of State Marco Rubio took to social media on Wednesday to tout the new rewards and visa restrictions.

“The United States is hunting down, dismantling, and destroying Cártel de Jalisco Nueva Generación,” he wrote on X.

U.S. Ambassador to Mexico Ron Johnson shared Rubio’s X post, writing above it:

“The pressure on the cartels and narcoterrorist organizations continues. … Under the leadership of @POTUS @realDonaldTrump, working alongside Mexican authorities, we are dismantling cartel leadership and holding accountable those who traffic deadly narcotics, such as fentanyl, and spread violence.”

The pressure on the cartels and narcoterrorist organizations continues. The United States announced criminal charges targeting senior CJNG leaders and more than $100 million in rewards for information leading to their capture. Under the leadership of @POTUS @realDonaldTrump,… https://t.co/2rfbMleFpT — Embajador Ronald Johnson (@USAmbMex) August 5, 2026

A blow to the CJNG in Spain

Separately, the National Police of Spain (CNP) announced on Wednesday that its agents, in a joint operation with the French Anti-Narcotics Office OFAST, had “broken up a branch of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) allegedly dedicated to the international trafficking of methamphetamine, and dismantled all its logistics infrastructure in Spain, including a clandestine laboratory.”

Thirteen people who allegedly belong to the criminal group were detained in operations in the cities of Lleida, Barcelona and Tarragona. Seven Mexicans, four Spaniards and two Colombians were arrested in the three cities, all of which are located in the Catalonia region of northeastern Spain.

The CNP said that the CJNG cell allegedly brought into Spain from Mexico “2.5 tonnes of methamphetamine camouflaged in approximately 12 tonnes of liquid vanilla flavoring.”

The confiscation of the meth was “one of the largest seizures” ever in Spain and Europe, the CNP said.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: How Guanajuato set the stage for Mexico’s independence from Spain
World.content:
The state of Guanajuato brings local and foreign tourists alike interested in exploring famous colonial towns and unique nature. But behind the manicured streets of San Miguel de Allende and Guanajuato City lie some of the most important stories in Mexican history.

On Sept. 28, 1810, Miguel Hidalgo y Castillo marched into Guanajuato with a ragtag army of tens of thousands at his back, kicking off the Mexican War of Independence. But why did it start here?

Just 12 days earlier in the town of Dolores, located approximately 60 kilometers from the capital city, Hidalgo issued his famous cry. The priest was fed up with Spanish colonial rule, which had conquered Mexico nearly 300 years prior. The cry was an urge to the people of Hidalgo’s congregation. He was pleading with them to revolt against the Spanish, and called his parish to arms.

The speech worked, and days later Hidalgo was the commander of an unofficial, untrained and unruly army, tens of thousands of soldiers strong. They were peasants, laborers and the poor. They had little equipment and even less training, but they had numbers.

The peasant army marched from Dolores to San Miguel de Allende and down to Celaya, where they looted and sacked Spanish homes, bringing more Indigenous and Creole people into their ranks.

Hidalgo’s forces reached Guanajuato with little resistance. Juan Antonio Riaño, the Spanish intendant of Guanajuato, chose to fight instead of surrendering the city. Riaño barricaded himself in the Alhóndiga de Granaditas, a massive, fortified stone structure made for storing grain.

Riaño’s force of around 400 men was greatly outnumbered. Spanish families moved into the granary, their wealth and belongings in tow, hoping to find shelter from the revolutionary horde. However, Riaño’s decision to only shelter Spanish families angered the local population in Guanajuato, who rallied behind Hidalgo.

With a massive force now ranging from 20,000 to 50,000 men, Hidalgo began the siege. He ordered his men to charge the gates of the fortress, where they took heavy losses but began to pound the front gate.

Riaño, now sensing defeat, tried to leave with a group of soldiers, but was shot and killed instantly. Riaño was previously a close friend of Hidalgo, who even wrote to Riaño before the siege to offer protection of him and his family, but the Spaniard had rejected — a decision which cost him his life.

The Spanish, however, still had one trick up their sleeve. They fitted a rifle with a white flag and waved it from the roof of the granary, signaling surrender. But as the rebellious forces began to drop their guard and approach the gates, the order was rescinded and the Spanish gunned down the unsuspecting soldiers.

It was too little too late, however, as the fortress was breached by insurgent soldier Juan José de los Reyes Martínez Amaro, the unlikeliest of heroes. A local miner — whose appearance, according to legend, resembled a turkey or guajolote, giving rise to the nickname “El Pípila” — strapped a large stone to his back and approached the gate with tar and a torch. The stone shielded him from gunfire, and he was able to burn through the door.

El Pípila’s statue now stands high above the city at Guanajuato’s famous viewpoint. He is honored for his bravery and as a hero of the city.

With the gate open, Hidalgo’s forces flew inside and mercilessly slaughtered the Spanish, including the huddled families who entered the granary seeking shelter. Their wealth was pillaged and the violence spread into the streets, where the resistance army spent days destroying Spanish and Creole homes and stealing their possessions. Over 3,000 insurgents were killed during the siege and the ensuing violence, along with hundreds of Spanish in the granary.

The attack on Guanajuato was brutal, but the rebels had won the first battle of the War of Independence. Hidalgo continued to lead his forces through the Bajío, and the battle set the stage for Mexican victory, with the Spanish abandoning the country in 1821.

The bullet holes from the siege are still riddled throughout the walls of the granary. They serve as both a reminder of the fight that led to a free Mexico and a monument to the lives lost from war.

World.title: Mexico in Numbers: The peso’s wildest swings since 2000
World.content:
Anyone who has been living in or visiting Mexico for an extended period of time knows that at certain times this century, one US dollar bought significantly fewer Mexican pesos than it does today.

I’m talking about 25 years ago, 20 years ago, 15 years ago.

I’m not talking about 10 years ago, when the greenback rose above 20 to the peso, or six years ago, when the USD:MXN exchange rate exceeded 25 at the onset of the COVID pandemic.

At the close of trading on Aug. 5 (i.e. yesterday), one US dollar was worth 17.24 Mexican pesos, according to the Bank of Mexico. That puts the current USD:MXN exchange rate more or less on par with the prevailing rates in December 2015 and June 2023.

This “Mexico in Numbers” article will show you how the USD:MXN exchange rate has changed this century. The aim is not to examine in depth why the rate has changed over the past 25 years, although I do mention a few factors that have caused the peso to appreciate or depreciate at different times this century.

Before we look closely at the USD:MXN exchange rate fluctuations since Jan. 1, 2001, here are two key numbers relevant to our topic.

* N.B. — All of the USD:MXN exchange rate data in this article comes from the Bank of Mexico (Banxico). Exchange rate data from 1954 to 2026 can be downloaded from the central bank’s website.

25.12

This is the highest USD:MXN exchange rate this century, and indeed of all time. This was the prevailing rate on March 24, 2020 — 13 days after the World Health Organization declared the COVID-19 outbreak a pandemic.

8.94

This is the lowest USD:MXN exchange rate this century. This was the prevailing rate on May 21, 2001 — 113 days before two planes crashed into the Twin Towers in New York City.

Changes in the USD:MXN exchange rate this century

For each of the five-year intervals that appear below, I note the prevailing USD:MXN exchange rates on the first trading day of each year and on June 30 (or on the closest trading day to that date). I also highlight the highest and lowest exchange rates in each period.

2001-2005: The peso weakens almost 9%

The Mexican peso traded at 9.71 to the US dollar on Jan. 2, 2001, the second calendar day of this century. On June 29, 2001, the USD:MXN exchange rate was 9.07. Just over a month earlier, as noted above, the peso traded at 8.94 to the greenback, its strongest position this century.

On Jan. 2, 2002, the USD:MXN exchange rate was 9.10, while on July 1 of that year it was 9.92. On September 4, 2002, the USD:MXN exchange rate went above 10 for the first time this century. The peso previously traded at more than 10 to the dollar in 1998 and early 1999.

On Jan. 2, 2003, the peso traded 10.36 to the dollar, while on June 30 of that year the USD:MXN rate was 10.43.

On Jan. 2, 2004, the USD:MXN rate was 11.08, while on June 30 of that year it was 11.52. The USD:MXN exchange rate reached its highest point of the 2001-2005 period on May 10, 2004, when one greenback bought 11.63 pesos.

On Jan. 3, 2005, one US dollar was worth 11.20 pesos, while the USD:MXN rate was 10.77 on June 30 of that year and 10.63 on Dec. 30.

Thus, the peso depreciated 92 centavos, or around 8.7%, against the US dollar between Jan. 1, 2001 and Dec. 30, 2005. The peso’s weakest point in the period (11.63 to the dollar) represented a 23.1% depreciation compared to its strongest point (8.94).

2006-2010: The pace of peso depreciation quickens

The USD:MXN exchange rate on Jan. 2, 2006, was 10.62, while on June 30 it was 11.27.

On the first trading day of 2007 — Jan. 2 — one US dollar bought 10.78 pesos, while a greenback purchased 10.79 pesos on June 29 of that year.

On Jan. 2, 2008, the peso traded at 10.89 to the dollar, while on June 30 of that year the Mexican currency was stronger at 10.30 to the greenback. On Aug. 5, 2008, the peso reached its strongest position of the 2006-10 period, trading at 9.91 to the dollar.

On Jan. 2, 2009, the peso traded at a much weaker 13.76 to the dollar and exactly two months later, on March 2 , the currency fell to its weakest point of the 2006-10 period — 15.36 to the dollar at a time when the global financial crisis had taken a heavy toll on the Mexican currency. By June 30, 2009, the peso had significantly recovered to trade at 13.17 to the dollar.

On the first trading day of 2010 — Jan. 4 — the peso was even stronger at 12.92 to the dollar. The USD:MXN exchange rate was 12.84 on June 30, 2010, and 12.34 on Dec. 31 of that year.

The peso depreciated 13.9% between Jan. 2, 2006 and December 31, 2010. The peso’s weakest point in the period (15.36 to the dollar) represented a 55% depreciation compared to its strongest point (9.91). That wild swing occurred in the space of just seven months.

2011-2015: The pace of peso depreciation quickens again, doubling to almost 30%

On Jan. 3, 2011, the USD:MXN exchange rate was 12.25, while on June 30 of that year it was 11.72. The peso’s strongest point in this five-year period was a rate of 11.50 to the greenback on May 2, 2011.

On the first trading day of 2012 — Jan. 2 — the peso traded at 13.93 to the greenback, whereas on June 29 the USD:MXN rate was 13.40

On Jan. 2, 2013, the peso was stronger at 12.74 to the greenback, while on July 1 of that year it traded at 12.91 to the dollar.

On Jan. 2, 2014, one greenback bought 13.10 pesos, while on June 30 the peso was slightly stronger at 12.97 to the dollar.

On the first trading day of 2015 — Jan. 2 — the USD:MXN rate was 14.82, while the dollar was significantly stronger on June 30 of that year, buying 15.68 pesos. The greenback continued strengthening in the second half of 2015, reaching its strongest point of the 2011-15 period on Dec. 14, when it bought 17.37 pesos.

A week before the peso tumbled to that point, Reuters reported that the Mexican currency had fallen to “a more than two-month low” as crude oil prices hovered near 7-year lows. Then-Bank of Mexico Governor Agustín Carstens said at the time that global volatility could continue to hit the peso in December 2015. And Carstens was right — the peso depreciated further from the 16.90 rate on Dec. 7, 2015, the date on which his remarks to Reuters were published.

In the five years between January 2011 and December 31, 2015 — when the USD:MXN rate was 17.24 — the peso depreciated 28.9%. The peso’s weakest point in the period (17.37 to the dollar) represented a 33.8% depreciation compared to its strongest point (11.50).

2016-2020: Pandemic drags peso down to its weakest level ever

On Jan. 4, 2016, the USD: MXN exchange rate was 17.35, while on June 30, one greenback bought 18.46 pesos.

On April 29, 2016, the peso traded at its strongest level in the 2016-2020 period — 17.17 to the greenback. However, later in 2016 — on Nov. 10 to be exact — the peso traded above 20 to the dollar for the first time ever. The peso’s depreciation to above 20 to the dollar came two days after Donald Trump won the 2016 presidential election.

On Nov. 10, 2016, Reuters reported that the Mexican peso had sunk again, “taking its biggest two-day tumble in more than 20 years as investors worried about how U.S. president-elect Donald Trump’s policies could hit exports from Latin America’s second largest economy.”

Earlier in 2016, as the peso approached 20 to the dollar, memes appeared showing the Mexican 20-peso banknote with the words “new one-dollar bill” superimposed on it.

On the first trading day of 2017 — Jan. 2 — the peso was still above 20 to the dollar, with the USD:MXN rate at 20.73. On June 30 of that year, the peso was significantly stronger at 18.06 to the greenback.

On Jan. 2, 2018, the USD:MXN exchange rate was 19.48, while on June 30 of that year it was 19.69.

On Jan. 2, 2019, one greenback bought 19.58 pesos while on July 1 of that year a dollar purchased 19.07 pesos.

On the first trading day of 2020 — Jan. 2 — the peso traded at 18.88 to the dollar, while on June 30 it was significantly weaker at 23.08 to the greenback.

As noted at the start of this article, the peso depreciated to its weakest level ever — 25.12 to the dollar — on March 24, 2020, at the onset of the COVID pandemic.

On March 23, 2020, Mexico News Daily reported that the peso had fallen to “a new record low” against the US dollar “as the coronavirus pandemic continues to take a heavy toll on economies around the world.”

At the time, MND reported: “The financial group Monex said that the peso is facing ‘considerable stress’ due to the economic impact of COVID-19 around the world. As the pandemic worsens, investors have rushed to free themselves of high-risk currencies, such as the peso, in favor of the US dollar, which is regarded as the ultimate safe-haven currency.”

By the end of 2020, the peso had substantially recovered, trading at 19.90 to the dollar on Dec. 31.

Between January 2016 and December 2020, the peso depreciated 12.8%. The peso’s weakest point in the period (25.12 to the dollar) represented a 31.6% depreciation compared to its strongest point (17.17).

2021-2025: The value of the peso against the dollar goes up, not down!

On Jan. 4, 2021 — the first trading day of this decade — the USD:MXN exchange rate was 19.84, while on June 30 of that year one dollar bought 19.90 pesos. Later in the year, on Nov. 26, the peso depreciated to its weakest level in the 2021-25 period — 21.82 to the greenback.

By the end of 2021, the peso had recovered somewhat to trade at 20.46 on Dec. 31. On that date, Reuters reported that the peso had gained “to above one-month highs … amid fewer concerns about the economic impact of a rise in coronavirus infections.”

Three days later, on Jan. 3, 2022, the peso traded at 20.58 to the dollar, while the USD:MXN exchange rate on June 30 of that year was 20.13.

On the first trading day of 2023 — Jan 2. — the peso traded at 19.48 to the greenback, an appreciation of over 3% for the Mexican currency compared to six months earlier. On June 30, 2023, the peso was significantly stronger again at 17.13 to the dollar.

At various times later in the year, the peso traded at below 17 to the dollar. MND reported on July 12, 2023, that the peso had “strengthened to 16.82 to the US dollar … on the back of data that showed that annual inflation in the United States slowed to 3% in June [of that year], its lowest level in over two years.”

On the first trading day of 2024, the peso was back above 17 to the dollar, but only just. On Jan. 2 of that year, the peso traded at 17.02 to the dollar, while on July 1, 2024, the USD:MXN rate was 18.38.

On April 8, 2024 — the day that a total solar eclipse mesmerized millions across Mexico — the peso appreciated to its strongest point of the 2021-2025 period, trading at 16.33 to the greenback. On that day, MND reported that the peso had “continued its hot streak…, appreciating to its strongest level against the dollar in almost nine years.”

At the time, Banco Base’s director of economic analysis, Gabriela Siller, attributed the appreciation of the peso to three factors: the inflow to Mexico of foreign currencies from exports, remittances and foreign direct investment; the “expectation” that the wide gap between interest rates in Mexico and the United States (11% in the former vs. 5.25%-5.50% in the latter at the time) would “attract capital to Mexico”; and the “expectation” that nearshoring would “attract waves of dollars” to Mexico.”

By the time the first trading day of 2025 rolled around, the peso was significantly weaker, trading at 20.69 to the greenback on Jan. 2 of that year. On June 30, 2025, the peso was stronger at 18.83 to the dollar, while the currency finished the year at 18.00 to the greenback on Dec. 31.

Between January 2021 and the end of 2025, the peso appreciated 10.2% against the dollar. Of the five-year periods considered in this article — five in total — the 2021-2025 interval was the only one in which the peso appreciated against the dollar. In addition, it was the only interval in which the peso’s strongest position came after its weakest position. The peso’s strongest point in the period (16.33 to the dollar in April 2024) represented a 33.6% appreciation compared to its weakest point (21.82 in November 2021).

2026: The peso continues to strengthen

Compared to the Bank of Mexico’s closing rate on Dec. 31, 2025 of 18.00 Mexican pesos to the dollar, the peso has appreciated 4.4% this year, based on the 17.24 closing rate on Aug. 5.

The El Economista newspaper reported on Wednesday, Aug. 5, that the appreciation of the peso, after closing at 17.26 on Aug. 4, was “supported by a greater appetite for risk” as currency traders remained “attentive to news about a possible [peace] agreement in the Middle East,” where the United States and Iran have been at war since late February.

Key numerical takeaways from the changes in the USD:MXN exchange rate this century

Between Dec. 29, 2000 and Aug. 5, 2026 — this century, in other words — the Mexican peso depreciated 44.3%.

Put differently, the US dollar appreciated 79.6% between the end of 2000 and Aug. 5, 2026.

The difference between the highest USD:MXN rate this century (25.12) and the lowest (8.94) is 16.18 pesos.

Between May 21, 2001, the day the USD:MXN rate was 8.94, and March 24, 2020, the day that the USD:MXN rate was 25.12, the peso depreciated 64.4%.

The appreciation of the US dollar between May 21, 2001 and March 24, 2020, was 181%.

By Mexico News Daily chief staff writer Peter Davies (peter.davies@mexiconewsdaily.com)

World.title: Dozens of UK cyclosporiasis victims had vacationed at Riviera Maya resorts
World.content:
Mexico is tightening health surveillance at more than a dozen hotels in Cancún and the Riviera Maya after the United Kingdom reported dozens of cases of cyclosporiasis in travelers, most of whom had recently stayed at all‑inclusive resorts in the state of Quintana Roo.

At the same time, Mexican officials are saying the country is not facing a domestic outbreak, nor has it been identified as the source of more than 10,000 laboratory-confirmed cyclosporiasis cases reported in the U.S. and 67 infections in British travelers.

Mensaje del secretario de Salud, David Kershenobich: Es importante mencionar que los casos de ciclosporiasis que existen actualmente en México representan el 0.00002% de la población, lo que significa que no tenemos un brote activo. pic.twitter.com/UN0wC6qmcH — SALUD México (@SSalud_mx) August 6, 2026

The Health Ministry has confirmed 33 cases of cyclosporiasis in 13 Mexican states between May 25 and July 31 and opened investigations into possible links with U.S. and U.K. infection reports.

Health Minister David Kershenobich said in a video posted Thursday that detected cases represent just 0.00002% of Mexico’s population. He also stressed that Cyclospora cayetanensis infections “are recurrent worldwide” and that there is no scientific evidence to date that Mexico is the origin of the outbreak.

The ministry, working with the Federal Commission for Protection against Sanitary Risks (Cofepris) and the General Directorate of Epidemiology (DGE), has deployed five inspection teams to 16 hotels in Quintana Roo.

The inspections follows a July 30 UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) alert reporting 67 cyclosporiasis cases between April 30 and July 15, with 48 of 51 patients who provided travel information reporting trips to Mexico — mainly to the Riviera Maya and Cancún.

UKHSA said the affected travelers stayed in “a range of different hotels” and consumed varied food and drink in all‑inclusive packages — emphasizing that investigations have not identified any single hotel or product as the source.

In response, Mexican inspectors conducted field visits this week in Quintana Roo during which they collected samples of food, water, fruits and vegetables, according to a Ministry of Health press release.

Laboratory analyses are still in process and authorities say results will be released when testing is complete.

Meanwhile, Mexican authorities are cooperating with U.S. counterparts on a multistate outbreak that officials say has sickened more than 10,000 people and is linked to shredded iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms de Mexico, grown in the central state of Guanajuato and distributed to Taco Bell and other outlets.

Product testing has not yielded any confirmed positive samples, though inspections are ongoing.

In tourist zones in Quintana Roo and elsewhere, Mexico’s Health Ministry has expanded surveillance, reinforced food safety protocols and reminded travelers and residents to wash and disinfect fruits and vegetables, drink potable water and seek medical attention for persistent diarrhea, especially after travel.

Officials also stress that identifying a country as a preliminary origin of a product under investigation “does not, in itself, constitute evidence that the contamination occurred in that place,” and say epidemiological work will continue until conclusive findings are available.

Cyclosporiasis is an intestinal infection usually acquired by eating or drinking contaminated food or water. Symptoms include watery “explosive diarrhea,” stomach cramps, nausea, loss of appetite, fatigue and low‑grade fever.

The 33 patients diagnosed in Mexico remain under observation; no deaths linked to the infection have been reported in Mexico.

With reports from El País, Infobae La Silla Rota and El Heraldo de México

—NNPC listing President Bola Tinubu said on Thursday that Nigeria’s state oil company will be reformed and listed on the Nigerian Exchange, without setting a date. —Market surge Nigeria’s market value has risen from about 30 trillion naira in 2023 to roughly 160 trillion, with the main index up from 52,000 to 244,000. —Pension money South Africa’s SA-H2 hydrogen fund closed a first round of 3 billion rand, backed by the pension fund of government employees. —Fuel prices Dangote cut its depot price of petrol to 1,165 naira a litre from 1,215, though filling stations have kept their old rates. —Namibia’s terms Namibia is seeking about 250 million dollars for industrial decarbonisation, insisting on processing lithium and rare earths at home. —A memorial Burkina Faso has budgeted 117 billion CFA francs for a memorial to the revolutionary leader Thomas Sankara.

An oil company, a pension fund, a hospital chain and the memory of a dead revolutionary all acquired a figure this week.

Nigeria – The State Takes Its Oil Company to Market

A promise made in the villa

President Bola Tinubu told the leadership of the Nigerian Exchange on Thursday that the state oil company will be reformed and listed on the market. He offered no timetable, which makes this a commitment rather than a plan.

The exchange had just presented him with its own scorecard. The market’s value has climbed from about 30 trillion naira in 2023 to roughly 160 trillion, and the main index from 52,000 points to 244,000.

Confidence upstairs, doubt at the pump

The mood in Abuja is that of a country that has decided it is investable again, willing to sell shares in the thing it once guarded most jealously. Tinubu tied the argument back to his early support for the Dangote refinery, casting private money as the engine rather than the guest.

Ordinary Nigerians spent the same day watching a different signal. Dangote cut its depot price of petrol to 1,165 naira a litre and diesel to 1,570, and filling stations simply kept charging the old rates.

Angola – The Exhale

Prices finally slow

Angola is approaching single-digit inflation for the first time in decades, and its central bank has begun cutting rates. For a country that spent a generation outrunning its own prices, that is less a data point than permission to stand still.

The national feeling is one of cautious relief rather than celebration. Angolans have seen disinflation promised before.

Courted for a railway

Luanda is also being courted, because its coastline is where a railway meets the sea. The Lobito corridor carries copper and cobalt from Congo and Zambia to Angolan ports, and it is the infrastructure Washington has backed most heavily on the continent.

American and Angolan naval commanders met in Rabat last month to discuss modernising that capability. Nothing was signed, and the relationship remains long on frameworks and short on hardware.

South Africa – Thoroughness Without Joy

Civil servants buy into hydrogen

The SA-H2 fund closed its first round at 3 billion rand, about 182 million dollars, on Thursday. Among the five backers is the Public Investment Corporation, investing on behalf of the pension fund of government employees.

The others are the European Commission through its Global Gateway strategy, the Dutch state investor Invest International, Sanlam and the Industrial Development Corporation. The fund is aiming for 12 billion rand by the middle of 2028.

A country doing the paperwork

Twenty million dollars has already gone to a green ammonia project at Coega in the Eastern Cape, and up to four million to a fuels producer in Gauteng. South Africa is turning ports, minerals and sunlight into an industrial argument, one committed rand at a time.

The temper is the same grim competence it showed a day earlier, sending its own police commanders towards prosecution. This is a country doing correct things without appearing to enjoy any of them.

Morocco – The Composed Transaction

Gulf money buys a stake

The private hospital group AKDITAL is opening 15% of its international holding to Arab Invest, a Saudi-based investor. It is a Moroccan company selling part of its expansion abroad to Gulf capital.

Separately, Saham Bank has launched a 500 million dirham programme to overhaul the lender. Two deals in one day, in two different industries.

Neither eager nor anxious

Morocco spent a decade making itself investable, through finance-centre rules, ports and energy contracts. The mood now is neither eager nor anxious but simply businesslike, a country that has stopped explaining itself to investors.

The buyers are increasingly from the Gulf rather than Europe. That shift is quiet, and it is the part worth watching.

An oil company, a pension fund, a hospital group and the memory of a dead revolutionary all acquired a number this week — the clearest sign yet of a continent that has stopped asking what it is worth and started saying it.

Namibia – Impatient Dignity

Terms, not just money

Namibia is chasing about 250 million dollars for industrial decarbonisation, having been chosen for a billion-dollar global programme aimed at hard-to-abate industries. Its stated priority is processing lithium and rare earths at home rather than shipping them out raw.

The country’s position is blunt and often repeated. It does not want to merely export raw materials, it wants to industrialise.

A small country setting conditions

That insistence sits inside a wider financing structure built with Dutch and European partners, including a fund targeting around a billion euros. The same Dutch managers appear in South Africa’s hydrogen vehicle, which tells you the machine is regional rather than national.

There is an awkward detail underneath. The official who framed Namibia’s hydrogen ambition left last November and now works for a German engineering group that sells electrolysers into exactly this market.

Burkina Faso – A Price on Self-Reliance

117 billion francs for a memory

Burkina Faso has budgeted 117 billion CFA francs for a memorial to Thomas Sankara, the revolutionary president killed in 1987. That is roughly 190 million dollars committed to remembrance.

Sankara is remembered above all for preaching that his country should owe nobody anything. The government is spending heavily to honour a man whose central argument was frugality.

Reverence as policy

The mood in Ouagadougou is reverent and defiant at once, using the past to explain the present. A military government leaning on a revolutionary’s memory is making an argument about legitimacy, not history.

It is the sharpest counterpoint on the continent today. Everywhere else states are selling stakes in themselves, and here one is buying back its own myth.

The Bigger Picture Today’s through-line is pricing. Nigeria has offered its state oil company to the market, Morocco has sold a slice of a hospital group to Riyadh, and South Africa has put the retirement savings of its civil servants behind green hydrogen. What is genuinely new is not the foreign money, which has always come. It is that African institutions are now on the other side of the table with capital of their own, and that Namibia feels able to name conditions rather than accept them. Against all of it stands Burkina Faso, budgeting 190 million dollars to honour a man who preached owing nothing to anyone. A continent that has stopped asking what it is worth is also arguing with itself about what should never have been for sale.

Africa Intelligence Brief August 7: What We Are Watching

Coming months – Whether Nigeria attaches an actual timetable to the promised NNPC listing.

Today – Whether Nigerian regulators force filling stations to pass on Dangote’s price cut.

13 August – Zambia’s presidential and parliamentary vote, six days away.

Mid-2028 – The SA-H2 fund’s target of 12 billion rand, against 3 billion committed so far.

Coming months – Whether Angola’s rate cuts continue as inflation approaches single digits.

Ongoing – Whether Namibia’s insistence on local processing survives contact with buyers.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Nigeria actually listing NNPC on the stock exchange?

President Bola Tinubu said on Thursday 6 August 2026, during a meeting with the board of Nigerian Exchange Group and his economic management team at the Presidential Villa in Abuja, that the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited would be reformed and listed on the Nigerian Exchange. No timetable, size or structure was announced, so it remains a stated commitment rather than a scheduled transaction.

How much has the Nigerian stock market grown?

Nigerian Exchange Group told the president that the total value of listed stocks has risen from just under 30 trillion naira in 2023 to about 160 trillion naira, while the All-Share Index has climbed from around 52,000 points to roughly 244,000. The exchange said it expects the market’s value to reach about 230 trillion naira by the end of this year on the strength of expected listings.

Who is funding South Africa’s SA-H2 green hydrogen fund?

The fund announced a first close of 3 billion rand, about 182 million United States dollars, on 6 August 2026, from five committers: the European Commission through Global Gateway, the Dutch state investor Invest International, the Public Investment Corporation on behalf of the Government Employees Pension Fund, Sanlam Life Insurance and the Industrial Development Corporation. It targets a final close of 12 billion rand by mid-2028 and has committed 20 million dollars to the Hive Hydrogen Coega green ammonia project and up to 4 million dollars to a fuels producer in Gauteng.

Why is Burkina Faso building a memorial to Thomas Sankara?

The government has budgeted 117 billion CFA francs, roughly 190 million United States dollars, for a memorial to the revolutionary president assassinated in 1987, whose central message was that Burkina Faso should be self-reliant and owe nothing to outside powers. The scale of the spending has drawn attention precisely because it honours a leader remembered for frugality, and because the current military government leans heavily on his legacy for its own legitimacy.

Sources: Nigerian Exchange Group, BusinessDay NG, Punch, Legit.ng

World.title: American Airlines Sets Daily Miami–Montevideo Return Dec. 3
World.content:
Uruguay · Travel

Key Facts —The return. American’s first Miami departure is scheduled for December 2, arriving in Montevideo on December 3. —The frequency. The route will operate daily through March 2, 2027, then three times weekly through March 28. —The aircraft. Boeing 787-8 Dreamliners will provide 234 seats: 20 Flagship Business, 28 Premium Economy and 186 economy. —The schedule. Overnight flights are timed for connections through American’s Miami hub. —The limit. This is a seasonal restoration, not a year-round route.

Uruguay will regain its only nonstop link to the United States in December, when American Airlines restores daily Dreamliner service between Montevideo and Miami for the southern summer.

American Airlines will restart nonstop flights between Miami International Airport and Montevideo’s Carrasco International Airport in early December 2026. The first Miami departure is scheduled for December 2, arriving in Montevideo on December 3; the first Montevideo departure is scheduled for December 3. The carrier plans one flight each day through March 2, 2027, before reducing the route to three weekly services until March 28.

An American Airlines Boeing 787-8, the aircraft scheduled for the seasonal Miami–Montevideo route. (Photo: The Boeing Company/American Airlines Newsroom)

A Daily Link for the Peak Season

The daily phase covers Uruguay’s main tourism season and the year-end travel rush. American’s published plan uses a 234-seat Boeing 787-8 with 20 Flagship Business seats, 28 Premium Economy seats and 186 economy seats, comprising 48 Main Cabin Extra and 138 Main Cabin.

During the daily phase, with all times local, the Miami departure is scheduled for 10:55 p.m., arriving in Montevideo at 10:10 a.m. the following day. The return leaves Carrasco at 10:30 p.m. and reaches Miami at 5:45 a.m. These overnight timings preserve daytime hours and feed American’s wider network from its South Florida hub.

Why the Route Matters to Uruguay

The service restores a direct U.S. connection that disappears outside American’s seasonal operating window. For Uruguayan travelers, Miami is both a destination and a major connecting point for North America, the Caribbean and Europe. For inbound visitors, a daily nonstop removes a connection through Panama City, Bogotá, Lima or São Paulo.

American listed Montevideo among the destinations in its expanded winter network for Mexico, the Caribbean and Latin America. The company has served Uruguay for nearly three decades, but recent Miami–Montevideo schedules have been seasonal rather than continuous.

Capacity Without a Year-Round Commitment

Daily operations would offer 1,638 seats in each direction during a full seven-day week. That is meaningful capacity for a relatively small market, but the March reduction also shows the airline is matching supply to seasonal demand.

The distinction matters: tickets are being sold for the announced period, yet the current schedule does not establish a permanent daily service. Continuation beyond March 28 would require a later timetable decision.

What to Watch Next

Booking performance. Advance demand may influence whether daily capacity holds through the full peak period.

March frequency. Montevideo departures are scheduled for Monday, Thursday and Saturday after March 2; Miami departures leave the preceding evenings.

Aircraft changes. Long-range schedules can be adjusted, so travelers should verify the operating aircraft before departure.

Next winter. A future extension would show whether American sees enough demand for a longer season.

Frequently Asked Questions

When will American Airlines resume Miami–Montevideo flights?

The first Miami departure is scheduled for December 2, arriving in Montevideo on December 3. The first Montevideo departure is scheduled for December 3.

Will the route operate every day?

Yes, from December 3 through March 2, 2027. It is then scheduled three times weekly through March 28.

Which aircraft will American use?

American plans to use a 234-seat Boeing 787-8 Dreamliner.

Is Miami–Montevideo becoming a year-round route?

No. The announced schedule is seasonal and currently ends on March 28, 2027.

How many seats will the daily service provide?

A daily 234-seat aircraft provides 1,638 seats in each direction during a full seven-day week.

World.title: Chile’s Copper Windfall Could Top US$9 Billion as the Price Passes US$14,000
World.content:
Chile · Mining

Key Facts The price. Three-month copper on the London Metal Exchange passed US$14,000 a tonne on 4 August and reached US$14,369.50 on Thursday, the highest since the record of US$14,527.50 set on 29 January.

The Chile copper windfall could reach US$9.7 billion above budget this year as copper tops US$14,000 a tonne — but the country is producing less of it, and Codelco says it cannot fund its own plan.

The Chile copper windfall is real and it is large. Copper on the London Metal Exchange passed US$14,000 a tonne on 4 August and reached US$14,369.50 on Thursday, and Chilean analysts now put the extra take for the treasury at close to US$9.7 billion this year. On the same afternoon, the chairman of Codelco told a mining conference the company faces four difficult years.

Chuquicamata, near Calama. Chile is earning more from copper while producing less of it. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

Where the Chile copper windfall comes from

Álvaro Merino, executive director of Núcleo Minero, puts each one-cent move in the annual average copper price at about US$120 million in extra exports and roughly US$60 million to the treasury, through private-mining tax and Codelco surpluses combined.

Chile’s 2026 budget was built on a reference price of US$4.38 a pound, set by the independent consultative committee. The year-to-date average is US$5.97. If the full-year average lands at US$6.00, the extra take works out at about US$9.7 billion. On a more conservative assumption of US$50 million per cent, it is closer to US$8.1 billion.

That is separate from a figure published in late July. The budget office projects large private mining will pay US$8,039 million in tax this year — a record, up 32 percent on 2025. That is a total, not an increase. Codelco transfers are forecast at US$3,188 million, up 58 percent in real terms.

Why the price is running

The trigger came from central Africa. On Thursday Reuters obtained an order signed by three Congolese ministers banning exports of copper and cobalt concentrates outright. The Democratic Republic of Congo is the world’s second-largest copper supplier.

The market was already tight. LME warehouse stocks fell to 226,650 tonnes, the lowest since mid-February, with on-warrant availability down to 94,200 tonnes — barely a day of world consumption. COMEX September copper set a record of US$6.723 a pound on Thursday.

One point of care. Reuters places the all-time high on the LME three-month contract at US$14,527.50 on 29 January, so Thursday was a six-month high rather than a record. Cochilco logged a record close of US$6.55 a pound the same day, which fits if it is quoting the cash price.

The problem the windfall hides

None of this comes from digging up more copper. Cochilco expects 5.3 million tonnes in 2026, down 2 percent, after output fell about 9 percent year-on-year through May.

On the same day the price hit its six-month high, Codelco’s chairman was explaining why the state miner cannot keep up. Speaking at the Ecos de la Minería conference in Santiago, Bernardo Fontaine said the five-year investment plan is US$34 billion and there is “no possibility, obviously, of financing US$34 billion given the debt Codelco carries”. He added: “This plan is going to bring us four difficult years, difficult years in production.”

His numbers are stark. Comparing the last four years with the previous four: production down 16 percent, cost per tonne up 82 percent and debt up 50 percent, all with copper 30 percent more expensive. Codelco will review the pipeline project by project and may sell stakes it holds in private companies.

Chile is collecting a windfall built entirely on price while its largest single asset shrinks. That reverses when the price does.

What it means if you live in or invest in Chile

Copper was 50.1 percent of Chilean exports in the first half, US$30,236 million and up 11.5 percent. It is the main reason the peso sits near 913 to the dollar rather than well above 950 — so dollar earners lose a little purchasing power and peso earners get cheaper imports.

The budget effect is bigger. An extra US$8 to 9.7 billion turns a strained fiscal position into a manageable one, which changes the odds on tax rises and the pricing of Chilean sovereign bonds. The risk underneath it is the production line: a country earning more from selling less has a problem a good year in the metals market postpones rather than solves. World.title: Chile Inflation Falls to 3.5% in July as Fuel Prices Drop
World.content:
Chile · Economy

Key Facts The print. July prices rose 0.1 percent on the month. Over twelve months, Chile inflation is 3.5 percent, down from 4.3 percent in June.

July prices rose 0.1 percent on the month. Over twelve months, Chile inflation is 3.5 percent, down from 4.3 percent in June. Back in the band. The central bank targets 3 percent with a 2 to 4 percent tolerance range. June breached the ceiling; July is inside again.

The central bank targets 3 percent with a 2 to 4 percent tolerance range. June breached the ceiling; July is inside again. What pulled it down. Transport fell 3.5 percent, with petrol down 8.5 percent, diesel down 13.5 percent and air fares down 9.4 percent.

Transport fell 3.5 percent, with petrol down 8.5 percent, diesel down 13.5 percent and air fares down 9.4 percent. What kept rising. Food and housing were both up 0.7 percent. Electricity rose 2.4 percent on the second-half tariff reset; rent rose 0.6 percent.

Food and housing were both up 0.7 percent. Electricity rose 2.4 percent on the second-half tariff reset; rent rose 0.6 percent. The rate. The policy rate stayed at 4.5 percent on 28 July, unanimously. The next meeting is 8 September.

The policy rate stayed at 4.5 percent on 28 July, unanimously. The next meeting is 8 September. Your UF. The unit rises 41 pesos to 40,885 (about US$45) by 9 September — one of the smallest steps in months.

Chile inflation eased to 3.5 percent in July as petrol and diesel prices fell, bringing it back inside the central bank’s target band for the first time since May.

Chile inflation fell to 3.5 percent over twelve months in July, down from 4.3 percent in June, after consumer prices rose just 0.1 percent on the month. The National Statistics Institute published the figures on Friday morning, and they put the country back inside the central bank’s 2 to 4 percent tolerance band.

Food prices rose 0.7 percent in July while fuel fell sharply, and the two roughly cancelled out. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What moved Chile inflation in July

The INE published the numbers at 8 a.m. on Friday. Ten of the thirteen divisions rose, two fell and one was flat, and almost all the relief came from one place: transport, down 3.5 percent, which alone took 0.47 percentage points off the index.

Fuel did the work. Petrol fell 8.5 percent, diesel 13.5 percent and air fares 9.4 percent. That is welcome and it is also fragile — those prices answer to oil markets and the Middle East, not to anything Santiago controls.

The other side of the ledger kept climbing. Food and non-alcoholic drinks rose 0.7 percent, with seasonal fruit up 6.6 percent and soft drinks up 3.6 percent. Housing and utilities also rose 0.7 percent, driven by a 2.4 percent jump in electricity as the second-half tariff reset landed, plus 0.6 percent on rent and 8.2 percent on accommodation services.

Underneath the headline, core prices were firmer than the top line suggests: the measure that strips out volatile items rose 0.5 percent on the month, and the food-and-energy-free measure 0.4 percent.

A four-month low, not a new floor

Three and a half percent is the lowest twelve-month reading since March, when it was 2.8 percent. It is not the lowest of the year — February came in at 2.4 percent, the softest since 2020.

The path in between explains why the central bank is cautious. Inflation climbed from 2.8 percent in March to 4.0 in April, 3.9 in May and 4.3 in June, before this month’s drop. One good print after a four-month climb is a turn, not a trend.

Why rates are not moving yet

The board held the policy rate at 4.5 percent on 28 July, unanimously. It flagged the June overshoot, oil back near US$100 a barrel on renewed tension between the United States and Iran, a weaker peso and a soft May Imacec reading. Two-year inflation expectations remain anchored at 3 percent.

Santander’s research team expects the rate to stay at 4.5 percent for the rest of the year, and traders are pricing no change across the next four meetings, with a possible quarter-point cut somewhere inside a year. The next decision is 8 September.

What it means if you live in Chile

This matters more in Chile than a CPI print does almost anywhere else, because so much of daily life is priced in UF rather than pesos. Rent, mortgages, school fees, health-plan premiums and a great many service contracts all track the unit, which follows last month’s inflation with a one-month lag.

A 0.1 percent print means the UF rises only about 41 pesos over the coming cycle, to 40,885 pesos (roughly US$45) by 9 September. In practice a rent of 25 UF — about 1.02 million pesos, or US$1,120 — resets by around a thousand pesos rather than ten thousand. That is the smallest indexation step in months.

Borrowing is the other half. With the policy rate stuck and the bank explicitly waiting for core inflation to cool, mortgage and consumer credit will not get cheaper before September at the earliest, and the market says not this year. If you earn in dollars, the peso sits near 913 with no strong signal either way from this print. This is general information, not financial advice.

Latin America · Business

Key Facts —The agreement. Liberty Latin America and Amdocs announced a 10-year strategic engagement on August 5, 2026. —The scope. Amdocs will manage Liberty Latin America’s end-to-end IT ecosystem across its regional footprint. —The technology. Operations will use Amdocs’ aOS platform in what the companies describe as an AI-driven model. —The partner. Amdocs will work with existing supplier Prodapt to support service continuity during and after the transition. —The forecast. The Liberty Latin America Amdocs deal hands one supplier responsibility for a regional telecom group’s full IT environment for a decade, making execution and service continuity as important as the promised AI efficiencies.

Liberty Latin America said on August 5 that Amdocs will manage its end-to-end IT ecosystem across Latin America and the Caribbean. The companies plan to move existing operations onto Amdocs’ Agentic Operating System, or aOS. They describe the target model as AI-driven; no independent performance evidence accompanied the announcement.

A Broad Outsourcing Decision

The scope matters more than the product label. Liberty operates consumer brands including BTC, Flow, Liberty and Más Móvil in more than 20 countries. Moving the full IT domain to a single long-term manager can standardize processes across those markets, but it also concentrates delivery risk with one vendor.

Prodapt, an existing Liberty supplier, will collaborate with Amdocs throughout the engagement. The companies said the transition should occur over the coming months, with Prodapt supporting continuity. They did not publish milestones, staffing effects or country-by-country implementation dates.

The Financial Claim

Liberty chief executive Balan Nair told investors the transaction is expected to generate more than US$250 million in net present value. That is management’s estimate of discounted benefits, not the amount Liberty will pay Amdocs. Neither company disclosed the contract price or the assumptions behind the forecast.

For Amdocs, the agreement expands a managed-services business that generated US$791 million, or about 67% of revenue, in its fiscal third quarter. Amdocs called the contract a meaningful expansion in the Caribbean and Latin American region; that characterization remains the vendor’s.

World.title: Peru Mexico Relations Restored as Betssy Chávez Flies Out on a Military Plane
World.content:
Peru · Diplomacy

Key Facts She left. Betssy Chávez flew out of the Grupo Aéreo N.º 8 base at Callao around midnight on 6–7 August, aboard a Mexican Air Force aircraft.

Betssy Chávez flew out of the Grupo Aéreo N.º 8 base at Callao around midnight on 6–7 August, aboard a Mexican Air Force aircraft. The legal basis. Peru granted a safe-conduct under Articles V and XII of the 1954 Caracas Convention on diplomatic asylum.

Peru granted a safe-conduct under Articles V and XII of the 1954 Caracas Convention on diplomatic asylum. The trade. Peru and Mexico announced the restoration of diplomatic relations the same morning, nine months after Lima broke them.

Peru and Mexico announced the restoration of diplomatic relations the same morning, nine months after Lima broke them. Her case. Sentenced in November 2025 to 11 years, 5 months and 15 days for conspiracy to rebel over Pedro Castillo’s 2022 attempt to dissolve Congress. The conviction is under appeal.

Sentenced in November 2025 to 11 years, 5 months and 15 days for conspiracy to rebel over Pedro Castillo’s 2022 attempt to dissolve Congress. The conviction is under appeal. Not an amnesty. Peru says the safe-conduct changes nothing about her judicial situation and reserves the right to seek extradition.

Peru says the safe-conduct changes nothing about her judicial situation and reserves the right to seek extradition. What to watch. Foreign Minister Carlos Espá has floated unwinding Mexico’s visa requirement for Peruvians “step by step”.

Peru Mexico relations resumed on Friday morning, hours after Betssy Chávez left Lima on a Mexican Air Force plane under a safe-conduct that changes nothing about her 11-year sentence.

Peru Mexico relations were restored on 7 August, and the price was a plane ticket. Around midnight, Betssy Chávez — Pedro Castillo’s last prime minister — left the Grupo Aéreo N.º 8 military base at Callao aboard a Mexican Air Force aircraft. By breakfast, Lima and Mexico City had published a joint communiqué ending a nine-month diplomatic rupture.

Betssy Chávez sheltered in the Mexican embassy compound in Lima for nine months before Peru granted a safe-conduct. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

How Peru Mexico relations came back in a single morning

Chávez had been inside the Mexican embassy compound in Lima since early November 2025 — roughly nine months, latterly with Brazil representing Mexican interests after Peru severed ties. The flight out was arranged quietly. Espá told Canal N the coordination was handled “with the greatest possible confidentiality”: his ministry issued the safe-conduct, the Defence Ministry cleared the Mexican aircraft to land, the Interior Ministry provided security, and Brazil acted as intermediary.

The sequence matters. The departure was agreed with Mexico’s foreign ministry before the joint communiqué on restoring relations was published. The plane went first; the diplomacy followed. President Claudia Sheinbaum opened her morning press conference in Mexico City by confirming Chávez was about to land, calling the safe-conduct an act of goodwill by President Keiko Fujimori.

Why the relationship broke in the first place

Peru cut diplomatic relations on 3 November 2025, the day Mexico granted Chávez asylum. Then foreign minister Hugo de Zela called it an unfriendly act. Consular relations were never severed, but the embassy in Lima has been run by Brazil since January 2026.

The friction goes back further — to December 2022, when Mexico criticised Castillo’s removal and took in his family. Peru declared Mexico’s ambassador persona non grata, withdrew its own envoy in March 2023, and Congress declared Sheinbaum persona non grata in 2024. Somewhere in all that, Peruvians picked up a visa requirement to enter Mexico.

Restoring relations was one of the first significant foreign-policy acts of Fujimori’s government, sworn in on 28 July 2026. Espá presented it as a straight trade: Lima honours the asylum convention, Mexico reopens its embassy.

What it does not do

It does not touch her conviction. Peru’s foreign ministry stated plainly that the safe-conduct leaves her judicial situation unchanged and that Peru may still request extradition. She also remains under a separate investigation by the Fiscalía over illicit enrichment.

Lima is meanwhile running a consultation at the Organisation of American States aimed at stopping what it calls the distortion of diplomatic asylum — in plain terms, an attempt to set a precedent that asylum should not shelter people with criminal convictions. Peru insists there is no political persecution in the country.

What changes for you

The concrete one is the visa. Mexico’s requirement for Peruvian travellers was collateral damage from this feud, and Espá has now publicly floated unwinding it step by step. If you are a dual national, run a Peru-based business with Mexican operations, or move staff between Lima and Mexico City, that is the file to watch over the next few months.

Embassies reopen too. Consular work involving Mexico — visas, apostilles, notarial acts, civil registry — should return to normal channels once ambassadors are named, though no date has been given. Both countries also invoked the Pacific Alliance and its free movement of people, goods, services and capital; two of the bloc’s four members had no diplomatic relations until Friday morning.

There is a governing signal here worth more than the case itself. Fujimori’s first big move was to hand a convicted Castillo minister a plane out in exchange for a diplomatic normalisation. That is a pragmatism datapoint for anyone trying to read the next five years of Peruvian policy. This is general information, not legal advice.

World.title: Colombia’s Amazon Mining Ban Lands Three Days Before a Pro-Drilling President
World.content:
Colombia · Environment

Key Facts The instrument. Resolution 0961 of 2026, signed by the Environment Ministry on 4 August, published 5 August — three days before the new government took office.

Resolution 0961 of 2026, signed by the Environment Ministry on 4 August, published 5 August — three days before the new government took office. The area. 483,283.55 km², about 42 percent of Colombia’s continental territory, across 61 municipalities in ten departments.

483,283.55 km², about 42 percent of Colombia’s continental territory, across 61 municipalities in ten departments. What stops. No new mining concessions and no new oil or gas contracts anywhere in the Amazon biome.

No new mining concessions and no new oil or gas contracts anywhere in the Amazon biome. What continues. Existing titles run to the end of their contracts — but cannot be extended.

Existing titles run to the end of their contracts — but cannot be extended. The weak spot. It is a ministerial resolution, the easiest instrument to undo, and the incoming environment minister says it will stay “on paper”.

Colombia’s Amazon mining ban closes an area the size of Spain to new extraction, signed by an outgoing government days before a president who campaigned on drilling was sworn in.

The Colombia Amazon mining ban arrived with three days to spare. On 4 August the Environment Ministry signed Resolution 0961 of 2026, declaring the entire Colombian Amazon a permanent reserve closed to new mining concessions and new oil contracts. It was published the next day. On 7 August, Abelardo De La Espriella — who campaigned on reopening exploration — took the presidential sash in Cali.

Mining in the Amazon basin. Colombia has closed its entire share of the biome to new mining and oil contracts. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What the Colombia Amazon mining ban covers

The resolution delimits 483,283.55 square kilometres — about 48.3 million hectares. The ministry calls it roughly 42 percent of Colombia’s continental territory. Read that carefully: it is 42 percent of the country, not of the Amazon.

Sixty-one municipalities in ten departments fall inside. All of Caquetá, Putumayo, Amazonas, Guainía, Guaviare and Vaupés, plus parts of Meta, Vichada, Cauca and Nariño.

No new mining authorisations, no new hydrocarbon contracts. Companies holding a valid title with the required environmental permits can operate to the end of their contract — but there is no extension. That is the part that bites. It does not stop current production; it shortens the life of everything already there. Indigenous rights and the national parks regime are untouched.

How fragile is it

Very. A ministerial resolution is the easiest of Colombia’s legal instruments to undo. María Aponte of Holland & Knight has said the new government could modify or repeal it through a fresh administrative act.

The incoming environment minister, Fabio Arjona, is blunt about his view. “Regulating is not governing,” he told El Espectador, arguing that sweeping mining exclusions mostly encourage illegality. He expects the declaration to stay on paper.

There is one procedural counterweight. When the ministry first announced this at COP30 in Belém in November 2025, the Interior Ministry ruled it needed prior consultation with 566 ethnic communities. That ran through June and July and was protocolised on 19 and 20 July. Whether repeal triggers the same ten-month requirement is unresolved, and it is the question that decides everything.

Not everyone in the green camp is cheering

Margarita Flórez of the Asociación Ambiente y Sociedad calls the measure easily dismantled and notes that illegal gold mining and mercury do far more damage than licensed operators. Alejandra Laina of WRI Colombia makes the same point: the resolution restricts legal activity while the forest is eaten by what was never legal. It is a real legal act with real consequences for permit holders, and it may do very little for the trees.

What it means if you live in or invest in Colombia

If you have upstream exposure, the production hit is small — Colombia’s oil comes from the Llanos and Magdalena Medio, not Amazonas. The sting is the renewal ban: any Amazon title now runs to expiry and stops, which changes reserve-life assumptions today, before any court rules.

The wider signal matters more. A ministry closed 42 percent of a country by resolution 72 hours before a handover, and the successor promised the opposite policy. Colombian resource permitting is now a political-cycle asset, not a legal-certainty one.

For residency, property and visas, nothing changes. This is a story for the extractive, carbon and conservation sectors — and for anyone running conservation or tourism projects in Leticia, Putumayo or Guaviare, where the resolution is a legal hook that did not exist last week. Colombia is now the first Amazon country to close its whole share of the biome, while Brazil went the other way and began drilling at the Morpho well this year. This is general information, not legal or investment advice.

World.title: Nexa Says Cerro Lindo Is Peru’s First Block-Caving Mine
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

Peru · Mining

Key Facts —The milestone. Nexa Resources says Cerro Lindo is the first mine in Peru to implement large-scale block caving. —The start. Operations began in an initial section at the end of the second quarter and reached regular operation in July 2026. —The method. Workers undercut a large ore column so gravity and rock pressure fracture it; broken ore is drawn through collection points below. —The technology. Teleoperated loaders, real-time geotechnical instruments and microseismic monitoring reduce employee exposure in production and caving zones. —The goal. Nexa expects lower unit costs, continuous extraction, access to deeper ore and reduced use of explosives and water. —The backdrop. Nexa reported second-quarter net income of US$98 million and adjusted EBITDA of US$286 million, up 78% year on year.

Nexa Resources has begun block-caving production at Cerro Lindo in Peru’s Ica region, introducing a high-volume underground method that the company says has never before been used by a Peruvian mine.

A load-haul-dump machine working underground. This archive image illustrates mechanized underground mining and does not show Cerro Lindo. (Photo: internal archive)
