Although Russia formally remains Armenia’s strategic ally, many Armenians have not forgotten that Russian peacekeepers effectively acted as bystanders, failing to fulfil their mission of protecting the Armenian population of Nagorno-Karabakh. Following the CSTO’s refusal to defend Armenia’s territorial integrity, relations between Moscow and Yerevan cooled even further. The Armenian leadership also adopted a more outspoken tone towards Russia, both in its rhetoric and in its actions.

At the same time, contacts between the Armenian government and its European partners intensified. Brussels allocated hundreds of millions of dollars to support political and economic reforms in Armenia, as well as strengthen the country’s borders. France also began supplying Armenia with military equipment. The culmination of these developments came on 17 October 2023, when speaking at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan declared:

“The Republic of Armenia is ready to be as close to the European Union as the European Union considers possible. Our joint statement with President von der Leyen says: ‘In these difficult times, the EU and Armenia stand shoulder to shoulder.'”

In the years that followed, Pashinyan repeatedly stated that Armenia would seek EU membership. The parliamentary elections held in June and their outcome only reinforced the government’s determination.

“Last year, we adopted a law launching the process of accession to the European Union, which, I would remind you, was initiated by civil society. I believe this provides an additional incentive to give new momentum to our democratic and institutional reforms so that we can achieve EU standards as quickly as possible.

This is our main intermediate goal because we understand that no country can become a full member of the European Union without meeting its standards. Therefore, our primary task is first and foremost to comply with EU standards. […]If we are admitted to the European Union, we will be happy. If we are not, we will still benefit, because Armenia will have become a country that meets European standards, with all the positive consequences that entails,” Pashinyan said at the time.

System administrator Artak Gaboyan shares his views. Video and editing: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews.

Russia pushes back

At the start of the crisis in Armenian-Russian relations, Moscow responded relatively cautiously to Yerevan’s efforts to move closer to Europe. The Kremlin sought to avoid further destabilising the situation, citing Armenia’s difficult historical circumstances. Even Armenia’s effective suspension of its participation in the CSTO did not result in a fundamental reassessment of bilateral relations.

However, Moscow appeared to change its approach in the run-up to the parliamentary elections held in June.

One of the defining moments came during Pashinyan’s meeting with Vladimir Putin in Moscow in April, when the Russian president openly asked him to allow pro-Russian political forces to participate in the elections. He was primarily referring to Russian-Armenian billionaire Samvel Karapetyan. However, as Karapetyan holds citizenship of several countries, not only Armenia, Armenian law bars him from serving as an MP or becoming prime minister. Pashinyan reportedly made this clear to Putin.

The Kremlin nevertheless continued to support pro-Russian political figures while also taking more concrete steps. Russian regulators began imposing restrictions on imports of Armenian products. Initially, the measures targeted specific companies and categories of goods, but they were later expanded to cover almost all agricultural produce from Armenia.

Businessman Suren Margaryan shares his views. Video and editing: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews.

The situation continued to escalate. Armenian officials began openly accusing Moscow of attempting to interfere in the country’s internal affairs and engineer a change of government.

At the same time, international media reported on alleged hybrid attacks against Armenia. Reuters also published a report alleging that the Kremlin had devised a plan to bring 100,000 Armenian citizens into the country to vote for pro-Russian political forces.

Following the elections, Moscow has stepped up its calls for Armenia to decide, once and for all, which direction it intends to take. Russian officials have specifically called for a referendum on whether the country should pursue integration with the European Union or the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), arguing that choosing the EU would require Armenia to leave the EAEU.

“No one is pushing Armenia out of the EAEU. They themselves have said they want to join the European Union. They need to make a choice. And the sooner that choice is made, the better it will be for everyone,” Russian Deputy Prime Minister Aleksey Overchuk said.

This culminated in a joint statement by the EAEU member states calling for Armenia to hold a referendum on whether the country should remain in the EAEU or pursue EU membership.

Central Yerevan. Photo: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews

Armenia says time is not right for referendum

In response to Moscow’s demands, the Armenian authorities say they have no plans to hold a referendum or withdraw from the EAEU—for now. The key word is “for now.” Yerevan intends to remain a member of the EAEU until there is a realistic prospect of joining the European Union. Moreover, under the EAEU’s founding rules, Armenia cannot be expelled from the bloc without its consent.

However, holding a referendum on EU membership appears to be a realistic prospect in the longer term. Opinion polls also suggest such a referendum could succeed. Since the 2020 war, Russia’s popularity in Armenia has declined markedly, while support for European integration has continued to grow.

According to a survey conducted by the International Republican Institute (IRI) in May 2026, 75% of Armenians support the country’s accession to the European Union, while 58% say they would vote in favour of joining the bloc in a referendum. The findings point to a sustained decline in trust in Russia and growing pro-European sentiment among the Armenian public.

Photographer Mane Sergoyan shares her views. Video and editing: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews.

What do experts say?

Which direction should Armenia take? That is arguably the country’s defining question today. Does Armenia have the capacity to make a definitive choice in favour of the European Union? How might Russia respond if it does? And what security risks could such a shift entail?

Political analyst Robert Gevondyan says Yerevan is pursuing a diversification of its foreign policy, a goal repeatedly articulated by the country’s leadership. In his view, this aligns with the interests of Armenia’s European partners.

“Armenia is already receiving a certain level of support, particularly through its cooperation with France. It is possible that, in the future, security cooperation will expand to include other countries, although there is not yet enough information at this stage to identify them. At the same time, it should be remembered that the EU operates under NATO’s security umbrella. While Armenia is not currently seeking rapid accession to the Alliance, if it succeeds in developing close ties with individual EU member states, it could gain access to additional opportunities as an indirect beneficiary of NATO’s resources,” he said.

Is Armenia ready to become part of the European Union today? Gevondyan argues that the question itself is misplaced, as every country must go through a lengthy accession process before joining the bloc.

“No country is ever fully prepared to begin the integration process overnight. By the time Armenia is ready, it will effectively already be part of Europe. States usually go through a long period of integration, during which they implement reforms across various sectors, align with European standards, improve product quality and reach agreements on mutual trade. This process takes years. Armenia is ready to embark on that journey. At the same time, it is impossible to reconcile EU requirements and the conditions for trading with the West with the standards and requirements that exist within the EAEU. We are only at the beginning of a long road.”

Journalist Marianna Mkrtchyan shares her views. Video and editing: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews.

“Armenia is still a long way from joining the European Union. But the current trajectory could already result in serious losses—not only economically, but also in terms of the country’s sovereignty,” argues political commentator Hayk Khalatyan, founder of the Analytical Centre for Strategic Studies and Initiatives.

Khalatyan also argues that the Armenian leadership will ultimately be unable to sustain its current course of deepening ties with the European Union while remaining a member of the EAEU:

“Pashinyan’s challenge now, after the elections, is to try to normalise relations with Moscow. He will be expected to take concrete steps demonstrating that he is abandoning his previous foreign policy course. But that would effectively mean turning his back on the powerful external actors who helped him remain in power. The question, then, is which path he will choose: to turn his back on the West and Turkey, or continue down the path of confrontation with Russia and the gradual breakdown of bilateral relations. I very much doubt that Pashinyan will abandon his Western partners and move towards normalising ties with Russia. He would like to preserve the policy he has pursued in recent years—reaping the economic benefits of EAEU membership while, in practice, steadily distancing Armenia politically from Russia. But we are now seeing that Moscow is no longer willing to tolerate that approach.”

Human rights activist and film director Hovhannes Ishkhanyan shares his views. Video and editing: Arman Gharajyan.

At the same time, relations between Brussels and Moscow remain deeply confrontational, with some political and security circles even discussing the possibility of a future conflict between Russia and the West.

Whatever the outcome, Armenia is now adapting to a new geopolitical reality while facing Russian trade restrictions. The country is seeking to redirect its exports towards European markets and diversify its trade partners. If it succeeds, Yerevan will remove what many see as its last major economic dependency on Russia.

Yasha Solomonyan, chairman of the Armenian Association of Professional Guides, shares his views. Video and editing: Arman Gharajyan/JAMnews

With the support of the Russian Language News Exchange

World.title: UK embassy in Georgia: Amaglobeli’s sentence ‘disproportionate’ and politically motivated
World.content:
UK embassy condemns Amaglobeli’s sentence

The UK embassy in Georgia has described the sentence handed down to journalist Mzia Amaglobeli as disproportionate and politically motivated, and has called for her immediate release.

“A year ago today Mzia Amaglobeli, a prominent Georgian journalist, was sentenced to two years in prison. We remain concerned that her sentence is disproportionate and politicised and call again for her immediate release,” the embassy’s post on Facebook read.

Mzia Amaglobeli was sentenced on 6 August 2025.

The journalist was arrested on 11 January 2025 on charges of assaulting Batumi police chief Irakli Dgebuadze. On 14 January, Batumi City Court granted the prosecution’s request to remand her in custody pending trial.

The defence’s requests to have the pre-trial detention measure changed were rejected by the courts. Batumi City Court ruled the request inadmissible, while on 19 February 2025 Kutaisi Court of Appeal upheld the decision to keep Amaglobeli in pre-trial detention.

According to Nona Kurdovanidze, chair of the Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association, the court relied on a falsified protocol when justifying her pre-trial detention.

Following her arrest, Mzia Amaghlobeli went on a hunger strike that lasted 38 days. On 18 February 2025, it was announced that she had ended the hunger strike and resumed eating under medical supervision.

World.title: US unexpectedly sheds 23,000 jobs in blow for Trump before midterms
World.content:
The United States has unexpectedly shed thousands of jobs, according to government data, despite President Donald Trump's claims he had led an economic revival in the country.

The world's largest economy lost 23,000 jobs in July, data published by the US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) showed, signalling a potential weak labour market after months of steady growth.

The unemployment rate has remained relatively steady though at 4.1 per cent, likely a result of falling labour supply as the US economy grapples with an aging population and lower net migration.

Since taking office for his second term, Mr Trump has unleashed a spate of policies aimed at reviving domestic manufacturing and curbing surging inflation.

The United States has unexpectedly lost thousands of jobs, despite President Donald Trump claiming he had led an economic revival in the country. (Reuters: Evelyn Hockstein)

But based on the new figures, job growth hit a peak in March before declining in the next three months and entering negative territory in July.

In addition to the loss of jobs in July, the BLS revised down job growth in the previous two months by 103,000.

Analysts had expected further job growth, with economists polled by Dow Jones Newswires and the Wall Street Journal expecting 83,000 new jobs to be added in July.

The decline and revisions to the previous months will spark concern that the labour market may not be as strong as was previously reported.

Employment declined in the local government education and retail trade sectors, while it continued to grow in healthcare with more Americans aging and requiring medical assistance, the BLS statement said.

Employment in health care grew with more Americans aging and requiring medical assistance. (Unsplash: Frederick Medina)

Retail trade lost 19,000 jobs, with employment declining in warehouse retailers and general merchandise stores.

Employment in the financial activities sector continued its downward trend, losing 14,000 jobs.

State of economy to be a key issue at midterm elections

But Republicans will be tested in November's midterm elections, with the state of the economy a key issue for Democrats who are seeking to wrest back control of both houses of Congress.

The data released on Friday will also pose a question to the US Federal Reserve, which has been signalling it was preparing for a rate hike later this year.

Policymakers at the US Federal Reserve watch the labour market closely, as their dual mandate requires the Fed to deliver maximum employment while ensuring inflation remains at a long-term target of two per cent.

Last month, the Fed held interest rates steady, but three regional Fed presidents dissented in favour of a rate hike.

Markets in Europe gained ground and markets in Asia were mixed.

AFP

World.title: Lawyers for Andrew and Tristan Tate urge US judge to release them from jail
World.content:
Lawyers for social media influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate have urged a US judge to release the brothers from a Miami jail as they fight the British government's efforts to extradite them to face charges of rape, assault and facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation.

In a filing in Miami federal court on Friday, the Tate brothers' lawyers said their "extraordinary public visibility" would make it impractical for them to try to flee, meaning there was no need to keep them behind bars until the extradition proceedings end.

"It would be extraordinarily difficult for Andrew or Tristan to travel undetected or avoid attention," their lawyers wrote.

They urged US Magistrate Judge Lauren Louis to release them on bail on condition that they surrender their passports and submit to location monitoring.

Tate brothers deny wrongdoing

Andrew Tate, 39, and Tristan Tate, 38, were arrested in Miami on July 18.

Britain's Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) said on July 19 it had brought new charges against the two relating to alleged offences involving four alleged victims between July 2010 and August 2017.

The Tate brothers, both former kickboxers who have dual US and British citizenship, have denied any wrongdoing.

Loading...

Their arrests marked a new chapter in the widening legal troubles for the brothers, who have built a large online following promoting their views on masculinity and wealth. Andrew Tate has previously described himself as a misogynist.

Prosecutors with the Miami US Attorney's Office are due to respond to the Tates' bid for release on bail by August 10, and Judge Louis has scheduled a court hearing over their possible release for August 13.

Prosecutors have previously said Judge Louis should keep the brothers detained because there was a risk they could flee and because they posed dangers to the community.

Andrew and Tristan Tate to be charged with rape, human trafficking in UK British prosecutors have approved 21 charges for social media influencer and self-described misogynist Andrew Tate, and his brother Tristan, including rape and human trafficking.

The legal process for determining whether the Tate brothers may be extradited could take months. Britain has until September 16 to submit its full extradition request to the State Department, US court records show.

Andrew Tate and Tristan Tate had previously faced rape and human trafficking charges in Britain related to three alleged victims, the CPS said.

A British judge issued a warrant for their arrests in January 2024.

They have not appeared in British court to enter a plea to those charges.

Britain is seeking to extradite the brothers to face both sets of charges.

Reuters

World.title: Unknown Australian soldiers identified decades after deaths in action
World.content:
A lot separates the stories of two Australian soldiers who died two decades apart in wars on opposite sides of the world, but there are some remarkable parallels.

Both were killed in action on the same date and both lay in graves marked "Unknown Australian", their families never knowing what became of them.

Now the men have been identified, one more than a century after he was killed.

Private Archibald "Blue" Hanley of the 30th Battalion was killed in the Battle of Amiens near Villers-Bretonnux in France on August 8, 1918.

Archibald Hanley (left) with his brother, John Hanley. (Supplied: Australian Defence via Allen Stokes)

For more than a century he lay unidentified in the Villers-Bretonneux Military Cemetery.

Twenty-four years later, Lieutenant Hercules William Crawford of the 39th Battalion, Citizens Military Forces, was killed during the Battle of Kokoda in Papua New Guinea.

He went missing on the Kokoda Track near Pirivi on August 8, 1942 and was buried at the Bomana War Cemetery.

Lieutenant Hercules Crawford of the 39th Battalion CMF. (Supplied: Austalian Defence Force via Natasha Read)

The identities of the men were confirmed after extensive investigations by the Australian Army's Unrecovered War Casualties team, in consultation with the Commonwealth War Graves Commission and the Office of Australian War Graves.

"When we say, 'Lest We Forget' at the end of the Ode we re-commit to remembering them in perpetuity," Veterans' Affairs Minister Matt Keogh said in a statement.

"The formal identification of Private Archibald Hanley and Lieutenant Hercules William Crawford reflects our enduring commitment to accounting for Australia's wartime missing, no matter how much time has passed."

Mystery of Australia's missing soldiers The final resting place of more than 30,000 Australian soldiers from World War I and II is unknown. With DNA breakthroughs, more families are trying to find their ancestors' graves.

Headstones bearing the names, ranks and unit details of the soldiers will be installed at their graves.

Chief of Army Lieutenant General Susan Coyle said the identification of the soldiers provided long-awaited answers to their families.

"[This] demonstrates that time does not diminish our determination to account for our missing and ensure their service and sacrifice are properly commemorated," she said.

World.title: Travis Head pips star duo to win second-straight Allan Border Medal
World.content:
Travis Head has pipped fellow Ashes hero Alex Carey to claim a second consecutive Allan Border Medal.

During a function in Brisbane on Friday night, held six months later than normal due to scheduling conflicts, the star batter was again crowned Australia's leading male cricketer.

Head had 153 votes, just ahead of his South Australian teammate Alex Carey on 152.

Player of the Ashes, Mitchell Starc, finished third on 150 votes despite having ditched one of the three international formats.

Head pipped Carey and Starc to the gong. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Still a force in Tests and ODIs, Starc ended his T20 international career last September in a bid to extend his red-ball career.

Starc won the Shane Warne Test player of the year award, while Mitchell Marsh took out the ODI award.

Big-hitting Tim David was named Australia's best T20 player.

Head joins Ricky Ponting, Michael Clarke, Shane Watson, Steve Smith and David Warner as multiple winners of the Allan Border Medal, which was first handed out in 2000.

The 32-year-old made 30 appearances for Australia across all three formats during the 2025/26 season, scoring 1,437 runs.

Head belted a famous 123 from 83 balls to guide Australia to a stunning victory in the opening Ashes Test in Perth.

He took that form into his home Test in Adelaide, flailing 170 in a memorable partnership with Carey.

During a career-best season, Carey scored 1,079 runs in 24 games across all formats.

Carey hit a stunning century at the Adelaide Oval, while his glovework during the Ashes was exceptional with 28 dismissals.

Normally held during a gala event in Melbourne at the end of summer, the Allan Border Medal was delayed due to organisers wanting the cricketers to be in the room for it.

Last year, the all-conquering women's team attended the event, but the men's players were in Sri Lanka for a Test tour, so Head had to accept the medal via video.

Earlier this year, Annabel Sutherland won a second-consecutive Belinda Clark Award and was also named the women's ODI player of the year.

AAP

World.title: Katherine residents gather en masse to protest rolling youth crime spree
World.content:
About 50 members of the Katherine community have gathered on the Northern Territory town's main street to express their fear and frustration at the region's crime rate after the latest in a string of car thefts.

It comes after a group of young people were seen driving around the town three hours south of Darwin yesterday, with footage posted to social media showing a black Volkswagen hatchback being driven dangerously for hours until about 9pm, when it eventually crashed on Stutterd Street.

An NT Police spokesperson said in statement "approximately seven" of the occupants were then seen exiting the allegedly stolen car, with investigators later identifying three suspects.

Loading...

The spokesperson said police "understood the frustration" of some community members but defended the choice not to initiate a pursuit prior to the crash, saying it could have escalated the situation and put more innocent people at risk.

In response to the incident, local businessman Ben Coutts took to social media this morning, asking residents to attend a planned "coffee with a cop" event at a local cafe to express their frustration with a perceived lack of action on youth crime.

Natalie Ellis says some social media commentary in the wake of the latest incident has been "vicious against Aboriginal people". (ABC News: James Elton)

"We need help, the community needs help, we're scared, and we're sick of paying the cost," he told the ABC.

"We are here as the people of Katherine."

Natalie Ellis, who works on the Katherine Justice Reinvestment project with a cohort of around 20 at-risk youth, said some of the commentary on social media had been "vicious against Aboriginal people".

Police in Katherine are investigating after a stolen car was allegedly driven recklessly around the town for several hours before eventually crashing. (ABC News: James Elton)

Ms Ellis asked the community to remember that "95 per cent of the kids in town are good", saying disengagement from school was the number one problem driving youth crime.

"Aboriginal people are victims too, and we need to not forget that," she said.

Police resourcing, curfews raised

The crowd gathered outside the cafe included members of the Katherine Town Council, who stressed they were appearing in their private capacity.

Among them was Toni Tapp Coutts, who said it was time the NT government considered a temporary youth curfew in Katherine like those seen in Alice Springs in recent years.

"I think we should have a curfew, the temperature of the town needs to be lowered," she said.

Toni Tapp Coutts says it is time the NT government considers imposing curfews. (ABC News: James Elton)

"Those kids need to have time to think about their actions, the families need to be forced to confront some of this behaviour in the town, and taking responsibility."

Speaking with community members and local media, NT Police Superintendent Virginia Read suggested there could be a case for more police resources in Katherine.

"If I had my way, it would be nice if we could have some more police," she said.

Member for Katherine Jo Hersey, who was also at the gathering, said she shared the community's frustration and would continue to raise the issue with Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro.

Virginia Read says "it would be nice if we could have some more police" on the beat in Katherine. (ABC News: James Elton)

"People are pissed off," she said.

"It's come time now where we do need some more resources in town here."

Ms Hersey said she understood the calls for a curfew but questioned whether it would be effective, saying the curfew in Alice Springs just pushed crime "further out" of the city centre.

But she said she would raise the option of a curfew with Mrs Finocchiaro "if that's what the community wanted".

Mother says she is lucky to be alive

Ashleigh Pugh said she was driving home with her two-year-old daughter yesterday when she had a close encounter with the black Volkswagen.

Ms Pugh said the car was coming towards her head-on, trying to overtake a road train while evading police before veering off the road at the last moment.

"There was absolutely no chance they were going to beat that road train before colliding with me and my daughter, even at the speed they were travelling at," she said.

Police say they have identied three suspects after up to seven youths were seen exiting the Volkswagon after it crashed on Stutterd Street. (ABC News: James Elton)

"I thank God and everything above that at the last second they did that.

"I pulled over, I caught my breath, I bawled my eyes out, and I turned to my girl and I just thanked everything that we were still there."

Mr Pugh said she "used to be proud" to call Katherine home, but no longer felt it was the same town she grew up in.

"Yesterday's incident was yet another key highlight of the seemingly never-ending escalation," she said.

Locals question crime statistics

NT Police crime statistics show overall offending rates in Katherine are down between the 12 months to May this year and the same period last year.

The figures show property crime dropped by 8 per cent while crimes against the person were down 14 per cent — with vehicle thefts the notable exception, rising 21 per cent in the same period.

But long-time locals Jim King and Patty Buntine both said in their view, overall crime was worse now than any time in their memories.

Jeff Usher says locals have "had a gutful" and he has stopped reporting crimes because "nothing happens". (ABC News: James Elton)

Local cabinet-maker Jeff Usher said he had seen repeated break-ins at his workshop, but often did not bother reporting crimes to police because "nothing happens".

"We've had a gutful," he said.

When asked whether Katherine's true crime rate was reflected in the official figures, Ms Hersey said statistics were "one thing" but her experience on the ground was "very different".

"It doesn't pass the pub test," she said.

Jo Hersey says her experience on the ground is "very different" to the picture painted by official statistics. (ABC News: James Elton)

"I absolutely get the anger and the frustration that everyone is feeling, it is absolutely not OK."

Ms Hersey promised to raise the community's frustration at the highest levels of government.

"We do not need any more deaths," she said.

World.title: Do dolphins grieve the way humans do?
World.content:
In a scene akin to a funeral procession, a pod of dolphins surrounds a grieving mother as it nudges along its deceased calf through a picturesque estuary at the bottom end of Western Australia.

The footage was captured by the non-profit conservation group Geographe Marine Research and was initially shared to create awareness of the situation for the coastal community of Bunbury.

It has since attracted thousands of responses from people struck by the seemingly human display of emotion.

The dolphin mother, Fraggle, tried to balance the dead calf on its back as other dolphins joined it in an 11-day "funeral". (Supplied: Geographe Marine Research)

Geographe Marine Research's Rodney Peterson was behind the drone footage widely shared online, which the organisation uses to monitor the region's frequent marine visitors.

He and the non-profit's head researcher, Capri Jolliffe, said they see dolphins mourning every year.

Do dolphins actually grieve?

The term epimeletic is used by experts to describe animal behaviours like those displayed by Fraggle, the dolphin mother attempting to balance its dead two-week-old calf on her back.

According to Ms Jolliffe the term also extends to acts of caregiving towards sick, injured or dying members in a group.

Experts believe dolphins genuinely experience bouts of grief. (Supplied: Geographe Marine Research)

She says scientists, while reluctant to attribute human characteristics to animal behaviours, are fairly confident dolphins and other animals are genuinely experiencing bouts of grief "as humans know it" after loss.

According to Ms Jolliffe, animals with high social cognition are recognised as being more intelligent and as a result more "vulnerable to mourning and grief".

Elephants, known for their curiosity and resourcefulness, rely on intricate social hierarchies that lend to epimeletic behaviours like burying deceased herd members, she says.

Whale saved by dolphins A pod of dolphins have guided a stranded juvenile whale out of an estuary.

Researchers have also recorded emotional responses in apes and canines like wolves and dingoes.

Orcas, tooth whales and baleen whales are also known to exhibit epimeletic behaviours.

In particular, dolphins, which do not produce many offspring in their lifetime, invest a lot of energy into the ones they do have and are naturally "highly bonded to their calves", she says.

"Of all the observation of marine mammal species, female dolphins carrying deceased offspring account [for] 75 per cent of recorded cases," Ms Jolliffe says.

How long do dolphins typically mourn?

According to experts, the standard period of time for a dolphin to hold onto their calf typically lasts between three and seven days.

During that time, the pod stays close and checks in on the grieving mother, who is likely to stop feeding altogether.

For Fraggle, the latest loss of the two-week-old calf marks the dolphin's fourth bout of grief after losing its third calf in March last year.

The footage was captured by the non-profit conservation group Geographe Marine Research based in Dunsborough, WA. (Supplied: Geographe Marine Research)

Mr Peterson says Fraggle was observed with last year's calf for a few days.

Remarkably, this time around, the dolphin held onto its two-week-old calf for 11 days, a period of time Ms Jolliffe says may never have been recorded in dolphins before.

At the end of the period, Fraggle appeared distressed and there were little remains of the calf left.

Despite this, Mr Peterson said Fraggle was back with the pod and a "happy" dolphin again the following day.

Why is this case so remarkable?

Fraggle has always given birth in cooler months and lost all four of its calves in seven years.

The team wonders whether the mother's extensive experience with grief might explain why this period endured longer.

Ocean Census discovers 1,000 species in a year Thousands of species have been discovered lurking and thriving in our oceans.

Mr Peterson also says it might have something to do with slowed decomposition rates which allowed Fraggle to hold on longer.

"You can have your theories," he says.

Either way, as one of the longest observations of a dolphin mother grieving, Ms Jolliffe says the group is hoping the case might be picked up for documentation.

"Dolphins have emotional lives that we don't fully understand," Ms Jolliffe says.

World.title: Ruthless Lions send ominous warning to AFL rivals by dismantling Hawks
World.content:
Jarrod Berry (left) and Ryan Lester (right) celebrated their milestone matches in style as the Lions recorded a 67-point win. (Getty Images)

Brisbane has bounced back from last week's thumping by Carlton to thrash Hawthorn by 67 points at the Gabba.

Led by Kai Lohmann's five-goal haul, the premiers stayed firmly in the top four hunt with a convincing 18.17 (125) to 8.10 (58) win over the third-placed Hawks.

The victory was a perfect response to the 76-point loss to the Blues as the Lions celebrated a double milestone night with Jarrod Berry making his 200th AFL appearance and veteran defender Ryan Lester marking his 250th AFL game with a late goal that delighted the sell-out crowd.

Defeat for Sam Mitchell's team ends a four-game winning run ahead of next weekend's clash with Collingwood at the MCG and will raise questions heading into the finals about their genuine premiership credentials.

In a week where his own visit to Magpies HQ was a focus, Lachie Neale was a standout for the Lions with 35 disposals, seven marks, eight tackles and six clearances.

As well as Lohmann, the Lions had four multiple goalkickers with Logan Morris kicking four majors in the first half, Charlie Cameron booting three and Eric Hipwood scored two including a booming third-quarter shot from well outside 50.

Will Ashcroft had a game-high 39 disposals including 13 score involvements while Harris Andrews delivered another defensive masterclass, snaffling 10 marks as the Hawks forward line struggled to get clean ball all night.

Hawthorn was no match for the rampant reigning premiers at the Gabba. (Getty Images)

The Hawks though were also guilty of missing crucial chances in the opening two quarters with Harry Morrison and Sam Butler both offending as the Lions surged into a winning position.

The hosts were only six clear at the end of the first term but scored three quickfire goals at the start of the second to break the game open and never looked back, the Hawks unable to mount any meaningful resistance.

In the end Jack Gunston finished with three majors while Josh Ward had 28 disposals but it was a disappointing night for the Hawks who were simply second-best across the park.

AAP

World.title: Perth business claims $250k loss over Metronet works disruption
World.content:
A Perth business owner says years of railway construction work have cost him hundreds of thousands of dollars.

Joe Mahon says the removal of the Oats Street Metronet level crossing and subsequent works to elevate the rail line and build a new train station have caused road closures and parking issues that have seriously affected his bottom line.

He told 102.5 ABC Perth he did not object to the public transport upgrades at East Victoria Park from late 2023 to mid-2025, but has asked the Public Transport Authority (PTA) for compensation.

The corner of Bank Street and Forward Street was chosen as the location for Reid's Remotes because of the visibility from the street, customer parking and ease of access.

When Oats Street was subject to closure, it forced prospective customers to access more complicated detours that were subject to frequent change.

"At the start it was gradual because it was issues like their workers taking up all the parking onsite so our customers couldn't actually park," Mr Mahon said.

"Then, once they introduced a road closure, it was like falling off the edge of a cliff. Basically, people couldn't access us.

"The one street that they were supposed to access us through, Forward Street, was full of trucks and cranes and concrete trucks. We even struggled to get there ourselves just to get to work."

The shop was extremely difficult to access at times, Joe Mahon said. (Supplied: Joe Mahon)

Mr Mahon said the sometimes roads were closed during certain times of the day and online maps and GPS services could not keep up.

"Customers would actually give up in frustration and just cancel their booking," he said.

Mr Mahon said in the four years before the level crossing removal works his turnover had been growing by 25 and 30 per cent per annum.

But in the 2024 and 2025 accounting years his turnover fell by 7.45 per cent and 8.75 per cent.

Mr Mahon attributes that decline to the loss of passing trade caused by the Metronet works.

"In 2018 we started documenting every customer who came to us how they found us. One of the main ones is that they're passing trade, so they just saw the signage on the building and came in," he said.

"At the point where the [Metronet] project started that started to decline.

" By about April in 2024 it had gone to zero, and so we had no passing trade for the next 18 months. "

The Metronet worksite on Bank Street, opposite Joe Mahon's business. (Supplied: Joe Mahon)

Mr Mahon said he did not learn that Oats Street would be closed for 18 months until after it was shut.

After the works finished he submitted a compensation claim for $250,000, which he believes his business would have made had it continued to grow at the rate measured before the works began.

The PTA recently denied his claim, saying the changes to traffic conditions were reasonable in the circumstances and undertaken for the benefit of the entire community.

Its legal representatives also said access to the property was continuously maintained and that there was no reasonable alternative way the works could have been carried out.

The PTA also said reasonable steps to mitigate the impact on the community were taken.

But Mr Mahon said he intended to continue his fight for compensation.

"I can't see any other option. I can't afford not to. My business almost closed last year," he said.

"I've sunk the last 19 years into that business.

"I have no problem with the works and the fact that they're essential. I think public transport is essential.

"But when a government department does work that knowingly will impact people and has no consideration for that impact, then that's a problem."

In a statement, a spokesperson for the PTA said: "All claims are assessed on an individual basis. As some claims are still being assessed, details of compensation payments will not be provided."

World.title: Four years overdue: The $4m social housing project left half-built
World.content:
NationalWAPublic housing Four years overdue: The $4m social housing project left half-built Indigo Lemay-Conway August 8, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Social housing in one of Perth’s southern suburbs has been left standing with no completion date in sight, even though it was due to be finished four years ago. The Hilton housing revitalisation project should have delivered 14 architecturally designed timber-frame social housing homes across the suburb by 2022. WA Greens leader Brad Pettitt at one of the half finished social homes in Hilton. Indigo Lemay-Conway But as of this month, construction has only begun – and stalled – on six of the Bernard Seeber Architects homes, with the remaining eight given a standard home-build design instead. WA Greens leader Brad Pettitt said the years of delays and multiple builders entering into liquidation resulted in half-finished homes that could have been used during the current housing crisis.



“There should be two families living in here now, but despite repeatedly pushing the state government on this, they’re failing to finish these properties,” Pettitt said. “Most depressingly, this is not an isolated incident. These are scattered all over this suburb, unfinished houses in the middle of a housing crisis. “The government needs to get on and actually finish this housing. It’s a really good design by a really great local architect, and it’s outrageous that it’s not completed.” Pettitt was the mayor of Fremantle when Bernard Seeber Architects won the design competition in 2017 for the social housing project. The 14 houses were to be built on seven different sites in Hilton and were anticipated to cost $200,000 per house at the time of the design.



But Pettitt says more than $4 million has been spent on the project to date. One of the half finished social homes designed by Bernard Seeber Architects in Hilton. Indigo Lemay-Conway “If they had delivered it on time, at the time, these would have been both inhabited and delivered much more cheaply than they have now. But instead, we’re going to spend way more than needed to be spent, whilst failing to even deliver these houses,” he said. “And you can see the amount of money that’s been wasted here on toilets and security, and all those things, rather than getting in and finishing houses.” Pettitt said the original builder assigned to the project went broke, as well as the builder who was hired after.



Small builder Jaguar Constructions currently holds the contract for the homes and told 9 News Perth it took over the project in 2024, but hasn’t worked on site since December. The company says it’s ready to finish the homes on a slim profit margin, but is waiting on the state government before construction can resume. Meanwhile, it’s covering the cost of maintaining the site. Hilton residents said it was frustrating to see homes sitting idle while so many people are searching for somewhere to live. “This has been going on for a number of years, and our poor neighbours on the street have been living right in front of a building site all this time with a young family, so that’s really unfortunate,” Louise Goodes said. “A lot of people are looking for somewhere to live now, and these houses could have been that answer.”



Rocky Terry said it was “totally ridiculous” the homes were still empty. “I’m a resident here, and Hilton’s a wonderful place to live, and these social houses here at the back have been going on for years,” Terry said. Hilton resident Louise Goodes. Indigo Lemay-Conway “It’s just totally ridiculous with the housing crisis that we haven’t got people in them. Now a lot of people say, ‘It’s good you haven’t got any neighbours’. No, I’d like to have neighbours, because that’s what we’re trying to do for people. And it’s got to happen. “They’re so close to finishing it now. I mean it’s past lockup, and they should be in there. They should have been in there a couple of years ago. It’s just not on. It’s just incompetence by someone.”



Bernard Seeber Architects director Georgina Willis said the idea behind the design for the homes was to create new infill density for rear strata lots at an affordable price. “The City of Fremantle granted special dispensation that allowed for two individual dwellings, so we set out to create inclusive, diverse, site-responsive architecture that is also humble and recognises the history and the culture of Hilton,” Willis said. She said the dwellings were meant to be built within a year of construction commencing. But despite the time it’s taken to get the buildings complete, the team would still like to see them come to fruition. “Ultimately, we’d like to see the completion of this project and whether that be this project or another new project with these sort of dwelling typologies, and that would be great if it’s in conjunction with the Department of Communities or Housing and Works,” she said.



An artist impression of what Bernard Seeber Architects social homes would have looked like. Bernard Seeber Architects “Because ultimately, it’s the community that benefits. The intention is to provide quality living for people who are vulnerable in communities and so Fremantle can benefit as well as the broader community.” Housing and Works Minister John Carey said the state government has delivered more than 4300 social and affordable homes to date. “In the vast majority of cases, projects are delivered without issue; however, we are not immune from the challenges in the construction market,” Carey said. He confirmed the original builders for the project went into administration and therefore had their build contracts terminated.



“Eight of the 14 Hilton homes were delivered under a new builder and tenanted after shifting to a design and construct model,” he said. “The Department of Housing and Works is also working with a new builder to complete the remaining six Hilton homes.” WA Premier Roger Cook said he didn’t know the details of the specific homes in Hilton, but there could be a range of reasons why a property might be vacant. “Firstly, it might be part of a broader development in the area. There may be other issues associated with the infrastructure for the area. So we’ll always make sure that we can get our social housing stock back into the market, so we can get roofs over the heads of people as soon as possible,” he said.

World.title: A hotel fit for a king, a tsar and Princess Di doesn’t disappoint
World.content:
★★★★½ Reviews & adviceHotel reviews A hotel fit for a king, a tsar and Princess Di doesn’t disappoint Michael Gebicki August 8, 2026 — 12:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The hotel Mandarin Oriental Old Cataract, Aswan, Egypt Checking in The hotel is perched on granite cliffs overlooking islands in the River Nile. I like a hotel that takes things in its stride without batting an eyelid, and I arrive at this venerable hotel in possibly the most beat-up Peugeot station wagon on the planet. Sitting beside the driver is a villainous looking teenager in a white gallabiyah with a red keffiyeh, with his sidekick – a mischievous but persuasive youth of about 10 – who have together procured this inelegant conveyance for me. The driver realises there is no possibility of being allowed inside the cool, manicured domain I am about to enter, and so I am dumped unceremoniously outside the gate, but the fez-topped staff are an unflappable breed and praise be, my name is on the guest list.



The look 



My garden suite, a step-down from the river-facing suites, has brown curtains and a separate sitting area with a brown couch and a brown desk. The dimensions are palatial, the bathroom is huge but the furnishings and fabrics might have come from the parlour of a dowager aunt whose taste atrophied in the 1950s. There are two separate buildings with very different rooms. The Palace Wing is the original while the Nile Wing was built in 1961 to house Russian engineers working on the Aswan High Dam. These are functional rooms, and while they share the Palace Wing rooms’ riverside location, they lack their grandeur and opulence. In May, management of the hotel was transferred from the Accor group to Mandarin Oriental. The hotel is currently undergoing a renovation expected to last until July 2027, and some rooms and suites will be unavailable in the meantime. Expect lighter, prettier colours, panache and a style uplift from the Mandarin Oriental makeover. Food + drink When the current makeover is complete the hotel will have six dining venues. Al Saraya serves an Ottolenghi-does-Egyptian dishes, handmade pasta, fish from the Nile and the yummy treats of the Levantine kitchen. A sundowner on the Terrace, perched high above the river, almost justifies the room rate. The bar is terrific. You can imagine Winston Churchill here with brandy and a cigar, or Orson Welles with Rita Hayworth, but the barman isn’t telling any tales. Some of the former restaurants are closed for renovation. When the current makeover is complete the hotel will have six dining venues. Out + about



A felucca ride is the proper thing to do in the late afternoon. You’re probably only staying two nights, with an early morning visit to Abu Simbel taking up most of one day. There’s not too much to tempt you into Aswan, the souk is nothing special and the merchants are merciless hagglers. The unfinished obelisk and the Nubian Museum are within walking distance of the hotel. Just to the south, the Temple of Isis at the Philae temple complex was the last major temple built in the classical Pharaonic Egyptian style. A felucca ride around Elephantine Island is the proper thing to do in late afternoon. The hotel will arrange it, with a bar on board. You’ll be besieged by small children on surfboards who will anchor themselves limpet-like to your vessel singing “Frere Jacques” in expectation of a reward. The song hasn’t changed in 20 years. The verdict There’s not too much in Aswan to tempt you away from the hotel. The location is sublime, the suites in the Palace Wing are palatial, the pedigree is uplifting, but it feels frozen in a time warp. It needs to shake off the stodge, and the Mandarin Oriental group has what it takes.





Highlight Sunset cocktails on the Terrace overlooking the swan-like feluccas on the Nile. Lowlight Service was glacial in the breakfast room when I stayed under Accor management, but hopefully the Mandarin Oriental will inspire waitstaff to lift their game. The writer stayed at his own expense.

World.title: ‘Smashed, outplayed, outhunted’: Lions put the Hawks, and the rest of the AFL, on notice
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘Smashed, outplayed, outhunted’: Lions put the Hawks, and the rest of the AFL, on notice Nick Wright August 7, 2026 — 11:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

In the ultimate response to a harrowing evening against Carlton last round, best mates Logan Morris and Kai Lohmann shone brightest on the night Chris Fagan’s side proved just how alive their three-peat hopes really are. The Lions sent shockwaves through the competition with a 67-point drubbing of the Hawks, 18.17 (125) to 8.10 (58) – leaving some of the game’s greats in awe. It was a day to remember for Ryan Lester – gifted a goal in his 250th game by Sam Draper. AFL Photos “This is the team you don’t want to be meeting in September,” said Australian Football Hall of Fame Legend Jason Dunstall, the Hawks’ all-time leading goalkicker who grew up in Queensland, in his role with Kayo Sports. “Whenever Hawthorn had it, Brisbane were on them, and they were on them big-time.



“This was a punishing victory... one that’s re-awakened the spirit within the whole group. “If they get into the top four with a double chance, look out. “They [Brisbane] took on a team that many had thought might be ready to challenge, and they showed them in no uncertain terms that they have a long way to go.” Work to do: Jack Gunston and Sam Mitchell’s Hawks. AFL Photos Melbourne great and fellow Australian Football Hall of Famer Garry Lyon said the Hawks, meanwhile, had been “smashed”, “outplayed and outhunted”.



“It looked a little bit too hard for them, which is a staggering thing to say about this Hawthorn side who have been so good for so long,” he said on Kayo. Never one to get too carried away with a single game’s result, Hawthorn coach Sam Mitchell said he was “pretty honest” to his playing group in the aftermath. “I thought we were outclassed tonight. I think we’re better than that. Kai Lohmann and his Lions teammates put on a prime-time show. AFL Photos “Brisbane are obviously a good side, they’ve won the last couple [of premierships] and they’re setting themselves again, so we saw it as an opportunity to compete against the best, and we weren’t up to it tonight ... I think we can execute better than that and play to a higher level, and we’re going to need to.”



Friday night’s victory edged Fagan just clear of great mate and three-time premiership winning Lions coach Leigh Matthews as the winningest in club history. They’ve both coached 237 Lions games, with Fagan winning 143 to Matthews’ 142. But Fagan’s response when asked on Kayo Sports about the feat said it all: “He’s got a statue, I haven’t”. Fagan said he had “no reason not to” back his side in after their showing against the Blues. “You’ve just got to remember our players are human – they’d won seven in a row, they had a bad day last week, but they’ve always been a group over the last seven or eight years who have been able to bounce back after disappointments,” he said in his post-game press conference. “We put that performance in the bin pretty quickly ... over the last nine games we’ve played, we’ve had one game where our defensive intensity wasn’t where it should be. When our energy is up, we tend to do that well.”



View post on X Morris’ four goals from 15 touches was conquered with a gamut of tricks – a brilliant overhead mark in a tight contest earning his first in the opening term, which he swiftly followed up with a clean strike on the edge of the 50. His third was arguably his best, spilling a shanked kick deep into the pocket, but holding his nerve and threading a grubber through the defence on a tight angle, before taking a mark in front of a contest and kicking his fourth. Morris’ exploits took his season tally to 51, just six goals off Coleman Medal leader Charlie Curnow, whose Swans will clash with Port Adelaide on Saturday afternoon. Fagan could only smile when asked about Morris on Kayo Sports.



“I’ll have to tip a bucket of water on him, I reckon, to keep him calm,” he said. Whether he garners the end-of-year honour or not, Morris is fast become a bona fide superstar. His efforts on Friday night were complemented by veteran duo Charlie Cameron and Eric Hipwood (five goals between them), as well as Lohmann – who kicked five majors of his own with some miracle moments thrown in the mix. It was a particularly telling return to form for Hipwood, who had a nightmare when moved into defence against the Blues. Two of Lohmann’s maximums came within a minute of each other in the third quarter – the first latching onto a loose ball and snapping on the run, with his second a clean set shot which earned a pump of the chest. View post on X



His off-balance snap as he was about to be crunched in a tackle in the final term for his fourth will be one that lands in his career highlights reel throughout the next decade, and while Hawks counterpart Josh Weddle scored soon after, the damage by that point was well and truly done. Lohmann was quick to prove that, snapping a set shot from a narrow long-range angle for his fifth to complete a bumper night out – one which featured 24 touches, two clearances and a congratulatory hug from a Hawks opponent in one of the more commanding displays of the 23-year-old’s career so far. Ryan Lester and Jarrod Berry were chaired from the ground after their 250th and 200th games respectively. AFL Photos These sides entered Friday night’s battle as two of the most lethal attacking outfits in the competition – each only trailing Sydney for points scored – but they were forced to wait nearly nine minutes for the first goal of the match through Hawks star, and former Lion, Jack Gunston. That was perhaps exactly the motivation the Lions needed to rebound from their 76-point capitulation against the Blues last week, after they were heavily criticised for their lack of pressure at the end of what had been a seven-game winning streak, and their premiership credentials called into question as a result.



Aside from that opening Gunston goal, the Lions never trailed, and a second quarter surge – kicking 6.5 to Hawthorn’s 3.1 – proved the momentum swing needed to put the foot down on their fellow top four threats. The hosts went on to kick five goals to two in the third quarter – beginning with Sam Draper’s snap at close range and ending with top-10 draftee Daniel Annable’s first AFL goal in his comeback from shoulder surgery – and consolidated in the final term, as 250-game milestone man Ryan Lester fittingly helped himself to a goal and Cam Rayner joined him on the scoreboard. “We love Ryan Lester, what he’s been able to do in his career is one of the great stories ... he’s just a tale of absolute persistence, and he’s playing his best footy in his 30s,” Fagan said of the man better known as “Froggy”, who has been dropped more than a dozen times throughout his career. If Morris, Lohmann, Hipwood and Cameron hitting their straps wasn’t good news enough for the Lions faithful, the sight of marquee recruit Oscar Allen back in the AFL – having returned from a three-month foot injury lay-off through the VFL in the past fortnight – only adds a new layer to the two-time reigning premiers’ forward line heading towards September.



“Oscar didn’t have a lot of the ball, but that’s often what happens when you have three of them [tall forwards] there, but between them, they caused a bit of chaos,” Fagan said. “I thought Kai Lohmann’s performance tonight was one of the most special performances I’ve seen from a small forward player. He got a lot of the ball, his tackle pressure was sensational, and he kicked five goals, so it’s a pretty good night by him too. “He’s just got his pressure right, he doesn’t have to worry about those freakish things – they just happen. When he focuses entirely on putting pressure on, his game seems to come together.” Every time Hawthorn struck throughout the contest and threatened to get back in the fight – Massimo D’Ambrosio, Jarman Impey and Connor Macdonald all scoring at key stages – the Lions were quick to respond and ensure they maintained a commanding lead. Despite the Hawks leading the inside-50 count at the major break (31 to 29), Lions co-captain Harris Andrews and his backline contingent were near impenetrable.



Even as the Lions’ superstar midfield was contained in the opening quarter, they eventually exploded to keep Hawthorn scrambling – Will Ashcroft leading the charge with 39 touches and seven clearances, with Lachie Neale (35 disposals, six clearances, three goal assists) hot on his tail. The 51-year-old woman was one of three arrested at Narvick Crescent, Heidelberg West on Friday, almost a week after an incident in nearby Blackwood Parade that left a 68-year-old man fighting for life.

World.title: Roosters pip Bulldogs to draw level with league leaders
World.content:
Sydney Roosters have edged past Canterbury in a 20-18 win that has blown the race for the NRL’s minor premiership wide open.

On a pivotal night in the make-up of the top four, the Roosters moved up to second with a late win at Allianz Stadium that puts Trent Robinson’s men level on 36 points with ladder-leading Penrith.

Loading

The Panthers, who sit first as a result of their superior for and against, host the Roosters next Thursday and look set to be without captain Isaah Yeo.

Even without facing Yeo, the Roosters will have to turn things up a notch against the Panthers as the race for the minor premiership looks set to go to the wire.

Robinson’s side led 8-2 at half-time on Friday but were stunned when a try from Lachlan Galvin and a Jacob Kiraz double in a 12-minute second-half spell catapulted the Bulldogs into an unlikely lead.

But a miscommunication at the back by Bulldogs fullback Connor Tracey allowed Salesi Foketi to dive on a loose kick and claim the match-winning try in the 69th minute.

Loading

The victory gave the Roosters a seventh-straight win but also puts a major dent in Canterbury’s top-eight aspirations after they threatened to upset the home side.

Stephen Crichton kicked a penalty to get the Bulldogs on the board after sixth minutes before Sam Walker and Hugo Savala combined down the left to send Billy Smith in at the corner.

Then after Matt Burton failed to gather a Daly Cherry-Evans bomb, Siua Wong touched down for the Roosters who led 8-2 at half-time after Walker failed to convert both kicks.

The Bulldogs had struggled for spark in the first half but they came back after half-time with a bang as hooker Bailey Hayward burst up the middle of the field and found a supporting Kiraz.

The Canterbury winger scored under the posts as Crichton converted to tie the game up.

Galvin then put the Bulldogs ahead for the first time when the five-eighth drifted across field and darted through a Reece Robson tackle to score.

Galvin set up Kiraz for his side’s third but Canterbury were unable to find a knockout blow and the Roosters clawed their way back into the game.

Smith added a second with 15 minutes left before Foketi was in the right place at the right time, touching down a Walker bomb that Tracey failed to take to score the decisive try.

World.title: ‘Doesn’t look great’: Fears Penrith co-captain Isaah Yeo’s season could be over
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 ‘Doesn’t look great’: Fears Penrith co-captain Isaah Yeo’s season could be over Christian Nicolussi Updated August 7, 2026 — 9:25pm ,first published 8:17pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Isaah Yeo suffered a suspected pectoral injury on Friday evening, with Penrith coach Ivan Cleary conceding: “It doesn’t look great.” And to make matters worse, their opponents next Thursday night, the Sydney Roosters, plucked a come-from-behind win over Canterbury – and now have the chance to move to the top of the ladder should they triumph at CommBank Stadium. Loading Panthers supporters will be hoping scans clear their co-captain of any serious damage after he came from the field late in the first half during the 28-12 loss to the New Zealand Warriors. Yeo reeled out of a tackle and immediately looked in pain. He is expected to have scans back in Sydney, which is most likely to be Sunday.



The competition leaders scored two tries in three minutes late in the game, and were rightfully denied a third when Liam Martin was ruled offside during a kick chase. But the immediate focus will be on inspirational leader Yeo, whose importance to the premiership favourites is the equal of Nathan Cleary. Panthers captain Isaah Yeo. Getty Images A ruptured pec would mean Yeo misses the rest of the season for Penrith, and also require Kevin Walters to find a new captain for Australia ahead of the World Cup. At the very least, Yeo is next to no chance to be available for the heavyweight showdown with the Roosters.



Lindsay Smith and Billy Phillips are early contenders to replace Yeo at lock forward. “Obviously ‘Yeoy’ is a big loss and hard to replace, but that’s how it goes; if that’s the case we’ll have to [move forward without him],” Cleary said. “You can’t win the game at the start, but you can sort of lose it. We missed the start tonight.” Luke Metcalf scores for the Warriors against Penrith. Getty Images The Panthers could also lose centre Paul Alamoti who was binned and placed on report for up-ending opposite centre Leka Halasima in the first half.



Penrith (shoulder) are likely to welcome back Dylan Edwards, but Casey McLean (hand) and Mitch Kenny (foot/ankle) will not be available until the eve of the finals. The Roosters trailed 18-8 with 15 minutes remaining against the Bulldogs before their halves Sam Walker and Daly Cherry-Evans built pressure through their kicking games. Billy Smith bagged a double, then Salesi Foketi won the race to a Walker kick that was bizarrely allowed to bounce by the Dogs. Cherry-Evans has played with and against Yeo, and said of him potentially being sidelined: “He’s a fantastic player, hopefully it’s not too serious for him, you never want to see the best players in the game get injured … I send out my best [wishes] to him.” When asked about winning the minor premiership, Roosters coach Trent Robinson said the goals for his side were very simple.



“I want to play our best footy that we can possibly play this year; the ultimate goal is to play the most beautiful footy on the biggest stage,” Robinson said. The 20-18 loss for the Bulldogs means they will finish the weekend outside the top eight, and potentially as low as 10th should Manly beat Melbourne in Perth on Saturday. Back-rower Sitili Tupouniua returned for the first time since round 16, but lasted five minutes before succumbing to a hamstring injury. The Warriors, meanwhile, also kept themselves in the minor premiership race, with coach Andrew Webster admitting the win would serve as a wonderful confidence boost, and timely reminder “we belong” at the pointy end of the year. Related Article Sydney Roosters 20 Canterbury 18

NRL 2026 Roosters pip Bulldogs to draw level with league leaders



They take on the Broncos and Rabbitohs in the next fortnight, and round out the regular season at home to Newcastle and Manly. Penrith take on the Roosters, followed by Melbourne, then the Bulldogs and Tigers. In his first game since April, out-of-favour Warriors half Luke Metcalf scored in the first half, then stepped inside to score his second try to seal the result inside a rocking Go Media Stadium. A top-two finish for the Warriors would be a huge bonus, with the intimidating atmosphere sure to help when hosting a qualifying final and potentially preliminary final.

World.title: Four years overdue: The $4m social housing project left half-built
World.content:
NationalWAPublic housing Four years overdue: The $4m social housing project left half-built Indigo Lemay-Conway August 8, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Social housing in one of Perth’s southern suburbs has been left standing with no completion date in sight, even though it was due to be finished four years ago. The Hilton housing revitalisation project should have delivered 14 architecturally designed timber-frame social housing homes across the suburb by 2022. WA Greens leader Brad Pettitt at one of the half finished social homes in Hilton. Indigo Lemay-Conway But as of this month, construction has only begun – and stalled – on six of the Bernard Seeber Architects homes, with the remaining eight given a standard home-build design instead. WA Greens leader Brad Pettitt said the years of delays and multiple builders entering into liquidation resulted in half-finished homes that could have been used during the current housing crisis.



“There should be two families living in here now, but despite repeatedly pushing the state government on this, they’re failing to finish these properties,” Pettitt said. “Most depressingly, this is not an isolated incident. These are scattered all over this suburb, unfinished houses in the middle of a housing crisis. “The government needs to get on and actually finish this housing. It’s a really good design by a really great local architect, and it’s outrageous that it’s not completed.” Pettitt was the mayor of Fremantle when Bernard Seeber Architects won the design competition in 2017 for the social housing project. The 14 houses were to be built on seven different sites in Hilton and were anticipated to cost $200,000 per house at the time of the design.



But Pettitt says more than $4 million has been spent on the project to date. One of the half finished social homes designed by Bernard Seeber Architects in Hilton. Indigo Lemay-Conway “If they had delivered it on time, at the time, these would have been both inhabited and delivered much more cheaply than they have now. But instead, we’re going to spend way more than needed to be spent, whilst failing to even deliver these houses,” he said. “And you can see the amount of money that’s been wasted here on toilets and security, and all those things, rather than getting in and finishing houses.” Pettitt said the original builder assigned to the project went broke, as well as the builder who was hired after.



Small builder Jaguar Constructions currently holds the contract for the homes and told 9 News Perth it took over the project in 2024, but hasn’t worked on site since December. The company says it’s ready to finish the homes on a slim profit margin, but is waiting on the state government before construction can resume. Meanwhile, it’s covering the cost of maintaining the site. Hilton residents said it was frustrating to see homes sitting idle while so many people are searching for somewhere to live. “This has been going on for a number of years, and our poor neighbours on the street have been living right in front of a building site all this time with a young family, so that’s really unfortunate,” Louise Goodes said. “A lot of people are looking for somewhere to live now, and these houses could have been that answer.”



Rocky Terry said it was “totally ridiculous” the homes were still empty. “I’m a resident here, and Hilton’s a wonderful place to live, and these social houses here at the back have been going on for years,” Terry said. Hilton resident Louise Goodes. Indigo Lemay-Conway “It’s just totally ridiculous with the housing crisis that we haven’t got people in them. Now a lot of people say, ‘It’s good you haven’t got any neighbours’. No, I’d like to have neighbours, because that’s what we’re trying to do for people. And it’s got to happen. “They’re so close to finishing it now. I mean it’s past lockup, and they should be in there. They should have been in there a couple of years ago. It’s just not on. It’s just incompetence by someone.”



Bernard Seeber Architects director Georgina Willis said the idea behind the design for the homes was to create new infill density for rear strata lots at an affordable price. “The City of Fremantle granted special dispensation that allowed for two individual dwellings, so we set out to create inclusive, diverse, site-responsive architecture that is also humble and recognises the history and the culture of Hilton,” Willis said. She said the dwellings were meant to be built within a year of construction commencing. But despite the time it’s taken to get the buildings complete, the team would still like to see them come to fruition. “Ultimately, we’d like to see the completion of this project and whether that be this project or another new project with these sort of dwelling typologies, and that would be great if it’s in conjunction with the Department of Communities or Housing and Works,” she said.



An artist impression of what Bernard Seeber Architects social homes would have looked like. Bernard Seeber Architects “Because ultimately, it’s the community that benefits. The intention is to provide quality living for people who are vulnerable in communities and so Fremantle can benefit as well as the broader community.” Housing and Works Minister John Carey said the state government has delivered more than 4300 social and affordable homes to date. “In the vast majority of cases, projects are delivered without issue; however, we are not immune from the challenges in the construction market,” Carey said. He confirmed the original builders for the project went into administration and therefore had their build contracts terminated.



“Eight of the 14 Hilton homes were delivered under a new builder and tenanted after shifting to a design and construct model,” he said. “The Department of Housing and Works is also working with a new builder to complete the remaining six Hilton homes.” WA Premier Roger Cook said he didn’t know the details of the specific homes in Hilton, but there could be a range of reasons why a property might be vacant. “Firstly, it might be part of a broader development in the area. There may be other issues associated with the infrastructure for the area. So we’ll always make sure that we can get our social housing stock back into the market, so we can get roofs over the heads of people as soon as possible,” he said.

World.title: A hotel fit for a king, a tsar and Princess Di doesn’t disappoint
World.content:
★★★★½ Reviews & adviceHotel reviews A hotel fit for a king, a tsar and Princess Di doesn’t disappoint Michael Gebicki August 8, 2026 — 12:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The hotel Mandarin Oriental Old Cataract, Aswan, Egypt Checking in The hotel is perched on granite cliffs overlooking islands in the River Nile. I like a hotel that takes things in its stride without batting an eyelid, and I arrive at this venerable hotel in possibly the most beat-up Peugeot station wagon on the planet. Sitting beside the driver is a villainous looking teenager in a white gallabiyah with a red keffiyeh, with his sidekick – a mischievous but persuasive youth of about 10 – who have together procured this inelegant conveyance for me. The driver realises there is no possibility of being allowed inside the cool, manicured domain I am about to enter, and so I am dumped unceremoniously outside the gate, but the fez-topped staff are an unflappable breed and praise be, my name is on the guest list.



The look 



My garden suite, a step-down from the river-facing suites, has brown curtains and a separate sitting area with a brown couch and a brown desk. The dimensions are palatial, the bathroom is huge but the furnishings and fabrics might have come from the parlour of a dowager aunt whose taste atrophied in the 1950s. There are two separate buildings with very different rooms. The Palace Wing is the original while the Nile Wing was built in 1961 to house Russian engineers working on the Aswan High Dam. These are functional rooms, and while they share the Palace Wing rooms’ riverside location, they lack their grandeur and opulence. In May, management of the hotel was transferred from the Accor group to Mandarin Oriental. The hotel is currently undergoing a renovation expected to last until July 2027, and some rooms and suites will be unavailable in the meantime. Expect lighter, prettier colours, panache and a style uplift from the Mandarin Oriental makeover. Food + drink When the current makeover is complete the hotel will have six dining venues. Al Saraya serves an Ottolenghi-does-Egyptian dishes, handmade pasta, fish from the Nile and the yummy treats of the Levantine kitchen. A sundowner on the Terrace, perched high above the river, almost justifies the room rate. The bar is terrific. You can imagine Winston Churchill here with brandy and a cigar, or Orson Welles with Rita Hayworth, but the barman isn’t telling any tales. Some of the former restaurants are closed for renovation. When the current makeover is complete the hotel will have six dining venues. Out + about



A felucca ride is the proper thing to do in the late afternoon. You’re probably only staying two nights, with an early morning visit to Abu Simbel taking up most of one day. There’s not too much to tempt you into Aswan, the souk is nothing special and the merchants are merciless hagglers. The unfinished obelisk and the Nubian Museum are within walking distance of the hotel. Just to the south, the Temple of Isis at the Philae temple complex was the last major temple built in the classical Pharaonic Egyptian style. A felucca ride around Elephantine Island is the proper thing to do in late afternoon. The hotel will arrange it, with a bar on board. You’ll be besieged by small children on surfboards who will anchor themselves limpet-like to your vessel singing “Frere Jacques” in expectation of a reward. The song hasn’t changed in 20 years. The verdict There’s not too much in Aswan to tempt you away from the hotel. The location is sublime, the suites in the Palace Wing are palatial, the pedigree is uplifting, but it feels frozen in a time warp. It needs to shake off the stodge, and the Mandarin Oriental group has what it takes.





Highlight Sunset cocktails on the Terrace overlooking the swan-like feluccas on the Nile. Lowlight Service was glacial in the breakfast room when I stayed under Accor management, but hopefully the Mandarin Oriental will inspire waitstaff to lift their game. The writer stayed at his own expense.
